deviation_from_documented: (1) Documented as 'equivalent to the partial correlation ... within [-1, 1]': the code returns raw precision entries Theta_ij, whose sign is opposite to the partial correlation -Theta_ij/sqrt(Theta_ii Theta_jj) and whose magnitude is unbounded (probe: bivariate_gaussian T=256 prec[2,3] = -2.385 vs partial correlation +0.811; up to |Theta_ij| ~ 49 on shared_envelope and ~95 for the CV variant on narrowband). (2) 'the matrix inverse of the covariance matrix': it is the l1-penalised estimate, and it is not the exact inverse of the reported cov_GraphicalLassoCV (solver iterates, see candidates). (3) The supplement says the l1 penalty sparsifies the covariance; it sparsifies this precision matrix. (4) Documented scikit-learn v0.24.1, executed 1.9.1. (5) -sq variants undocumented. (6) 'five splits' confirmed: KFold(5), unshuffled contiguous blocks.
deviation_from_canonical: Variant of Friedman et al. 2008: the diagonal is not penalised (sklearn docstring _graph_lasso.py:328-329; W_ii = S_ii exactly, probe), which matches Yuan & Lin 2007 / R glasso(penalize.diagonal=FALSE). S uses divisor T on ddof=1 z-scored data. Optimisation is approximate: default tol=1e-4 on the absolute dual gap, 100 sweeps, and the result is returned even without convergence; on ill-conditioned inputs the output can be measurably sub-optimal (candidate). CV rule is sklearn-specific (contiguous KFold, 10-iteration warm-started fold fits, ties to smaller alpha, alpha=0 never selectable). Reported value is Theta_ij, a precision entry, not a partial correlation.

metric_name_standard: graphical-lasso sparse precision (inverse covariance) estimate Theta_hat, raw off-diagonal entries (not partial correlations); alpha chosen by 5-fold CV; prec-sq is its square
canonical_ref: Friedman J, Hastie T, Tibshirani R 2008, 'Sparse inverse covariance estimation with the graphical lasso', Biostatistics 9(3):432-441, eq. (1)/(2.1) (diagonal penalised); off-diagonal-only penalty: Yuan M, Lin Y 2007, 'Model selection and estimation in the Gaussian graphical model', Biometrika 94(1):19-35, eq. (4); Banerjee O, El Ghaoui L, d'Aspremont A 2008, JMLR 9:485-516 CV variant: alpha chosen by K-fold cross-validated Gaussian log-likelihood (e.g. Friedman et al. 2008 §4; sklearn GraphicalLassoCV, iteratively refined log grid); there is no single canonical CV rule.
canonical_definition: Theta_hat = argmin_{Theta > 0} -log det Theta + tr(S Theta) + alpha * sum_{i != j} |Theta_ij| (Friedman 2008 sums over all i,j incl. the diagonal; Yuan & Lin 2007 penalise off-diagonals only); Sigma_hat = W = Theta_hat^{-1}; KKT: W_ii = S_ii (+alpha if diagonal penalised), W_ij = S_ij + alpha*sign(Theta_ij) if Theta_ij != 0, |W_ij - S_ij| <= alpha otherwise; partial correlation rho_ij|rest = -Theta_ij / sqrt(Theta_ii Theta_jj)
documented_definition: supplement §1.1.2, p.4: 'The precision matrix is the matrix inverse of the covariance matrix ... For normalized time-series data, the precision matrix is equivalent to the partial correlation between each pairwise time series, conditioned on all other time series, and is within [-1, 1]. The precision matrix is computed via the same module as the covariance matrix (in scikit-learn [2]), and has the same estimators.' Estimator described in §1.1.1, p.3-4 ('Lasso technique, which uses an l1-regularization to sparsify the covariance matrix'; CV variant 'with five splits'); keywords 'undirected, linear, signed, multivariate, contemporaneous'. GitBook basic-statistics.md (Precision) same text. The -sq identifiers are not described in the supplement. Identifiers: prec_GraphicalLassoCV, prec-sq_GraphicalLassoCV.

implemented_as: Each channel z-scored (ddof=1, optional detrend); X = (T, P) array; sklearn.GraphicalLassoCV() with library defaults: S = biased empirical covariance (divide by T, so S_ii=(T-1)/T); alpha selected by 5-fold contiguous KFold CV on Gaussian test log-likelihood over 16 alphas from 4 refinement rounds of a 4-point log grid starting at [0.01, 1]*max|S_offdiag|, training-fold fits capped at 10 iterations and warm-started; then a full-data fit at alpha_ (max_iter 100). Solver: sklearn block coordinate descent (Friedman 2008 glasso algorithm) with off-diagonal-only l1 penalty, start 0.95*S off-diagonal, stop when |dual gap| < 1e-4 or after 100 sweeps (warning silenced). Returns precision_ (the solver's Theta iterate, not inv(covariance_)) with diagonal set to NaN; -sq returns the elementwise square. Fit shared through data.covariance['GraphicalLassoCV'] by cov, cov-sq, prec, prec-sq; exactly symmetric because rows/columns are written together.

deviation_from_documented: (1) Documented as 'equivalent to the partial correlation ... within [-1, 1]': the code returns raw precision entries Theta_ij, whose sign is opposite to the partial correlation -Theta_ij/sqrt(Theta_ii Theta_jj) and whose magnitude is unbounded (probe: bivariate_gaussian T=256 prec[2,3] = -2.385 vs partial correlation +0.811; up to |Theta_ij| ~ 49 on shared_envelope and ~95 for the CV variant on narrowband). (2) 'the matrix inverse of the covariance matrix': it is the l1-penalised estimate, and it is not the exact inverse of the reported cov_GraphicalLassoCV (solver iterates, see candidates). (3) The supplement says the l1 penalty sparsifies the covariance; it sparsifies this precision matrix. (4) Documented scikit-learn v0.24.1, executed 1.9.1. (5) -sq variants undocumented. (6) 'five splits' confirmed: KFold(5), unshuffled contiguous blocks.
deviation_from_canonical: Variant of Friedman et al. 2008: the diagonal is not penalised (sklearn docstring _graph_lasso.py:328-329; W_ii = S_ii exactly, probe), which matches Yuan & Lin 2007 / R glasso(penalize.diagonal=FALSE). S uses divisor T on ddof=1 z-scored data. Optimisation is approximate: default tol=1e-4 on the absolute dual gap, 100 sweeps, and the result is returned even without convergence; on ill-conditioned inputs the output can be measurably sub-optimal (candidate). CV rule is sklearn-specific (contiguous KFold, 10-iteration warm-started fold fits, ties to smaller alpha, alpha=0 never selectable). Reported value is Theta_ij, a precision entry, not a partial correlation.

metric_name_standard: inverse of the Ledoit-Wolf shrinkage covariance estimate
canonical_ref: Dempster 1972, Biometrics 28(1):157-175 (covariance selection; concentration/precision matrix); partial-correlation relation rho_ij|rest = -Theta_ij / sqrt(Theta_ii Theta_jj) in Whittaker 1990, Graphical Models in Applied Multivariate Statistics, Wiley, ch. 5. Covariance estimator: Ledoit & Wolf 2004, J. Multivariate Analysis 88(2):365-411, §3 (estimator S* = (b^2/d^2) m I + (a^2/d^2) S, with m = <S,I>, d^2 = ||S - mI||^2, b^2 = min(bbar^2, d^2), bbar^2 = n^-2 sum_k ||x_k x_k^T - S||^2, normalised Frobenius norm ||A||^2 = tr(AA^T)/p)
canonical_definition: Theta = Sigma_hat^{-1} where Sigma_hat is: Sigma_LW = (1 - s) S + s (tr(S)/p) I with s = min(bbar^2, d^2)/d^2, S = (1/n) sum x_k x_k^T on (assumed) zero-mean data; partial correlation is -Theta_ij/sqrt(Theta_ii Theta_jj), not Theta_ij itself
documented_definition: supplement §1.1.2, p.4 (supplement.txt:158-171): 'The precision matrix is the matrix inverse of the covariance matrix ... For normalized time-series data, the precision matrix is equivalent to the partial correlation between each pairwise time series, conditioned on all other time series, and is within [-1, 1].' GitBook basic-statistics.md:101-122 has the same text. Neither source documents the '-sq' (squared) variants generated by pyspi/config.yaml.
delegate_lib: scikit-learn==1.9.1 sklearn.covariance.LedoitWolf().fit(X).precision_ (scipy==1.17.1 scipy.linalg.pinvh); numpy==2.5.4
implemented_as: Same cached sklearn.covariance.LedoitWolf() fit as cov_LedoitWolf; returns precision_ = scipy.linalg.pinvh(covariance_) computed at fit time (Moore-Penrose pseudo-inverse via eigh with relative cutoff max(P,P)*eps*max|eig|), diagonal NaN. Off-diagonals are raw inverse-covariance entries, not normalised; on the default pipeline Theta = T/(T-1) * [(1-s)R + sI]^{-1} with R the Pearson correlation matrix. Not symmetrised (Estimators.multivariate bypasses Undirected.multivariate). Squared variant (prec-sq_*) = np.square of the same matrix.

deviation_from_documented: Docs say precision is the matrix inverse and, for normalised data, 'equivalent to the partial correlation ... within [-1, 1]'. Implemented value is the unnormalised inverse entry Theta_ij: sign opposite to the partial correlation and magnitude unbounded (probe bivariate_gaussian T=1024 pair (2,3): prec = -2.061 vs partial correlation +0.786). Inverse is of the shrunk estimate, so even after normalisation it would be a shrunk partial correlation. The '-sq' squared variants are undocumented.

metric_name_standard: Off-diagonal entry of the inverse of the reweighted MCD robust covariance (robust precision matrix); prec-sq_MinCovDet is its square
canonical_ref: Rousseeuw P.J. 1985, "Multivariate estimation with high breakdown point", in Mathematical Statistics and Applications Vol. B, 283-297 (MCD definition); Rousseeuw P.J. & Van Driessen K. 1999, Technometrics 41(3):212-223 (FAST-MCD: C-step theorem, raw consistency factor med(d^2)/chi2_{p,0.5}, reweighting with hard weights d^2 <= chi2_{p,0.975}); consistency factor c_alpha = alpha / F_{chi2_{p+2}}(chi2_{p,alpha}): Croux C. & Haesbroeck G. 1999, J Multivar Anal 71:161-190; small-sample factors: Pison G., Van Aelst S., Willems G. 2002, Metrika 55:111-123; precision -> partial correlation: Whittaker J. 1990, Graphical Models in Applied Multivariate Statistics, Wiley, ch. 5 (Prop. 5.7.1 scaled-inverse identity)
canonical_definition: Omega = Sigma_MCD^{-1} (reweighted robust MCD scatter, see Covariance unit); the partial correlation is rho_ij|rest = -Omega_ij / sqrt(Omega_ii Omega_jj) (Whittaker 1990, Graphical Models in Applied Multivariate Statistics, ch. 5; Lauritzen 1996, Graphical Models). Omega_ij itself is not bounded and has the opposite sign of the partial correlation.
documented_definition: supplement §1.1.2, p.4: "The precision matrix is the matrix inverse of the covariance matrix ... For normalized time-series data, the precision matrix is equivalent to the partial correlation between each pairwise time series, conditioned on all other time series, and is within [-1, 1]. The precision matrix is computed via the same module as the covariance matrix (in scikit-learn [2]), and has the same estimators." Items 10 prec_EllipticEnvelope, 11 prec_MinCovDet. GitBook basic-statistics.md:107 same text. The -sq variant is not described.

implemented_as: Data z-scored per channel over the full sample (ddof=1; optional detrend first). z (T x P) passed to sklearn MinCovDet() with all defaults and random_state=None (global numpy RNG). FAST-MCD raw search: h = ceil((T+P+1)/2); T<=500: 30 random h-subsets x 2 C-steps, best 10 refined; T>500: random partition into T//300 subsets, 500 trials, merge on <=1500 samples. Raw distances divided by the Croux-Haesbroeck factor c(P,h/T); rows with d2 < chi2_{P,0.975} kept; Sigma = c(P,0.975) * MLE covariance (divisor n_w) of kept rows; precision_ = scipy.linalg.pinvh(Sigma). pyspi returns the precision_ matrix as is (no normalisation to correlation / partial correlation, no sign flip), diagonal set to NaN in place on the cached fit; prec-sq_MinCovDet returns its elementwise square. One fit per Data object per estimator name, shared by cov/prec and squared/unsquared identifiers.

deviation_from_documented: Version: documented sklearn v0.24.1, executed 1.9.1; the MCD correction and reweighting changed (raw median factor -> Croux-Haesbroeck factor; reweighted covariance now multiplied by c(P,0.975) = 1.055-1.104 for P=5..2), so values are not those of the documented version (probe p4.py, ratios 1.055-1.10). Definition: documented "equivalent to the partial correlation ... within [-1,1]" is false: the raw precision entry is returned, Omega_ij = -rho_ij|rest * sqrt(Omega_ii Omega_jj), opposite in sign to the partial correlation and unbounded (probe -2.63 vs partial correlation +0.81; up to 368 on narrowband). prec-sq_MinCovDet undocumented in the supplement. Stochastic output (global RNG) not documented in the supplement (documented in tests/README.md).
deviation_from_canonical: Close variant of reweighted FAST-MCD: (1) the search is a stochastic approximation of the MCD optimum (inherent to FAST-MCD) but the random starts come from the global numpy RNG, so the selected h-subset and hence values vary run to run (spread up to 0.34 at T=64); (2) h = ceil((n+p+1)/2) instead of floor; (3) reweighted covariance uses the MLE divisor n_w (robustbase: n_w - 1) and no small-sample correction (Pison et al. 2002); (4) raw consistency factor is the asymptotic Croux-Haesbroeck factor rather than RVD 1999 median rescaling; (5) the input is z-scored with non-robust mean/SD over the full sample before the robust fit, so the output is a robust covariance in units of the contaminated SD, not a robust correlation. (6) precision via pseudo-inverse pinvh: for singular scatter (collinear channels) a Moore-Penrose inverse is returned silently instead of failing.
units_and_range: prec: dimensionless (inverse z-score units), signed (sign opposite to partial correlation), symmetric up to round-off, unbounded (observed |value| up to 368 on narrowband_f0-0.25 T=64); prec-sq >= 0. Diagonal NaN. Finite pseudo-inverse values for singular scatter.

metric_name_standard: Off-diagonal entry of the inverse of the reweighted MCD robust covariance (robust precision matrix); prec-sq_MinCovDet is its square
canonical_ref: Rousseeuw P.J. 1985, "Multivariate estimation with high breakdown point", in Mathematical Statistics and Applications Vol. B, 283-297 (MCD definition); Rousseeuw P.J. & Van Driessen K. 1999, Technometrics 41(3):212-223 (FAST-MCD: C-step theorem, raw consistency factor med(d^2)/chi2_{p,0.5}, reweighting with hard weights d^2 <= chi2_{p,0.975}); consistency factor c_alpha = alpha / F_{chi2_{p+2}}(chi2_{p,alpha}): Croux C. & Haesbroeck G. 1999, J Multivar Anal 71:161-190; small-sample factors: Pison G., Van Aelst S., Willems G. 2002, Metrika 55:111-123; precision -> partial correlation: Whittaker J. 1990, Graphical Models in Applied Multivariate Statistics, Wiley, ch. 5 (Prop. 5.7.1 scaled-inverse identity)
canonical_definition: Omega = Sigma_MCD^{-1} (reweighted robust MCD scatter, see Covariance unit); the partial correlation is rho_ij|rest = -Omega_ij / sqrt(Omega_ii Omega_jj) (Whittaker 1990, Graphical Models in Applied Multivariate Statistics, ch. 5; Lauritzen 1996, Graphical Models). Omega_ij itself is not bounded and has the opposite sign of the partial correlation.
documented_definition: supplement §1.1.2, p.4: "The precision matrix is the matrix inverse of the covariance matrix ... For normalized time-series data, the precision matrix is equivalent to the partial correlation between each pairwise time series, conditioned on all other time series, and is within [-1, 1]. The precision matrix is computed via the same module as the covariance matrix (in scikit-learn [2]), and has the same estimators." Items 10 prec_EllipticEnvelope, 11 prec_MinCovDet. GitBook basic-statistics.md:107 same text. The -sq variant is not described.
delegate_lib: scikit-learn==1.9.1 (scipy==1.17.1 linalg.pinvh, numpy==2.5.4): sklearn.covariance.MinCovDet().fit -> MinCovDet.fit -> fast_mcd, correct_covariance, reweight_covariance; attribute precision_
implemented_as: Data z-scored per channel over the full sample (ddof=1; optional detrend first). z (T x P) passed to sklearn MinCovDet() with all defaults and random_state=None (global numpy RNG). FAST-MCD raw search: h = ceil((T+P+1)/2); T<=500: 30 random h-subsets x 2 C-steps, best 10 refined; T>500: random partition into T//300 subsets, 500 trials, merge on <=1500 samples. Raw distances divided by the Croux-Haesbroeck factor c(P,h/T); rows with d2 < chi2_{P,0.975} kept; Sigma = c(P,0.975) * MLE covariance (divisor n_w) of kept rows; precision_ = scipy.linalg.pinvh(Sigma). pyspi returns the precision_ matrix as is (no normalisation to correlation / partial correlation, no sign flip), diagonal set to NaN in place on the cached fit; prec-sq_MinCovDet returns its elementwise square. One fit per Data object per estimator name, shared by cov/prec and squared/unsquared identifiers.

deviation_from_canonical: Close variant of reweighted FAST-MCD: (1) the search is a stochastic approximation of the MCD optimum (inherent to FAST-MCD) but the random starts come from the global numpy RNG, so the selected h-subset and hence values vary run to run (spread up to 0.34 at T=64); (2) h = ceil((n+p+1)/2) instead of floor; (3) reweighted covariance uses the MLE divisor n_w (robustbase: n_w - 1) and no small-sample correction (Pison et al. 2002); (4) raw consistency factor is the asymptotic Croux-Haesbroeck factor rather than RVD 1999 median rescaling; (5) the input is z-scored with non-robust mean/SD over the full sample before the robust fit, so the output is a robust covariance in units of the contaminated SD, not a robust correlation. (6) precision via pseudo-inverse pinvh: for singular scatter (collinear channels) a Moore-Penrose inverse is returned silently instead of failing.

metric_name_standard: inverse of the OAS shrinkage covariance estimate
canonical_ref: Dempster 1972, Biometrics 28(1):157-175 (covariance selection; concentration/precision matrix); partial-correlation relation rho_ij|rest = -Theta_ij / sqrt(Theta_ii Theta_jj) in Whittaker 1990, Graphical Models in Applied Multivariate Statistics, Wiley, ch. 5. Covariance estimator: Chen, Wiesel, Eldar & Hero 2010, IEEE Trans. Signal Processing 58(10):5016-5029, Eq. 22-23 (arXiv:0907.4698v1 Eq. 23); target F = tr(S)/p I (Eq. 3), S = (1/n) sum x_i x_i^T (Eq. 2)
canonical_definition: Theta = Sigma_hat^{-1} where Sigma_hat is: Sigma_OAS = (1 - rho) S + rho (tr(S)/p) I, rho = min( [(1 - 2/p) tr(S^2) + tr^2(S)] / [(n + 1 - 2/p)(tr(S^2) - tr^2(S)/p)], 1 ); partial correlation is -Theta_ij/sqrt(Theta_ii Theta_jj), not Theta_ij itself
documented_definition: supplement §1.1.2, p.4 (supplement.txt:158-171): 'The precision matrix is the matrix inverse of the covariance matrix ... For normalized time-series data, the precision matrix is equivalent to the partial correlation between each pairwise time series, conditioned on all other time series, and is within [-1, 1].' GitBook basic-statistics.md:101-122 has the same text. Neither source documents the '-sq' (squared) variants generated by pyspi/config.yaml.

metric_name_standard: inverse of the fixed-coefficient (0.1) shrunk covariance
canonical_ref: Dempster 1972, Biometrics 28(1):157-175 (covariance selection; concentration/precision matrix); partial-correlation relation rho_ij|rest = -Theta_ij / sqrt(Theta_ii Theta_jj) in Whittaker 1990, Graphical Models in Applied Multivariate Statistics, Wiley, ch. 5. Covariance estimator: Pedregosa et al. 2011, J. Mach. Learn. Res. 12:2825-2830 (scikit-learn; supplement ref [2]) user guide 'Basic shrinkage'; the shrinkage form (1-s)S + s(tr S/p)I is the convex-combination family of Ledoit & Wolf 2004, J. Multivariate Analysis 88(2):365-411, with s fixed rather than estimated
canonical_definition: Theta = Sigma_hat^{-1} where Sigma_hat is: Sigma_shrunk = 0.9 S + 0.1 (tr(S)/p) I; partial correlation is -Theta_ij/sqrt(Theta_ii Theta_jj), not Theta_ij itself
documented_definition: supplement §1.1.2, p.4 (supplement.txt:158-171): 'The precision matrix is the matrix inverse of the covariance matrix ... For normalized time-series data, the precision matrix is equivalent to the partial correlation between each pairwise time series, conditioned on all other time series, and is within [-1, 1].' GitBook basic-statistics.md:101-122 has the same text. Neither source documents the '-sq' (squared) variants generated by pyspi/config.yaml.

implemented_as: Same cached sklearn.covariance.ShrunkCovariance() fit as cov_ShrunkCovariance; returns precision_ = scipy.linalg.pinvh(covariance_) computed at fit time (Moore-Penrose pseudo-inverse via eigh with relative cutoff max(P,P)*eps*max|eig|), diagonal NaN. Off-diagonals are raw inverse-covariance entries, not normalised; on the default pipeline Theta = T/(T-1) * [(1-s)R + sI]^{-1} with R the Pearson correlation matrix. Not symmetrised (Estimators.multivariate bypasses Undirected.multivariate). Squared variant (prec-sq_*) = np.square of the same matrix.

metric_name_standard: Spearman's rank correlation coefficient rho_S (tie-corrected: Pearson correlation of mid-ranks); spearmanr-sq is its square
canonical_ref: Spearman C. 1904, 'The proof and measurement of association between two things', Am J Psychol 15(1):72-101; tie handling by mid-ranks: Kendall & Gibbons 1990, Rank Correlation Methods, 5th ed., ch. 3
canonical_definition: rho_S = Pearson correlation of R(x) and R(y), R = rank with ties given average rank; equals 1 - 6 sum d_i^2 / (n(n^2-1)) only without ties
documented_definition: supplement §1.1.3, p.4 (supplement.txt:172-178): 'Spearman's rho is a nonparametric measure of rank correlation ... implemented via function spearmanr in SciPy [6], and has a value in [-1, 1]'; keywords 'undirected, nonlinear, signed, bivariate, contemporaneous'. GitBook basic-statistics.md:126-140 same text; table-of-spis.md:35 lists identifiers spearmanr and spearmanr-sq. The squared variant is not described in the supplement (only '17. spearmanr').

deviation_from_documented: Value: none (scipy.stats.spearmanr as documented, range [-1,1]). Metadata: class labels carry 'linear' whereas supplement/config keywords say 'nonlinear' (candidate); labels carry both 'signed' and 'unsigned' (bug 4). spearmanr-sq is listed in the GitBook table but its definition (rho^2, range [0,1]) is not documented in the supplement.
deviation_from_canonical: none for the coefficient (mid-rank Pearson is the standard tie-corrected rho_S; probe on tied data matched a from-scratch mid-rank Pearson exactly: 0.35395114622767243). spearmanr-sq (rho_S^2) is a pyspi-specific transform without a standard name. Detrending (if enabled) is a non-monotone transform applied before ranking, so the pipeline-detrend value is rho_S of residuals, not of the raw series. Numerics: with ties the two mid-rank SDs differ and np.corrcoef divides by them in sequence (numpy _function_base_impl.py:3036-3038), so spearmanr(x, y) and spearmanr(y, x) can differ in the last bits; continuous data give two permutations of 1..n with bit-identical SDs and no difference.
units_and_range: dimensionless; spearmanr signed in [-1,1]; spearmanr-sq in [0,1]; symmetric in exact arithmetic (kernel reciprocal calls can differ by a few ulp with ties; pipeline output exactly symmetric via the mirror, base.py:137); NaN on the diagonal; NaN only if a channel is constant, which the Data loader rejects earlier with ValueError (data.py:199-203)

metric_name_standard: Spearman's rank correlation coefficient rho_S (tie-corrected: Pearson correlation of mid-ranks); spearmanr-sq is its square
canonical_ref: Spearman C. 1904, 'The proof and measurement of association between two things', Am J Psychol 15(1):72-101; tie handling by mid-ranks: Kendall & Gibbons 1990, Rank Correlation Methods, 5th ed., ch. 3
canonical_definition: rho_S = Pearson correlation of R(x) and R(y), R = rank with ties given average rank; equals 1 - 6 sum d_i^2 / (n(n^2-1)) only without ties
documented_definition: supplement §1.1.3, p.4 (supplement.txt:172-178): 'Spearman's rho is a nonparametric measure of rank correlation ... implemented via function spearmanr in SciPy [6], and has a value in [-1, 1]'; keywords 'undirected, nonlinear, signed, bivariate, contemporaneous'. GitBook basic-statistics.md:126-140 same text; table-of-spis.md:35 lists identifiers spearmanr and spearmanr-sq. The squared variant is not described in the supplement (only '17. spearmanr').

Lower triangle overwritten from upper (i<j). Zero lag only; no multi-realisation handling (R=1 assumed).

deviation_from_documented: Value: none (scipy.stats.spearmanr as documented, range [-1,1]). Metadata: class labels carry 'linear' whereas supplement/config keywords say 'nonlinear' (candidate); labels carry both 'signed' and 'unsigned' (bug 4). spearmanr-sq is listed in the GitBook table but its definition (rho^2, range [0,1]) is not documented in the supplement.
deviation_from_canonical: none for the coefficient (mid-rank Pearson is the standard tie-corrected rho_S; probe on tied data matched a from-scratch mid-rank Pearson exactly: 0.35395114622767243). spearmanr-sq (rho_S^2) is a pyspi-specific transform without a standard name. Detrending (if enabled) is a non-monotone transform applied before ranking, so the pipeline-detrend value is rho_S of residuals, not of the raw series. Numerics: with ties the two mid-rank SDs differ and np.corrcoef divides by them in sequence (numpy _function_base_impl.py:3036-3038), so spearmanr(x, y) and spearmanr(y, x) can differ in the last bits; continuous data give two permutations of 1..n with bit-identical SDs and no difference.
units_and_range: dimensionless; spearmanr signed in [-1,1]; spearmanr-sq in [0,1]; symmetric in exact arithmetic (kernel reciprocal calls can differ by a few ulp with ties; pipeline output exactly symmetric via the mirror, base.py:137); NaN on the diagonal; NaN only if a channel is constant, which the Data loader rejects earlier with ValueError (data.py:199-203)

metric_name_standard: Kendall's tau-b (tie-adjusted Kendall rank correlation); kendalltau-sq is its square
canonical_ref: Kendall M.G. 1938, 'A new measure of rank correlation', Biometrika 30(1-2):81-93 (tau-a); tie adjustment tau-b: Kendall M.G. 1945, 'The treatment of ties in ranking problems', Biometrika 33(3):239-251; O(n log n) algorithm: Knight W.R. 1966, JASA 61:436-439
canonical_definition: tau_a = (C - D) / (n(n-1)/2); tau_b = (C - D) / sqrt((n0 - n1)(n0 - n2)), n0 = n(n-1)/2, n1/n2 = pairs tied in x/y; tau_a == tau_b when there are no ties

metric_name_standard: maximum of the sample cross-correlation function over lags |h| <= T/4 restricted to significant lags (and of its square for the -sq identifier)
canonical_ref: Brockwell & Davis, Time Series: Theory and Methods (Springer Science & Business Media, 2009, as cited in the supplement; edition not stated there), the supplement's reference [8] (supplement.txt:1987-1988): sample cross-covariance gamma_hat_ij(h), sample cross-correlation rho_hat_ij(h) and the +-1.96 n^-1/2 bound for two independent series of which one is white noise. UNVERIFIED locator: the section/theorem numbers (§11.2, Theorem 11.2.2) were recalled from memory and no copy of the book was consulted; see Open questions. Lag truncation: the supplement (§1.1.5, p.5; supplement.txt:197-198) cites [9] Afyouni, Smith & Nichols 2019, NeuroImage 199:609 and [10] Cliff, Novelli, Fulcher, Shine & Lizier 2021, Phys Rev Res 3:013145 (supplement.txt:1990-1995) for the practice of truncating the CCF "at a given level"; the specific T/4 cut is pyspi's choice, and no canonical source for it was consulted.
canonical_definition: rho_hat_xy(h) = gamma_hat_xy(h) / sqrt(gamma_hat_xx(0) gamma_hat_yy(0)), gamma_hat_xy(h) = (1/n) sum_{t=1}^{n-h} (x_{t+h} - xbar)(y_t - ybar) for 0 <= h < n and gamma_hat_xy(h) = gamma_hat_yx(-h) for h < 0 (mean-centred, divisor n at every lag, so |rho_hat| <= 1); lag-h sample CCF considered significant when |rho_hat| > 1.96/sqrt(n) (valid under independence with at least one white series). The scalar summary (max or mean of the CCF over a lag window) is a pyspi construction with no canonical source.
documented_definition: supplement §1.1.5, p.5 (pack lines 197-213; heading at supplement.txt line 192): "The cross-correlation function is defined as the Pearson correlation between two time series for all lags [8], giving values in [-1, 1] for each lag ... the correlation from the MLE of the cross-covariance at a given lag, normalised by the autocovariance ... we do by only using the first T/4 lags ... a correlation below 1.96/sqrt(T) is considered statistically insignificant [8], thus we optionally cut-off the lags at this level (sig-True means we only use the statistically significant values, and sig-False means we use all values) ... the maximum over the considered lags (max), and the average over the considered lags (mean)." deviation_from_documented: (1) Normalisation: documented as 'Pearson correlation ... giving values in [-1, 1]', but r = z/(std_ddof0(x) std_ddof0(y)(T-1)) on ddof=1 z-scored input equals T/(T-1) times the sample correlation at every lag (probe T=64: lag-0 ratio to Pearson r 1.0158730 = 64/63; ratio to the B&D CCF 1.0158730 at every lag), so identical series give 1.0159 > 1 at T=64. (2) Lag window: documented 'first T/4 lags'; implemented lags -(T//4-1)..+T//4 (both sides, 2*(T//4) lags, asymmetric by one lag). (3) Threshold: documented 1.96/sqrt(T), implemented 1.96/sqrt(T//4) ~= 3.92/sqrt(T) (basic.py:118-119; probe thresholds T=256 0.245 vs 0.1225). (4) Window centre: N = len//2 is the element at lag +1, lag 0 is at N-1 (probe). (5) Negative-side cut: start index N - fzr uses the position of the last insignificant left-half value counted from the far-left end, so the cut is mirrored: when lag 0 itself is insignificant (fzr = N-1) the window starts at lag -(T//4-2) and covers ~T//4 insignificant lags; crafted probe with significance only at |lag| <= 2 gives window lags -11..2 (T=64) and mean 0.321 instead of 0.9. (6) If one half has no insignificant lag the code raises IndexError (not documented); if fzr = 0 and fzf = 0 the window is empty: mean -> NaN with RuntimeWarning, max -> ValueError (crafted probe). (7) The resulting value depends on which channel has the higher index (probe below).
deviation_from_canonical: Constant inflation by T/(T-1) relative to the B&D sample CCF (divisor (T-1)^2/T instead of T-1 for z-scored data); window not symmetric about lag 0 (+T//4 included, -T//4 excluded); with normalise=False no centring at all (non-centred cross-product), whereas rho_hat is mean-centred; the max/mean summary over lags has no canonical definition (pyspi construction); signed max ignores negative peaks (max |rho_hat| is the more common peak-CCF summary; -sq covers it). The significance-restricted window is neither the documented rule nor a canonical one (threshold doubled, centre off by one, negative cut mirrored).
units_and_range: Dimensionless, signed (plain) / non-negative (-sq). Nominally in [-1, 1] / [0, 1] but scaled by T/(T-1) so can slightly exceed 1 (1.0159 at T=64 for identical series). Symmetric by construction (mirror), yet the value depends on channel order. Can raise IndexError (whole matrix NaN in Calculator) or ValueError on an empty window; never NaN.
direction_convention: Undirected; A is symmetric by the mirror in pyspi/base.py:137. A[i,j] = A[j,i] = statistic over a lag window of r from scipy.signal.correlate(x_hi, x_lo) where hi = max(i,j), lo = min(i,j) (first bivariate call is (i=hi, j=lo), and the cache at basic.py:113 returns the same unreversed array for (lo,hi)); probe: data.xcorr[(0,1)] equals the slice computed from correlate(x1, x0). Sign convention of the lag axis (probe and scipy docstring :168): a peak at positive lag k in correlate(x, y) means x(t) ~ y(t-k), i.e. y leads x by k; so positive lags in the stored r mean the LOWER-index channel leads. Same orientation as Brockwell & Davis gamma_12(h) = Cov(X_{t+h,1}, X_{t,2}) with series 1 = x_hi.

score_rubric_note: It is the maximum over a window set by a doubled threshold, a lag +1 centre and a mirrored left cut. The documented reading agrees on 0/20 runs. Channel order moves delayed_noise A[0,3] from 0.081 to 0.993.
what_changed: On top of T/(T-1), the sigonly rule differs from the documented one in four ways. (a) The threshold is 1.96/sqrt(T//4), twice the documented 1.96/sqrt(T): 0 null exceedances against 3.7%. (b) The centre is lag +1. (c) The left cut is mirrored (start N - fzr), so the kept window almost always spans the whole negative half (254-256 of 256 lags at T=1024, none significant on null data). (d) The positive side stops at the first insignificant lag from +1, so a lag-k peak with k>=2 on the positive side is never seen. The result is the maximum of the CCF over about lags -(T//4-2)..0 plus the significant run from +1. It depends on which channel has the higher index: delayed_noise A[0,3] 0.081 against 0.993 reversed. It raises IndexError, which makes the Calculator matrix all NaN, on periodic, trending and long-memory data. It agrees with the documented quantity (up to T/(T-1)) only when the peak sits at lag 0 or the significant lags run contiguously from +1 (var2_bivariate, gauss_ar1_pair, bivariate_gaussian rho pairs). Rubric anchor 4 (related but different quantity) rather than 6: anchor 6 covers the threshold/origin deviations, and the checks show the mirrored cut and order dependence on top of them.

metric_name_standard: maximum of the sample cross-correlation function over lags |h| <= T/4 restricted to significant lags (and of its square for the -sq identifier)
canonical_ref: Brockwell & Davis, Time Series: Theory and Methods (Springer Science & Business Media, 2009, as cited in the supplement; edition not stated there), the supplement's reference [8] (supplement.txt:1987-1988): sample cross-covariance gamma_hat_ij(h), sample cross-correlation rho_hat_ij(h) and the +-1.96 n^-1/2 bound for two independent series of which one is white noise. UNVERIFIED locator: the section/theorem numbers (§11.2, Theorem 11.2.2) were recalled from memory and no copy of the book was consulted; see Open questions. Lag truncation: the supplement (§1.1.5, p.5; supplement.txt:197-198) cites [9] Afyouni, Smith & Nichols 2019, NeuroImage 199:609 and [10] Cliff, Novelli, Fulcher, Shine & Lizier 2021, Phys Rev Res 3:013145 (supplement.txt:1990-1995) for the practice of truncating the CCF "at a given level"; the specific T/4 cut is pyspi's choice, and no canonical source for it was consulted.
canonical_definition: rho_hat_xy(h) = gamma_hat_xy(h) / sqrt(gamma_hat_xx(0) gamma_hat_yy(0)), gamma_hat_xy(h) = (1/n) sum_{t=1}^{n-h} (x_{t+h} - xbar)(y_t - ybar) for 0 <= h < n and gamma_hat_xy(h) = gamma_hat_yx(-h) for h < 0 (mean-centred, divisor n at every lag, so |rho_hat| <= 1); lag-h sample CCF considered significant when |rho_hat| > 1.96/sqrt(n) (valid under independence with at least one white series). The scalar summary (max or mean of the CCF over a lag window) is a pyspi construction with no canonical source.
documented_definition: supplement §1.1.5, p.5 (pack lines 197-213; heading at supplement.txt line 192): "The cross-correlation function is defined as the Pearson correlation between two time series for all lags [8], giving values in [-1, 1] for each lag ... the correlation from the MLE of the cross-covariance at a given lag, normalised by the autocovariance ... we do by only using the first T/4 lags ... a correlation below 1.96/sqrt(T) is considered statistically insignificant [8], thus we optionally cut-off the lags at this level (sig-True means we only use the statistically significant values, and sig-False means we use all values) ... the maximum over the considered lags (max), and the average over the considered lags (mean)." Same text on GitBook basic-statistics.md:55-57 (Cross Correlation), which lists xcorr_max_sig-True, xcorr_mean_sig-True, xcorr_mean_sig-False and their -sq versions (lines 63-75). [8] = Brockwell & Davis, Time Series: Theory and Methods (supplement.txt:1987).

deviation_from_documented: (1) Normalisation: documented as 'Pearson correlation ... giving values in [-1, 1]', but r = z/(std_ddof0(x) std_ddof0(y)(T-1)) on ddof=1 z-scored input equals T/(T-1) times the sample correlation at every lag (probe T=64: lag-0 ratio to Pearson r 1.0158730 = 64/63; ratio to the B&D CCF 1.0158730 at every lag), so identical series give 1.0159 > 1 at T=64. (2) Lag window: documented 'first T/4 lags'; implemented lags -(T//4-1)..+T//4 (both sides, 2*(T//4) lags, asymmetric by one lag). (3) Threshold: documented 1.96/sqrt(T), implemented 1.96/sqrt(T//4) ~= 3.92/sqrt(T) (basic.py:118-119; probe thresholds T=256 0.245 vs 0.1225). (4) Window centre: N = len//2 is the element at lag +1, lag 0 is at N-1 (probe). (5) Negative-side cut: start index N - fzr uses the position of the last insignificant left-half value counted from the far-left end, so the cut is mirrored: when lag 0 itself is insignificant (fzr = N-1) the window starts at lag -(T//4-2) and covers ~T//4 insignificant lags; crafted probe with significance only at |lag| <= 2 gives window lags -11..2 (T=64) and mean 0.321 instead of 0.9. (6) If one half has no insignificant lag the code raises IndexError (not documented); if fzr = 0 and fzf = 0 the window is empty: mean -> NaN with RuntimeWarning, max -> ValueError (crafted probe). (7) The resulting value depends on which channel has the higher index (probe below).
deviation_from_canonical: Constant inflation by T/(T-1) relative to the B&D sample CCF (divisor (T-1)^2/T instead of T-1 for z-scored data); window not symmetric about lag 0 (+T//4 included, -T//4 excluded); with normalise=False no centring at all (non-centred cross-product), whereas rho_hat is mean-centred; the max/mean summary over lags has no canonical definition (pyspi construction); signed max ignores negative peaks (max |rho_hat| is the more common peak-CCF summary; -sq covers it). The significance-restricted window is neither the documented rule nor a canonical one (threshold doubled, centre off by one, negative cut mirrored).
units_and_range: Dimensionless, signed (plain) / non-negative (-sq). Nominally in [-1, 1] / [0, 1] but scaled by T/(T-1) so can slightly exceed 1 (1.0159 at T=64 for identical series). Symmetric by construction (mirror), yet the value depends on channel order. Can raise IndexError (whole matrix NaN in Calculator) or ValueError on an empty window; never NaN.
direction_convention: Undirected; A is symmetric by the mirror in pyspi/base.py:137. A[i,j] = A[j,i] = statistic over a lag window of r from scipy.signal.correlate(x_hi, x_lo) where hi = max(i,j), lo = min(i,j) (first bivariate call is (i=hi, j=lo), and the cache at basic.py:113 returns the same unreversed array for (lo,hi)); probe: data.xcorr[(0,1)] equals the slice computed from correlate(x1, x0). Sign convention of the lag axis (probe and scipy docstring :168): a peak at positive lag k in correlate(x, y) means x(t) ~ y(t-k), i.e. y leads x by k; so positive lags in the stored r mean the LOWER-index channel leads. Same orientation as Brockwell & Davis gamma_12(h) = Cov(X_{t+h,1}, X_{t,2}) with series 1 = x_hi.

score_rubric_note: It is the maximum over a window set by a doubled threshold, a lag +1 centre and a mirrored left cut. The documented reading agrees on 0/20 runs. Channel order moves delayed_noise A[0,3] from 0.081 to 0.993.
what_changed: On top of T/(T-1), the sigonly rule differs from the documented one in four ways. (a) The threshold is 1.96/sqrt(T//4), twice the documented 1.96/sqrt(T): 0 null exceedances against 3.7%. (b) The centre is lag +1. (c) The left cut is mirrored (start N - fzr), so the kept window almost always spans the whole negative half (254-256 of 256 lags at T=1024, none significant on null data). (d) The positive side stops at the first insignificant lag from +1, so a lag-k peak with k>=2 on the positive side is never seen. The result is the maximum of the CCF over about lags -(T//4-2)..0 plus the significant run from +1. It depends on which channel has the higher index: delayed_noise A[0,3] 0.081 against 0.993 reversed. It raises IndexError, which makes the Calculator matrix all NaN, on periodic, trending and long-memory data. It agrees with the documented quantity (up to T/(T-1)) only when the peak sits at lag 0 or the significant lags run contiguously from +1 (var2_bivariate, gauss_ar1_pair, bivariate_gaussian rho pairs). Rubric anchor 4 (related but different quantity) rather than 6: anchor 6 covers the threshold/origin deviations, and the checks show the mirrored cut and order dependence on top of them.

metric_name_standard: mean of the sample cross-correlation function over lags |h| <= T/4 restricted to significant lags (and of its square for the -sq identifier)
canonical_ref: Brockwell & Davis, Time Series: Theory and Methods (Springer Science & Business Media, 2009, as cited in the supplement; edition not stated there), the supplement's reference [8] (supplement.txt:1987-1988): sample cross-covariance gamma_hat_ij(h), sample cross-correlation rho_hat_ij(h) and the +-1.96 n^-1/2 bound for two independent series of which one is white noise. UNVERIFIED locator: the section/theorem numbers (§11.2, Theorem 11.2.2) were recalled from memory and no copy of the book was consulted; see Open questions. Lag truncation: the supplement (§1.1.5, p.5; supplement.txt:197-198) cites [9] Afyouni, Smith & Nichols 2019, NeuroImage 199:609 and [10] Cliff, Novelli, Fulcher, Shine & Lizier 2021, Phys Rev Res 3:013145 (supplement.txt:1990-1995) for the practice of truncating the CCF "at a given level"; the specific T/4 cut is pyspi's choice, and no canonical source for it was consulted.
canonical_definition: rho_hat_xy(h) = gamma_hat_xy(h) / sqrt(gamma_hat_xx(0) gamma_hat_yy(0)), gamma_hat_xy(h) = (1/n) sum_{t=1}^{n-h} (x_{t+h} - xbar)(y_t - ybar) for 0 <= h < n and gamma_hat_xy(h) = gamma_hat_yx(-h) for h < 0 (mean-centred, divisor n at every lag, so |rho_hat| <= 1); lag-h sample CCF considered significant when |rho_hat| > 1.96/sqrt(n) (valid under independence with at least one white series). The scalar summary (max or mean of the CCF over a lag window) is a pyspi construction with no canonical source.
documented_definition: supplement §1.1.5, p.5 (pack lines 197-213; heading at supplement.txt line 192): "The cross-correlation function is defined as the Pearson correlation between two time series for all lags [8], giving values in [-1, 1] for each lag ... the correlation from the MLE of the cross-covariance at a given lag, normalised by the autocovariance ... we do by only using the first T/4 lags ... a correlation below 1.96/sqrt(T) is considered statistically insignificant [8], thus we optionally cut-off the lags at this level (sig-True means we only use the statistically significant values, and sig-False means we use all values) ... the maximum over the considered lags (max), and the average over the considered lags (mean)." Same text on GitBook basic-statistics.md:55-57 (Cross Correlation), which lists xcorr_max_sig-True, xcorr_mean_sig-True, xcorr_mean_sig-False and their -sq versions (lines 63-75). [8] = Brockwell & Davis, Time Series: Theory and Methods (supplement.txt:1987).

No mean removal inside the SPI. Result mirrored to a symmetric matrix from the (hi, lo) orientation.

deviation_from_documented: (1) Normalisation: documented as 'Pearson correlation ... giving values in [-1, 1]', but r = z/(std_ddof0(x) std_ddof0(y)(T-1)) on ddof=1 z-scored input equals T/(T-1) times the sample correlation at every lag (probe T=64: lag-0 ratio to Pearson r 1.0158730 = 64/63; ratio to the B&D CCF 1.0158730 at every lag), so identical series give 1.0159 > 1 at T=64. (2) Lag window: documented 'first T/4 lags'; implemented lags -(T//4-1)..+T//4 (both sides, 2*(T//4) lags, asymmetric by one lag). (3) Threshold: documented 1.96/sqrt(T), implemented 1.96/sqrt(T//4) ~= 3.92/sqrt(T) (basic.py:118-119; probe thresholds T=256 0.245 vs 0.1225). (4) Window centre: N = len//2 is the element at lag +1, lag 0 is at N-1 (probe). (5) Negative-side cut: start index N - fzr uses the position of the last insignificant left-half value counted from the far-left end, so the cut is mirrored: when lag 0 itself is insignificant (fzr = N-1) the window starts at lag -(T//4-2) and covers ~T//4 insignificant lags; crafted probe with significance only at |lag| <= 2 gives window lags -11..2 (T=64) and mean 0.321 instead of 0.9. (6) If one half has no insignificant lag the code raises IndexError (not documented); if fzr = 0 and fzf = 0 the window is empty: mean -> NaN with RuntimeWarning, max -> ValueError (crafted probe). (7) The resulting value depends on which channel has the higher index (probe below).
deviation_from_canonical: Constant inflation by T/(T-1) relative to the B&D sample CCF (divisor (T-1)^2/T instead of T-1 for z-scored data); window not symmetric about lag 0 (+T//4 included, -T//4 excluded); with normalise=False no centring at all (non-centred cross-product), whereas rho_hat is mean-centred; the max/mean summary over lags has no canonical definition (pyspi construction); signed max ignores negative peaks (max |rho_hat| is the more common peak-CCF summary; -sq covers it). The significance-restricted window is neither the documented rule nor a canonical one (threshold doubled, centre off by one, negative cut mirrored); the mean over a variable-length window mixes window length with correlation strength.
units_and_range: Dimensionless, signed (plain) / non-negative (-sq). Nominally in [-1, 1] / [0, 1] but scaled by T/(T-1) so can slightly exceed 1 (1.0159 at T=64 for identical series). metric_name_standard: mean of the sample cross-correlation function over lags |h| <= T/4 restricted to significant lags (and of its square for the -sq identifier)
canonical_ref: Brockwell & Davis, Time Series: Theory and Methods (Springer Science & Business Media, 2009, as cited in the supplement; edition not stated there), the supplement's reference [8] (supplement.txt:1987-1988): sample cross-covariance gamma_hat_ij(h), sample cross-correlation rho_hat_ij(h) and the +-1.96 n^-1/2 bound for two independent series of which one is white noise. UNVERIFIED locator: the section/theorem numbers (§11.2, Theorem 11.2.2) were recalled from memory and no copy of the book was consulted; see Open questions. Lag truncation: the supplement (§1.1.5, p.5; supplement.txt:197-198) cites [9] Afyouni, Smith & Nichols 2019, NeuroImage 199:609 and [10] Cliff, Novelli, Fulcher, Shine & Lizier 2021, Phys Rev Res 3:013145 (supplement.txt:1990-1995) for the practice of truncating the CCF "at a given level"; the specific T/4 cut is pyspi's choice, and no canonical source for it was consulted.
canonical_definition: rho_hat_xy(h) = gamma_hat_xy(h) / sqrt(gamma_hat_xx(0) gamma_hat_yy(0)), gamma_hat_xy(h) = (1/n) sum_{t=1}^{n-h} (x_{t+h} - xbar)(y_t - ybar) for 0 <= h < n and gamma_hat_xy(h) = gamma_hat_yx(-h) for h < 0 (mean-centred, divisor n at every lag, so |rho_hat| <= 1); lag-h sample CCF considered significant when |rho_hat| > 1.96/sqrt(n) (valid under independence with at least one white series). The scalar summary (max or mean of the CCF over a lag window) is a pyspi construction with no canonical source.
documented_definition: supplement §1.1.5, p.5 (pack lines 197-213; heading at supplement.txt line 192): "The cross-correlation function is defined as the Pearson correlation between two time series for all lags [8], giving values in [-1, 1] for each lag ... the correlation from the MLE of the cross-covariance at a given lag, normalised by the autocovariance ... we do by only using the first T/4 lags ... a correlation below 1.96/sqrt(T) is considered statistically insignificant [8], thus we optionally cut-off the lags at this level (sig-True means we only use the statistically significant values, and sig-False means we use all values) ... the maximum over the considered lags (max), and the average over the considered lags (mean)." Same text on GitBook basic-statistics.md:55-57 (Cross Correlation), which lists xcorr_max_sig-True, xcorr_mean_sig-True, xcorr_mean_sig-False and their -sq versions (lines 63-75). [8] = Brockwell & Davis, Time Series: Theory and Methods (supplement.txt:1987).

For the pair (x=x_hi, y=x_lo) pyspi computes z = scipy.signal.correlate(x, y, 'full'), r = z / (std0(x) std0(y) (T-1)) which for z-scored input equals T/(T-1) times the Brockwell-Davis sample CCF at every lag, keeps lags -(T//4-1)..+T//4 (2*(T//4) values, one more positive than negative lag); sig-True then sets N = T//4 (the element at lag +1, not lag 0), threshold 1.96/sqrt(T//4), positive-side end = first insignificant lag at or after +1 (exclusive), negative-side start = N - fzr where fzr is the index (from the far-left end) of the last insignificant value in the left half, i.e. a mirrored index rather than fzr+1; returns np.mean of r (signed) or of r**2 (-sq). No mean removal inside the SPI. Result mirrored to a symmetric matrix from the (hi, lo) orientation.

deviation_from_documented: (1) Normalisation: documented as 'Pearson correlation ... giving values in [-1, 1]', but r = z/(std_ddof0(x) std_ddof0(y)(T-1)) on ddof=1 z-scored input equals T/(T-1) times the sample correlation at every lag (probe T=64: lag-0 ratio to Pearson r 1.0158730 = 64/63; ratio to the B&D CCF 1.0158730 at every lag), so identical series give 1.0159 > 1 at T=64. (2) Lag window: documented 'first T/4 lags'; implemented lags -(T//4-1)..+T//4 (both sides, 2*(T//4) lags, asymmetric by one lag). (3) Threshold: documented 1.96/sqrt(T), implemented 1.96/sqrt(T//4) ~= 3.92/sqrt(T) (basic.py:118-119; probe thresholds T=256 0.245 vs 0.1225). (4) Window centre: N = len//2 is the element at lag +1, lag 0 is at N-1 (probe). (5) Negative-side cut: start index N - fzr uses the position of the last insignificant left-half value counted from the far-left end, so the cut is mirrored: when lag 0 itself is insignificant (fzr = N-1) the window starts at lag -(T//4-2) and covers ~T//4 insignificant lags; crafted probe with significance only at |lag| <= 2 gives window lags -11..2 (T=64) and mean 0.321 instead of 0.9. (6) If one half has no insignificant lag the code raises IndexError (not documented); if fzr = 0 and fzf = 0 the window is empty: mean -> NaN with RuntimeWarning, max -> ValueError (crafted probe). (7) The resulting value depends on which channel has the higher index (probe below).
deviation_from_canonical: Constant inflation by T/(T-1) relative to the B&D sample CCF (divisor (T-1)^2/T instead of T-1 for z-scored data); window not symmetric about lag 0 (+T//4 included, -T//4 excluded); with normalise=False no centring at all (non-centred cross-product), whereas rho_hat is mean-centred; the max/mean summary over lags has no canonical definition (pyspi construction); signed max ignores negative peaks (max |rho_hat| is the more common peak-CCF summary; -sq covers it). The significance-restricted window is neither the documented rule nor a canonical one (threshold doubled, centre off by one, negative cut mirrored); the mean over a variable-length window mixes window length with correlation strength.
units_and_range: Dimensionless, signed (plain) / non-negative (-sq). Nominally in [-1, 1] / [0, 1] but scaled by T/(T-1) so can slightly exceed 1 (1.0159 at T=64 for identical series). Symmetric by construction (mirror), yet the value depends on channel order. Can raise IndexError (whole matrix NaN in Calculator) or return NaN (with RuntimeWarning) on an empty window.
direction_convention: Undirected; A is symmetric by the mirror in pyspi/base.py:137. A[i,j] = A[j,i] = statistic over a lag window of r from scipy.signal.correlate(x_hi, x_lo) where hi = max(i,j), lo = min(i,j) (first bivariate call is (i=hi, j=lo), and the cache at basic.py:113 returns the same unreversed array for (lo,hi)); probe: data.xcorr[(0,1)] equals the slice computed from correlate(x1, x0). Sign convention of the lag axis (probe and scipy docstring :168): a peak at positive lag k in correlate(x, y) means x(t) ~ y(t-k), i.e. y leads x by k; so positive lags in the stored r mean the LOWER-index channel leads. Same orientation as Brockwell & Davis gamma_12(h) = Cov(X_{t+h,1}, X_{t,2}) with series 1 = x_hi.

metric_name_standard: mean of the sample cross-correlation function over lags |h| <= T/4 (and of its square for the -sq identifier)
canonical_ref: Brockwell & Davis, Time Series: Theory and Methods (Springer Science & Business Media, 2009, as cited in the supplement; edition not stated there), the supplement's reference [8] (supplement.txt:1987-1988): sample cross-covariance gamma_hat_ij(h), sample cross-correlation rho_hat_ij(h) and the +-1.96 n^-1/2 bound for two independent series of which one is white noise. UNVERIFIED locator: the section/theorem numbers (§11.2, Theorem 11.2.2) were recalled from memory and no copy of the book was consulted; see Open questions. Lag truncation: the supplement (§1.1.5, p.5; supplement.txt:197-198) cites [9] Afyouni, Smith & Nichols 2019, NeuroImage 199:609 and [10] Cliff, Novelli, Fulcher, Shine & Lizier 2021, Phys Rev Res 3:013145 (supplement.txt:1990-1995) for the practice of truncating the CCF "at a given level"; the specific T/4 cut is pyspi's choice, and no canonical source for it was consulted.
canonical_definition: rho_hat_xy(h) = gamma_hat_xy(h) / sqrt(gamma_hat_xx(0) gamma_hat_yy(0)), gamma_hat_xy(h) = (1/n) sum_{t=1}^{n-h} (x_{t+h} - xbar)(y_t - ybar) for 0 <= h < n and gamma_hat_xy(h) = gamma_hat_yx(-h) for h < 0 (mean-centred, divisor n at every lag, so |rho_hat| <= 1); lag-h sample CCF considered significant when |rho_hat| > 1.96/sqrt(n) (valid under independence with at least one white series). The scalar summary (max or mean of the CCF over a lag window) is a pyspi construction with no canonical source.
documented_definition: supplement §1.1.5, p.5 (pack lines 197-213; heading at supplement.txt line 192): "The cross-correlation function is defined as the Pearson correlation between two time series for all lags [8], giving values in [-1, 1] for each lag ... the correlation from the MLE of the cross-covariance at a given lag, normalised by the autocovariance ... we do by only using the first T/4 lags ... a correlation below 1.96/sqrt(T) is considered statistically insignificant [8], thus we optionally cut-off the lags at this level (sig-True means we only use the statistically significant values, and sig-False means we use all values) ... the maximum over the considered lags (max), and the average over the considered lags (mean)." Same text on GitBook basic-statistics.md:55-57 (Cross Correlation), which lists xcorr_max_sig-True, xcorr_mean_sig-True, xcorr_mean_sig-False and their -sq versions (lines 63-75). [8] = Brockwell & Davis, Time Series: Theory and Methods (supplement.txt:1987).

deviation_from_documented: (1) Normalisation: documented as 'Pearson correlation ... giving values in [-1, 1]', but r = z/(std_ddof0(x) std_ddof0(y)(T-1)) on ddof=1 z-scored input equals T/(T-1) times the sample correlation at every lag (probe T=64: lag-0 ratio to Pearson r 1.0158730 = 64/63; ratio to the B&D CCF 1.0158730 at every lag), so identical series give 1.0159 > 1 at T=64. (2) Lag window: documented 'first T/4 lags'; implemented lags -(T//4-1)..+T//4 (both sides, 2*(T//4) lags, asymmetric by one lag).
deviation_from_canonical: Constant inflation by T/(T-1) relative to the B&D sample CCF (divisor (T-1)^2/T instead of T-1 for z-scored data); window not symmetric about lag 0 (+T//4 included, -T//4 excluded); with normalise=False no centring at all (non-centred cross-product), whereas rho_hat is mean-centred; the max/mean summary over lags has no canonical definition (pyspi construction); signed max ignores negative peaks (max |rho_hat| is the more common peak-CCF summary; -sq covers it). The mean over 2*(T//4) lags is dominated by dilution (a single-lag correlation rho contributes rho/(2*(T//4))).
units_and_range: Dimensionless, signed (plain) / non-negative (-sq). Nominally in [-1, 1] / [0, 1] but scaled by T/(T-1) so can slightly exceed 1 (1.0159 at T=64 for identical series). Symmetric by construction (mirror), yet the value depends on channel order. No error path; finite for finite input. In the EEG selection.
direction_convention: Undirected; A is symmetric by the mirror in pyspi/base.py:137. A[i,j] = A[j,i] = statistic over a lag window of r from scipy.signal.correlate(x_hi, x_lo) where hi = max(i,j), lo = min(i,j) (first bivariate call is (i=hi, j=lo), and the cache at basic.py:113 returns the same unreversed array for (lo,hi)); probe: data.xcorr[(0,1)] equals the slice computed from correlate(x1, x0). Sign convention of the lag axis (probe and scipy docstring :168): a peak at positive lag k in correlate(x, y) means x(t) ~ y(t-k), i.e. y leads x by k; so positive lags in the stored r mean the LOWER-index channel leads. Same orientation as Brockwell & Davis gamma_12(h) = Cov(X_{t+h,1}, X_{t,2}) with series 1 = x_hi.

score_rubric_note: The constant factor T/(T-1) plus the one-lag-shifted window account for the whole gap (gap_d2 <= 6.1e-18 once both are applied). The shift changes the value (relative gap_d0 up to 0.54), so anchor 8 fails. Anchor 7 fails as well, because its first clause needs the supplement's variant and pyspi differs from it in a value-changing way (the supplement documents a Pearson correlation in [-1, 1] averaged over the 'first T/4 lags', while pyspi carries the T/(T-1) factor, 1.0159 for identical series at T=64, and averages over lags -(T//4-1)..T//4; documentation_status misdescribed). Anchor 6, a library formula that deviates from both the supplement and the canonical CCF in an interpretable way, is the highest anchor whose conditions all hold.
what_changed: The quantity is the supplement's 'average over the considered lags', computed as T/(T-1) times the mean of the Brockwell-Davis CCF over lags -(T//4-1)..T//4. The documented symmetric 'first T/4 lags' differs by one end lag, and the value depends on channel order by up to 1.6e-3, about 10-20% of the typical |A| on short-memory data. For z-scored data the CCF sums to 0 over all lags, so the value equals -(sum outside the window)/(2 T//4). It therefore tracks long-memory or trend mass outside +-T//4 (0.46-0.63 on cointegrated and trending) and not the dependence at small lags: the rho=0.8 pair scores -0.0002, below the rho=0.3 pair's 0.0013. normalise=False gives a non-centred quantity. These are properties of the documented quantity, recorded here and not scored. Rubric anchor 6: the library formula deviates from both the supplement ('average over the considered lags', 'first T/4 lags') and the canonical CCF in an interpretable way, a constant factor T/(T-1) plus the one-lag-shifted window -(T//4-1)..T//4 (gap_d2 <= 6.1e-18 after both are applied); the window shift changes the value (relative gap_d0 up to 0.54), so anchor 8 (constant factor only) does not apply.

metric_name_standard: Euclidean (L2) distance between the two z-scored time series viewed as vectors in R^T
canonical_ref: Deza & Deza 2016, Encyclopedia of Distances (4th ed., Springer), entry 'Euclidean metric' (l2-metric)
canonical_definition: d(x,y) = sqrt( sum_{t=1..T} (x_t - y_t)^2 )
documented_definition: GitBook distance-similarity.md 'Pairwise Distance' (lines 297-321): "Pairwise distance between time-series, computed using sklearn's pairwise distance function using the following distance metrics: Euclidean, Cityblock, Cosine, Chebyshev, Canberra, Braycurtis"; keywords "undirected, nonlinear, unsigned, unordered". No formula is given. pdist is absent from the supplement: supplement §1.2 'Distance similarity (26 SPIs)', p.5 (heading line 209) lists SPIs 22-47 (dcorr, dcorrx, mgc, mgcx, hsic, hhg, dtw, lcss, softdtw, bary) and no pdist entry.
delegate_lib: scikit-learn==1.9.1 sklearn.metrics.pairwise.euclidean_distances (dot-product expansion, float64 BLAS)
implemented_as: Rows z-scored (ddof=1) by Data by default; sklearn computes D^2 = ||x||^2 + ||y||^2 - 2 x.y via row_norms and a matrix product X X^T, clamps negatives to 0, sets only the true diagonal to 0, then takes sqrt. On z-scored rows ||x||^2 = T-1, so d = sqrt(2 (T-1) (1 - r)) with r the Pearson correlation (probe: max deviation 0.0 at T=256).

deviation_from_documented: None in substance: the code is sklearn.metrics.pairwise_distances with metric='euclidean' as the GitBook page states. Not stated on the page: inputs are z-scored per process (ddof=1) by Data by default (optionally detrended first), and the Calculator sets the diagonal to NaN. No formula or normalisation (e.g. per-sample scaling) is documented.
deviation_from_canonical: Formula: none. Numerics: the dot-product expansion suffers cancellation for near-identical rows: two identical (non-diagonal) rows give ~1e-7 instead of 0 (shared_envelope x0 vs x2: 1.19e-7 at T=64, 9.54e-7 at T=4096; direct difference gives 0.0), and relative error reaches 4.5e-2 when 1-r ~ 5e-15. Reciprocal entries can differ in the last bits (7.1e-15 on a 64x1024 probe; REVIEW M2). Domain: with default z-scoring the value is a deterministic monotone function of Pearson r, so it measures linear correlation only.
units_and_range: Same units as the z-scored data (dimensionless); range [0, 2 sqrt(T-1)] with 0 for r=1, sqrt(2(T-1)) for r=0, 2 sqrt(T-1) for y=-x (probe T=256: 31.937 = 2 sqrt(255)). Grows like sqrt(T); never negative; finite for finite input.
direction_convention: A[i,j] = d(z_i, z_j) for rows i, j of the (z-scored) M x T data; the metric is symmetric so A[i,j] = A[j,i]; no direction is encoded; diagonal NaN after Calculator.compute (confirmed in the check stage: sym runs).

what_changed: Canonical Bray-Curtis is sum|x-y| / sum(x+y) for non-negative abundances with range [0, 1]. pyspi (via SciPy) computes sum|x-y| / sum|x+y| on z-scored signed data: identical to the canonical index only for non-negative data. On default input the value is unbounded, exceeds 1 for negative correlation (3.0 in population for rho = -0.8), and is +inf without any warning for y = -x; for an affine pair (-x, 2x+1) z-score rounding decides between +inf and ~1e16. For Gaussian pairs it converges to sqrt((1-rho)/(1+rho)). Score 7: matches the documented (sklearn/SciPy) variant fp-exactly but differs from the canonical index in a value-changing way on pyspi's default input. Rubric reading is nearest-anchor 7 (score_rubric_note), because anchor 7's supplement-variant clause is met only through the GitBook sklearn form; the score-7 sentence above is the original reasoning for score_0_10.

metric_name_standard: bias-corrected squared distance correlation (R*_n, energy::bcdcor); the unbiased (U-statistic) dCov^2 normalised by the unbiased dVar^2 terms
canonical_ref: Szekely & Rizzo 2014, Ann. Statist. 42(6):2382-2412, Sec. 2-3 (U-centring, unbiased dCov^2 estimator, Prop. 1); bias-corrected dCor R*_n in Szekely & Rizzo 2013, J. Multivariate Anal. 117:193-213; population dCor: Szekely, Rizzo & Bakirov 2007, Ann. Statist. 35(6):2769-2794, Theorem 7(ii) (bivariate-normal closed form; arXiv 0803.4101 text, p.18, checked against the paper)
canonical_definition: U-centre a_ij=|x_i-x_j|: A~_ij = a_ij - a_i./(n-2) - a_.j/(n-2) + a_../((n-1)(n-2)) for i != j, 0 on the diagonal; (X.Y)_n = 1/(n(n-3)) sum_{i!=j} A~_ij B~_ij (unbiased for dCov^2(X,Y)); R*_n = (X.Y)_n / sqrt((X.X)_n (Y.Y)_n), an estimator of dCor^2 (squared scale), may be negative
documented_definition: supplement §1.2.1, p.5: 'The sample distance correlation is computed by summing over the entry-wise product of Euclidean distance matrices. This statistic is biased, however an unbiased estimator can be obtained by first double-centering the distance matrices [14]. ... We compute both the biased and unbiased statistics from the hyppo package' (identifier 22, dcorr). GitBook distance-similarity.md 'Distance Correlation' (same wording, ref arXiv 0803.4101). GitBook glossary-of-terms.md:21 (keyword table, 'Signed' row): 'Other SPIs, such as distance correlation (defined in the range [0,1]) are unsigned.'
delegate_lib: hyppo==0.5.2 hyppo.independence.Dcorr(bias=False).statistic (numba 0.68.0 jit _dcorr / _center_distmat); distances via scikit-learn==1.9.1 pairwise_distances('euclidean')
implemented_as: Default preprocessing: z-score each series (ddof=1), no detrend (irrelevant for the value: dCor is invariant to per-variable positive scaling and shifts). The T time points are treated as T iid samples of a 1-D variable (time order ignored). Euclidean (=|x_i-x_j|) distance matrices are U-centred (zero diagonal) and stat = sum(A~B~)/sqrt(sum(A~A~) sum(B~B~)) with NO square root, i.e. the bias-corrected dCor^2 R*_n. Returns exactly 0 when either U-centred variance <= 0; negative values are returned unchanged. Both ordered pairs are computed and the upper triangle (x = lower-index process) is mirrored.

deviation_from_documented: (1) The supplement says the unbiased estimator is obtained 'by first double-centering the distance matrices'; the code U-centres (n-2 and (n-1)(n-2) denominators, zero diagonal; dcorr.py:273-280), while the biased variant is the one that double-centres. (2) It says the sample statistic is a sum over the product of 'Euclidean distance matrices'; the product is of centred matrices. (3) The documentation does not say that this SPI is on the SQUARED scale (dCor^2) while dcorr_biased is on the root scale (dCor), so the two 'biased/unbiased' SPIs are not estimators of the same quantity. (4) The unbiased-estimator citation [14] is Shen, Priebe & Vogelstein (MGC), not Szekely & Rizzo 2013/2014. (5) Labelled 'unsigned' (config.yaml keywords; GitBook glossary-of-terms.md:21 gives distance correlation 'defined in the range [0,1]' as the example of an unsigned SPI) but returns negative values.
deviation_from_canonical: none for the estimator itself: matches the bias-corrected dCor^2 R*_n of Szekely & Rizzo (probe: hyppo 0.25339647074002397 vs from-scratch U-centred formula 0.25339647074002286). Convention notes: it estimates dCor^2, not dCor; clamps to 0 when a U-centred variance is <= 0 (canonical R*_n is undefined there).
units_and_range: dimensionless; in [-1, 1] (Cauchy-Schwarz in the U-centred inner-product space); negative values occur under independence (probe: 64.5% of 200 iid N(0,1) pairs at T=64 negative, min -0.0297; pyspi matrix entry -0.005393 on an independent pair); exactly 0 if either series has non-positive U-centred variance; invariant to per-variable affine maps with nonzero scale; symmetric in (x, y).
direction_convention: undirected: A[i, j] = A[j, i] = bivariate(x = process min(i, j), y = process max(i, j)) via the mirror in base.py:136-137; the kernel itself is symmetric (probe: bivariate(0,1) = bivariate(1,0) = 0.2180361011).

metric_name_standard: Sample multiscale graph correlation (Sample MGC): smoothed maximum local distance correlation over k/l-nearest-neighbour scales
canonical_ref: Shen C, Priebe CE, Vogelstein JT (2020) From distance correlation to multiscale graph correlation. J Am Stat Assoc 115(529):280-291, §3.1 eq.(6) and the local covariance/correlation definitions, §4.1 eqs.(7)-(9), Corollary 3 (threshold); see also Vogelstein et al. 2019 eLife 8:e41690
canonical_definition: A_ij = D^x_ij - (1/(n-1)) sum_s D^x_sj for i!=j, A_ii = 0 (column centring), B likewise. R^A_ij is the ascending rank of D^x_ij within column j, with minimal (consecutive) rank for ties. A^k = A ∘ I(R^A <= k), B^l = B ∘ I(R^B <= l), and Ê(M) = (1/(n(n-1))) sum_{i!=j} M_ij. dCov^{k,l} = Ê(A^k ∘ B^l') - Ê(A^k)Ê(B^l'), where ' is the transpose, and dVar is analogous. dCorr^{k,l} = dCov/sqrt(dVar^k dVar^l), set to 0 if a local variance < ε. Sample MGC is the max of dCorr over R, where R is the largest connected component of {dCorr^{k,l} > max(τ_n, dCorr^{n,n})}. τ_n = 2 F^{-1}_{Beta((v-1)/2,(v-1)/2)}(1 - 0.02/n) - 1 with v = n(n-3)/2. The statistic falls back to dCorr^{n,n} if |R| < 2n or if the max is <= dCorr^{n,n}.
documented_definition: supplement §1.2.3, p.6 (supplement.txt:243-252; the pack listed 249-259): keywords 'undirected, nonlinear, unsigned, bivariate, contemporaneous'; 'Multiscale graph correlation (MGC) [14] is a generalization of distance correlation ... the algorithm truncates the Euclidean distance matrices ... at an optimal threshold. MGC also includes a smoothing function that is intended to remove any bias introduced by disconnected components ... Only this unbiased estimator is included here (as in hyppo)'. [14] = Shen, Priebe, Vogelstein, JASA 115, 280 (2020). GitBook spi-descriptions/distance-similarity.md:251-266 has the same text, but its 'Key References' link (line 257) points to researchgate '3943235_Discovering_similar_multidimensional_trajectories', an LCSS paper, not MGC.

implemented_as: Preprocessing is the Calculator default: per-process z-score (ddof=1) and no detrend. Each pair uses x = process i and y = process j as (T,1) arrays, with sklearn dot-product Euclidean distance matrices, which are not exactly |x_a - x_b| and not bit-symmetric. Column-wise dense ranks come from np.unique(return_inverse)+1, so the diagonal (self, distance 0) gets rank 1. Column centring is D - colmean*n/(n-1) with the diagonal zeroed. The local covariance sum_{ab} A_ab B_ba I(rA_ab <= k) I(rB_ba <= l) - S_A(k) S_B(l)/n^2 is computed by rank binning, cumsum and a 2-D cumulative recurrence. Local variances are the diagonals of the same construction with (A, A'), and correlation = cov/sqrt(varx vary), clipped to <= 1, with rows or columns whose variance is <= 0 set to 0. The map is m x n', where m and n' are the numbers of distinct ranks (equal to T for continuous data). The threshold uses samp_size = n-1: Beta shape (n-1)(n-4)/4 - 1/2 at percentile 1 - 0.02/(n-1), maxed with the global-scale value. R is the largest 4-connected component (scipy.ndimage.label, first label on size ties). It is used only if |R| >= ceil(0.02*max(m,n'))*min(m,n'), and then stat = max(global, max over R). The permutation test is skipped (reps=0, warnings suppressed). Undirected: all ordered pairs are computed, and then the lower triangle is overwritten by the upper.

deviation_from_documented: (1) The supplement says 'Only this unbiased estimator is included here (as in hyppo)'. The global-scale value of the map is the column-centred dCorr^{n,n} of Shen et al. eq. (6), not hyppo's U-centred unbiased Dcorr. Probe on iid_gaussian T=256 pair (0,1): MGC global -0.0059473 vs Dcorr unbiased -0.0059357, close but different. (2) The label is 'unsigned' (supplement keywords, config.yaml and class; GitBook glossary-of-terms.md:21, 'Signed' keyword row, gives distance correlation 'defined in the range [0,1]' as the example of an unsigned SPI), but values are negative whenever the statistic falls back to the global scale under near-independence. Probe minimum was -0.0264 on iid_gaussian T=64, and most iid pairs were negative. (3) The GitBook 'Key References' link (distance-similarity.md:257) points to 'Discovering similar multidimensional trajectories', an LCSS paper; the supplement cites Shen et al. 2020 as the MGC source. (4) The verbal description of truncation and smoothing is consistent with the code.
deviation_from_canonical: The code follows the authors' R reference implementation (neurodata/r-mgc, GitHub master fetched 2026-10-14) rather than the paper text on three constants. (a) Subtractive centring term: /n^2 (_stats.pyx:444, matching r-mgc MGCLocalCorr.R:167) instead of the paper's Ê = 1/(n(n-1)). This is irrelevant at the global scale, where column sums are 0, and changes local correlations by O(1/n). Probe: nonlinear_dependence T=64 0.58183 vs 0.58028 with n(n-1), T=1024 0.534318 vs 0.534201. (b) Threshold sample size n-1 (_mgc.py:418, 454-456; R MGCSampleStat.R:99, 122-126) instead of n (Corollary 3). No effect was seen in the probes. (c) Minimum region size: ceil(0.02*max(m,n))*min(m,n) (_mgc.py:509), versus the paper's 2n and r-mgc's 2*min(m,n) (MGCSampleStat.R:172). For continuous data (m = n = T) this means n (T<=50), 2n (51-100), 6n (T=256), 21n (T=1024) or 82n (T=4096): stricter than the paper for T > 100. With tied data (m < n) it can be far laxer: on logistic_maps T=64 (map 64x8) the code gives 0.3707 vs 0.3157 under the 2n rule. (d) Equal-size largest components: the code takes the first label (argmax at _mgc.py:469), whereas the paper takes the union. (e) Variance cut-off is <= 0 rather than < ε. (f) Dense rank equals the paper's 'minimal rank' consecutive indexing (consistent). (g) Input distances are sklearn dot-product distances: rounding reorders near-tied neighbours. Probe on shared_envelope T=256 pair (0,1): 0.708 (pyspi) vs 0.769 with exact |x_a - x_b| (optimal scale (2,2)); logistic_maps T=256: 0.3176 vs 0.3221. Check-stage correction to (c): the SciPy region rule DOES change values on continuous data. At T=256 (required region 6n) the r-mgc rule 2*min(m,n) and the paper rule 2n accept local regions that SciPy rejects: anm pair (1,3), independent by construction, gives 0.0319 under the r-mgc rule vs pyspi 0.0051 (global fallback), and narrowband_f0-0.1 pair (1,2) gives 0.5364 vs pyspi 0.4751 (distance.mgc|anm|256|kernel|rmgc, distance.mgc|narrowband_f0-0.1|256|kernel|rmgc). On logistic_maps the r-mgc rule coincides with SciPy's (map 64 x 8: ceil(0.02*64)*8 = 16 = 2*min(m,n); identical values at T=64 and T=256), so the 0.3157 value is the paper's 2n rule only, not r-mgc's.

what_changed: pyspi computes SciPy's multiscale_graphcorr statistic exactly as SciPy's code states. That statistic deviates from the Shen et al. 2020 text in an interpretable way: the minimum region size ceil(0.02*max(m,n))*min(m,n) is SciPy's own rule, matching neither the paper (2n) nor the authors' r-mgc code (2*min(m,n)), and it changes values by up to 0.061 at T=256 on continuous data; the centring term n^2 and threshold size n-1 follow r-mgc, not the paper (<= 2.4e-3). It also deviates from the supplement: the label 'unsigned' (and the glossary's 'distance correlation (defined in the range [0,1])') is contradicted by negative values on 80-90% of independent pairs, and 'unbiased estimator (as in hyppo)' is inaccurate because the global fallback is the column-centred dCorr^{n,n}, not hyppo's U-centred dCor^2. The same-lineage cap does not apply and is not the basis of the score: the reference does not import or port SciPy's multiscale_graphcorr or hyppo (check_method independent-impl); it takes only three constants (n^2, n-1, the region rule) from SciPy's code, and those constants are what is being described, while the paper's and r-mgc's constants are measured as deviations. metric_name_standard: normalised unbiased HSIC with a Gaussian median-heuristic kernel (kernel analogue of bias-corrected dCor^2; an unbiased-centred kernel alignment)
canonical_ref: HSIC: Gretton, Bousquet, Smola & Scholkopf 2005, ALT, LNCS 3734:63-77 (HSIC_b = (m-1)^-2 tr(KHLH)); Gretton et al. 2007, NIPS 20 'A kernel statistical test of independence' (= supplement ref [15]): eq. (2) population HSIC, eq. (3) unbiased estimator as a sum of three U-statistics, eq. (4) biased HSIC_b = m^-2 tr(KHLH); Sec. 4 Gaussian kernel with 'kernel size set to the median distance between points in input space' (whether per variable is not stated); unbiased estimator in matrix form: Song, Smola, Gretton, Bedo & Borgwardt 2012, JMLR 13:1393-1434, eq. (5) (numerically identical to Gretton 2007 eq. (3): brute-force probe at m=9 differs by 1.8e-16); kernel/distance equivalence: Sejdinovic et al. 2013, Ann. Statist. 41(5):2263-2291; normalisation used here: Shen & Vogelstein 2020 (hyppo docs) / centred kernel alignment (Cortes, Mohri & Rostamizadeh 2012, JMLR 13:795-828)
canonical_definition: Unbiased HSIC (Song et al. 2012 eq. 5): with K~, L~ = Gram matrices with zeroed diagonal, HSIC_u = [tr(K~L~) + 1'K~1 1'L~1/((n-1)(n-2)) - 2/(n-2) 1'K~L~1] / (n(n-3)); Gaussian kernel k(x,x') = exp(-|x-x'|^2/(2 sigma^2)) with sigma = median inter-sample distance (Gretton et al. 2007 Sec. 4; applying it separately to each variable is the common reading, not stated explicitly there). Song eq. (5) equals the three-U-statistic estimator of Gretton et al. 2007 eq. (3). The quantity is an unnormalised dependence measure (HSIC itself, not a correlation).
documented_definition: supplement §1.2.5, p.6: 'The Hibert-Schmidt Independence Criterion (HSIC) [15] is an RKHS-based statistic that quantifies a statistical dependence between random variables via a sample kernel matrix. As with distance correlation, HSIC yields a biased statistic, where the unbiased (and consistent) estimator can be derived by double centering the kernel distance matrix [15]. Both biased and unbiased estimators are computed using hyppo' (identifier 29, hsic). GitBook distance-similarity.md 'Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion' (ref Gretton et al. NIPS 2007). GitBook glossary-of-terms.md:21 (keyword table, 'Signed' row): 'Other SPIs, such as distance correlation (defined in the range [0,1]) are unsigned.'
delegate_lib: hyppo==0.5.2 hyppo.independence.Hsic(bias=False).statistic -> hyppo.tools.compute_kern (median heuristic) -> scikit-learn==1.9.1 pairwise_kernels('rbf') -> hyppo Dcorr(bias=False, compute_distance=None).statistic (numba _dcorr)
implemented_as: Default preprocessing: z-score (ddof=1), no detrend. T time points treated as iid 1-D samples. sigma = median of the off-diagonal |x_i - x_j| of x (the FIRST argument, i.e. the lower-index process after the mirror) and gamma = 1/(2 sigma^2) is used for BOTH Gram matrices (med = 1 if the median is 0). D = 1 - K (max K = 1 on the diagonal) is U-centred and stat = <U(Dx),U(Dy)>/sqrt(<U(Dx),U(Dx)> <U(Dy),U(Dy)>) with no square root. Since U-centring removes the constant and D has zero diagonal, this equals HSIC_u(K,L)/sqrt(HSIC_u(K,K) HSIC_u(L,L)) of Song et al. (probe: 0.7662620588623132 both ways). Returns 0 if a centred variance <= 0. Upper triangle mirrored.

deviation_from_documented: (a) The supplement and GitBook describe HSIC as 'an RKHS-based statistic' with biased and unbiased estimators; neither says that the returned value is NORMALISED (HSIC(x,y)/sqrt(HSIC(x,x) HSIC(y,y)), a correlation-like number), nor that the Gaussian kernel bandwidth is the median heuristic computed from the first argument only and reused for the second. (b) 'the unbiased (and consistent) estimator can be derived by double centering the kernel distance matrix [15]': citing [15] for an unbiased estimator is supported, since Gretton et al. 2007 eq. (3) is an unbiased U-statistic estimator (eq. (4) is the biased one). The deviation is the 'double centering' wording only: the code's unbiased estimator U-centres 1-K (equal to Gretton 2007 eq. (3) and Song et al. 2012 eq. (5) before normalisation), and double centring is what the biased variant does. (c) Labelled 'undirected' but the bivariate value depends on argument order (made symmetric only by mirroring). (d) The unbiased value is on the squared-correlation scale while hsic_biased is square-rooted; the documentation presents them as two estimators of one quantity. (e) Labelled 'unsigned' (config.yaml keywords; the GitBook glossary, glossary-of-terms.md:21, defines unsigned SPIs by the example of distance correlation 'defined in the range [0,1]') but can be negative.
deviation_from_canonical: (1) Normalised: returns HSIC_u(x,y)/sqrt(HSIC_u(x,x) HSIC_u(y,y)), not HSIC_u (probe: 0.7663 vs raw HSIC_u 0.0570 on the same arrays); dimensionless, bounded. (2) Bandwidth: median heuristic computed from x only and applied to y (hyppo/tools/common.py:321-333, 342-343); a separate median for each variable (the common reading of Gretton et al. 2007 Sec. 4, which does not state it explicitly) would give 0.7720 instead of 0.7663 on the probe pair (x ~ N(0,1), y = exp(x) + noise). (3) Consequently the estimator is not symmetric in (x, y). The unbiased centring itself matches Song et al. 2012 eq. (5), equivalently Gretton et al. 2007 eq. (3), exactly.
