metric_name_standard: Summary (time-mean or time-max) of the soft-DTW barycenter (gamma = 1) of two z-scored series; squared variant summarises its square
canonical_ref: Cuturi & Blondel 2017, ICML, PMLR 70:894-903 (soft-DTW, §2 eq. 1-2 and barycenter §4 eq. 4, Alg. 1-2 forward/backward recursions); bias of soft-DTW (sdtw_gamma(x,x) != 0): Blondel, Mensch & Vert 2021, AISTATS, PMLR 130:3853-3861. Mean/max summary: pyspi construction.
canonical_definition: b* in argmin_b sum_k lambda_k dtw_gamma(b, x_k), dtw_gamma(b,x) = -gamma log sum_{A in paths} exp(-<A, Delta(b,x)>/gamma), Delta_ts = (b_t - x_s)^2; smooth and differentiable, recovers the DTW barycenter as gamma -> 0; SPI = mean_t b(t) or max_t b(t) (squared: of b(t)^2).
documented_definition: supplement §1.2.10, p.7 (supplement.txt lines 321-335): "A barycenter (or Fréchet mean) [21, 22] is a (univariate) time series that minimizes the sum of squared distances between MTS ... For each pair of (bivariate) time series ... we compute the raw barycenters then summarize them by taking their mean (modifier mean) and maximum (max), yielding seven SPIs" (keywords: undirected, nonlinear, unsigned, bivariate, time-dependent). GitBook distance-similarity.md:41-75 repeats this, adds "timepoint at which the maximum occurs (max_time)" and lists 12 identifiers bary_{euclidean,dtw,softdtw,sgddtw}_{mean,max,max_time}; neither source documents the squared (bary-sq_*) variants. Mode softdtw is documented as "alignment via a differential loss function"; supplement §1.2.9 (p.6-7) gives the soft-DTW default gamma = 1.
delegate_lib: tslearn==0.9.0 tslearn.barycenters.softdtw_barycenter (defaults gamma=1.0, weights=None -> ones, method="L-BFGS-B", tol=1e-3, max_iter=50, init = Euclidean barycenter) via scipy==1.17.1 scipy.optimize.minimize, numba soft-DTW kernels
implemented_as: z-scored pair (ddof=1). Init b0 = (x+y)/2. Objective f(b) = sum_k sdtw_1(D(b,x_k)) with D squared Euclidean and unit (unnormalised) weights; gradient by the soft-DTW backward recursion and Jacobian 2(b_t - x_s)E_ts; scipy L-BFGS-B with ftol = gtol = 1e-3 and maxiter 50; res.x returned without checking res.success. gamma = 1 is fixed (pyspi exposes no parameter). Deterministic and order-invariant (probe2 order-diff 0). Then nanmean/nanmax of b or b**2.

metric_name_standard: GW-tau (GWτ) distance between time series: 2-Wasserstein distance between the distributions of intrinsic (arc-length) distances from the trajectory start, a Gromov-Wasserstein-type upper bound
canonical_ref: Kravtsova N, McGee RL II, Dawes AT (2023) "Scalable Gromov-Wasserstein Based Comparison of Biological Time Series", Bull Math Biol 85:77, doi:10.1007/s11538-023-01175-y (PMC10326159): Def. 1 Eq. 5 (GWτ, general case); Def. 2 Eqs. 6-7 (point sets X, Y), Eqs. 8-9 (polygonal arc length d_X, d_Y), Eq. 10 (empirical GWτ), with the uniform measures mu_X, mu_Y given as an unnumbered display after Eq. 9; closed forms Eqs. 11 (equal sizes) and 12 (unequal sizes, lambda_ij weights) in the proof of Prop. 1(e); Prop. 1(a) GWτ = W_p of root-distance push-forwards, Prop. 1(b) GW <= GWτ. Equation labels read from the Europe PMC JATS full text (ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC10326159/fullTextXML, <label> of Equ1-Equ12; the measure display Equ16 has no label); the journal PDF was not separately consulted. Authors' reference code: github.com/kravtsova2/GWtau, GWtau_tutorial/vec_geo_dist.m, wass_sorted.m, gwtau_tutorial_main.m.
canonical_definition: For a 1-D series {(t_i, h(t_i))}, i=1..n, the trajectory is f(t)=(t,h(t)) in R^2; X={x_i=f(t_i)} with uniform measure mu_X = sum_{i=1}^n (1/n) delta_{x_i} (unnumbered display in Def. 2); intrinsic distance d_X(x_i,x_j) = sum_{k=i}^{j-1} ||f(t_{k+1})-f(t_k)|| (polygonal arc length, Eq. 8); root r_X = f(t_1). GWτ_p(X,Y) = inf over couplings of (sum |d_X(r_X,x) - d_Y(r_Y,y)|^p mu(x,y))^{1/p} = W_p(d_X(r_X,.)#mu_X, d_Y(r_Y,.)#mu_Y), no factor 1/2; experiments use p=2. Equal n: W_2^2 = (1/n) sum_i (z_(i) - w_(i))^2 over sorted root distances (n values per series, the root's own value 0 included by the empty-sum convention of Eq. 8).
documented_definition: No supplement section covers gwtau (supplement.txt has no Gromov/Wasserstein/gwtau entry; it predates the SPI). GitBook distance-similarity.md lines 164-180 ("Gromov-Wasserstein Distance", base identifier gwtau, keywords undirected, nonlinear, unsigned, unordered, distance): "represents each time series as a metric space and computing the distances from the start of each time series to every point. These distance distributions are then compared using the Wasserstein distance ... making it robust to shifts and perturbations ... based on the algorithm proposed by Kravtsova et al. (2023)." Docstring distance.py:267 "Gromov-Wasserstain distance (GWTau)".
delegate_lib: pyspi (native numpy: np.diff, np.linalg.norm, np.cumsum, np.sort, np.mean, np.sqrt); a Python port of the authors' MATLAB functions vec_geo_dist.m and wass_sorted.m
implemented_as: Calculator default Data(normalise=True, detrend=False): each series z-scored with ddof=1 (data.py:193-195). For a pair (i,j), x=z_i, y=z_j (shape (T,1) from the 3-D data array). Trajectory (k, x_k), k=0..T-1 (sample index as time, unit step, amplitude in SD units). vec_geo_dist returns the T-1 cumulative segment lengths L_x(k) = sum_{t<k} sqrt(1+(x_{t+1}-x_t)^2), k=1..T-1 (the root, value 0, is NOT included). wass_sorted sorts both vectors descending and, for equal lengths (always the case in pyspi), returns sqrt(mean_k (L_x(k)-L_y(k))^2) over T-1 entries. Because every segment has length >= 1 the vectors are already strictly increasing, so the sort is a no-op and the value is exactly the RMS over time of the difference of the two cumulative arc-length curves. The unequal-length branch (quantile-overlap coupling lambda_ij, Eq. 12) is unreachable from pyspi. Undirected.multivariate computes every ordered pair and then copies the upper triangle into the lower.

deviation_from_documented: (1) Keyword "unordered" (distance.py:271, config.yaml:314-320, GitBook line 166): neither "unordered" nor "temporal" is defined anywhere in the documentation. The GitBook keyword table (spis/glossary-of-terms.md:21) defines Undirected, Directed, Linear, Nonlinear, Signed, Univariate, Bivariate, Multivariate, Contemporaneous, Time-dependent, Frequency-dependent and Time-frequency dependent only, and development/development/incorporating-new-spis.md:430,546 describes labels only as "descriptive keywords" used for filtering (that page uses gwtau's own label list as its worked example, lines 441, 516, 558). There is therefore no documented definition to deviate from. The inconsistency is with sibling usage: the value depends on the temporal order of samples through the increments x_{t+1}-x_t (probe: jointly permuting both series with one permutation changed the value from 13.527 to 5.126 at T=256), while the order-dependent distances in the same file carry "temporal" (dcorrx distance.py:119, mgcx :139, TimeWarping (dtw, lcss, softdtw) :156, bary :215; xcorr basic.py:78). Read as the opposite of "temporal", "unordered" does not describe the computation. (2) GitBook "distances from the start ... to every point": the code omits the start point itself (T-1 distances, not T). (3) GitBook "robust to shifts" does not say what is shifted (time, phase, amplitude). For time shifts it contradicts the cited source paper, whose design intent is the opposite: Kravtsova et al. 2023, section "Empirical Results on Synthetic, Model-Based, and Publicly Available Real-World Data": "GWτ is able to distinguish between shifts since a shifted version of a trajectory has a different distribution of intrinsic distances, and the larger the shift, the easier it is for GWτ to distinguish between the trajectories", and "successfully capturing time shifts as class indicators is a desirable property". The paper's only robustness statement is narrower: for oscillations with "slight phase shifts within the class", "Slightly shifted versions of qualitatively similar trajectories will be matched by an optimal transport routine producing a small distance". Separately, on sampled data even that narrower statement fails for a phase shift relative to the sampling grid (see candidates: sampled sinusoid at f0=0.25 shifted by pi/4 gives a distance growing ∝ T). The constant offset x -> x + c is the one shift the value is exactly invariant to (z-scoring removes it, and gwtau(z, z + c) ~ 1e-14 without z-scoring). Otherwise the computation matches the GitBook prose.
deviation_from_canonical: (a) Root exclusion: the paper's discrete measure is uniform on all n points including the root (distance 0); vec_geo_dist returns n-1 values, so for equal lengths pyspi = canonical * sqrt(T/(T-1)) exactly (probe T=256: canonical/pyspi = 0.998044963916957 = sqrt(255/256)). This is a constant factor at fixed T (ranking-preserving) and is inherited verbatim from the authors' own MATLAB vec_geo_dist.m. (b) Time coordinate: pyspi always uses sample index 0..T-1 with unit spacing against z-scored amplitude (an implicit time/amplitude scale ratio of 1 sample : 1 SD); the paper allows actual (unequally spaced) times t_i and does not prescribe normalisation; matches the authors' tutorial (time=(0:n-1)'). (c) p fixed at 2 (paper's experimental choice). Descending sort is equivalent to the paper's ascending Eq. 11 (both vectors sorted the same way). Otherwise none.
units_and_range: Non-negative real, unbounded, in units of the trajectory metric (samples combined with SD units after z-scoring); 0 for identical increment-magnitude sequences (e.g. x vs -x, x vs x+c). Not normalised by length: under independence the value grows roughly ∝ sqrt(T) (probe: mean over 20 iid pairs 4.09, 8.67, 15.2, 32.6 at T=64, 256, 1024, 4096). A pseudometric on series (zero for distinct series). No NaN for finite input with T>=2; NaN diagonal set by Calculator.
direction_convention: Undirected: A[i,j] = gwtau(z_i, z_j) = A[j,i]; formula symmetric in its arguments ((a-b)^2 == (b-a)^2 bitwise) and Undirected.multivariate mirrors the upper triangle (base.py:136-137). Probe: bivariate(i=0,j=1) == bivariate(i=1,j=0) exactly; A == A.T exactly on 5 datasets.

score_rubric_note: Anchor 8 names a constant factor such as T/(T-1): pyspi leaves the root out of the uniform measure, so pyspi = canonical * sqrt(T/(T-1)) (0.79 % at T=64, 0.012 % at T=4096). The authors' MATLAB code does the same.
what_changed: pyspi's output agrees with the authors' MATLAB GWtau formula (checked against an independent merged-quantile W2, POT and closed forms), which differs from the paper's Def. 2 by a constant factor at fixed T: the root point (distance 0) is left out of the uniform measure, so pyspi = canonical * sqrt(T/(T-1)) (rubric 8, constant factor; 0.79 % at T=64, 0.012 % at T=4096). The GitBook's "distances from the start ... to every point" also includes the start, so the same factor separates pyspi from the documentation. The descending sort is a no-op (every segment length sqrt(1 + dx^2) >= 1), so the value is the RMS over time of the difference of the two cumulative arc-length curves; the closed-form sinusoid references, which never sort, match to 1e-11. Properties of the canonical construction, measured here: the value grows about as sqrt(T) under independence, depends on the sampling rate because time is the sample index (unit step against z-scored amplitude), and depends on the phase relative to the sampling grid for oscillations at frequencies p/q with small q (f0 = 0.25). Labelling: the "unordered" keyword is inconsistent with the order dependence (siblings that depend on order carry "temporal"; the pdist SPIs, which are order-invariant, carry "unordered").

metric_name_standard: additive-noise-model (ANM) residual-independence score for the hypothesis x -> y: HSIC between the GP-regression residual of y on x and x (Hoyer et al. 2008); here a single-direction HSIC statistic
canonical_ref: Hoyer, Janzing, Mooij, Peters & Scholkopf 2008, NIPS 21:689-696, sections 4-5 (procedure; GP regression "using a Gaussian kernel and independent Gaussian noise, optimizing the hyperparameters", HSIC test with gamma approximation of the null, accept/reject both directions); HSIC_b: Gretton, Bousquet, Smola & Scholkopf 2005, ALT, LNCS 3734:63-77; gamma-approximation test statistic m*HSIC_b: Gretton et al. 2008, NIPS 20 (hsicTestGamma)
canonical_definition: Fit y = f(x) + n by GP regression with RBF kernel plus a white-noise term (hyperparameters by marginal likelihood); residual n_hat = y - f_hat(x); test n_hat independent of x with HSIC (p-value); accept x -> y if independence is not rejected and y -> x is rejected. A score version uses the HSIC statistic HSIC_b(n_hat, x) = (1/m^2) tr(K H L H) (lower = more consistent with x -> y).
documented_definition: supplement §1.3.1, p.8: 'we use the statistic from cdt as our SPI, which is computed by first predicting y from x via a Gaussian process (with a radial basis function kernel), and then computing the normalized HSIC test statistic from the residuals (see Sec. 1.2.5 above)'; keywords 'directed, nonlinear, unsigned'; cdt stated as v0.5.23 (supplement p.7). GitBook causal-inference.md 'Additive Noise Model' repeats the text.
delegate_lib: cdt==0.6.0 cdt.causality.pairwise.ANM.normalized_hsic -> FastHsicTestGamma; scikit-learn==1.9.1 GaussianProcessRegressor (default kernel, fmin_l_bfgs_b via scipy==1.17.1 scipy.optimize.minimize L-BFGS-B); the GP+residual step is pyspi's own monkeypatch AdditiveNoiseModel.corrected_anm_score (replaces cdt ANM.anm_score)
implemented_as: A[i, j] = corrected_anm_score(x = z[i], y = z[j]) on z-scored (ddof=1) data, single direction only (cdt predict_proba, which differences both directions and applies sklearn.scale, is NOT used). GP: GaussianProcessRegressor(random_state=42) with default kernel ConstantKernel(1.0, bounds 1e-5..1e5) * RBF(1.0, bounds 1e-5..1e5), alpha = 1e-10 jitter and NO noise kernel, hyperparameters by one L-BFGS-B run from theta = (0, 0). Residual r = gp.predict(x).reshape(-1, 1) - y. Score = normalized_hsic(r, x): both standardised (ddof=0), stride-subsampled to 200 points when T > 200 (indices floor(0 : m : (m-1)/199)), Gaussian kernels with sigma = sqrt(0.5 * median of positive squared pairwise distances) per variable, statistic = (1/m) * sum(Kc * Lc) = m * HSIC_b with m = min(T, 200); non-finite -> 0. Probe: on every tested pair the optimiser drives the RBF length scale to ~1e-5..8.3e-4 (max on anm_T64 pair 2 -> 3: 8.33e-4) (lower bound 1e-5, sklearn ConvergenceWarning), R^2 = 1.0 and residual std ~1e-10 with r ~= -(alpha / c^2) * y (median ratio 1.000001), so the score is essentially m*HSIC_b(y, x) of the raw pair. Exactly, r = K(K + alpha I)^-1 y - y = -alpha (K + alpha I)^-1 y, so the score is m*HSIC_b(x, standardised (K + alpha I)^-1 y); it equals m*HSIC_b(x, y) when K ~ c I (no x-spacings below the fitted length scale) and departs from it where near-coincident x values are smoothed together (check stage: contaminated, nonlinear_dependence_T64).

deviation_from_documented: (a) 'see Sec. 1.2.5' points to pyspi's hsic SPI (hyppo, normalised and square-rooted HSIC with x-only bandwidth); anm uses cdt's own statistic m*HSIC_b (m = min(T, 200), stride subsample to 200 points, per-variable median-heuristic bandwidth on squared distances), which is neither normalised nor bounded and scales with m up to 200. (b) 'Gaussian process (with a radial basis function kernel)' is accurate, but the GP has no noise term and its fitted length scale collapses to the 1e-5 bound, so the 'residuals' are ~1e-10*y roundoff-level quantities, not noise estimates (candidate below). (c) Class label 'linear' (causal.py:15) contradicts the documented keyword 'nonlinear' and config.yaml:329. (d) Documented cdt v0.5.23; installed cdt 0.6.0 (already documented). (e) Only one direction is returned; the documentation does not say that cdt's ANM decision (score(b,a) - score(a,b)) is not used, nor that lower values mean 'more consistent with i -> j'.
deviation_from_canonical: (1) Regression lacks the independent Gaussian noise term that Hoyer et al. 2008 §5 use; with alpha = 1e-10 the marginal-likelihood optimum interpolates the data (length scale -> 1e-5 bound, R^2 = 1.0), which is exactly the overfitting Hoyer et al. §4 warn 'may lead one to falsely accept models'; the resulting score tracks HSIC(x, y) of the raw pair rather than residual independence (probe: anm_T64 9/12 entries equal the plain m*HSIC_b(y, x) to 4 decimals, the exceptions being (2,0), (2,1), (2,3); max relative difference 0.09-0.24 across 5 datasets). (2) Returns the test statistic m*HSIC_b, not a p-value or a two-direction comparison. (3) HSIC computed on a deterministic 200-point stride subsample for T > 200. (4) Time-series samples treated as iid (as in the original method).
units_and_range: dimensionless; >= 0 (centred Gaussian Gram matrices are PSD); scales with m = min(T, 200) (statistic is m*HSIC_b), so values are not comparable across T < 200; set to 0 if non-finite; observed 0.078-0.35 on independent pairs (check stage) and 2-23 on strongly dependent pairs; not symmetric by construction but nearly symmetric in practice because of the collapse (anm_T256: A[0,1] = 8.017, A[1,0] = 8.201; A[2,3] = 22.16, A[3,2] = 20.03); NaN matrix if the Cholesky fails.
direction_convention: A[i, j] = score for the hypothesis i -> j (x = process i regressed onto, y = process j predicted); under the ANM principle LOWER means more consistent with i -> j. Code-derived; to be confirmed empirically on the anm dataset (x0 -> x1, x2 -> x3).

what_changed: The GP has no noise term, so the marginal-likelihood fit interpolates (length scale at or near the 1e-5 bound) and the 'residual' is r = -alpha (K + alpha I)^-1 y ~ -(alpha/c) y. The score is therefore m*HSIC_b(x, (K + alpha I)^-1 y), a near-symmetric dependence score between x and y, not the residual-independence statistic of Hoyer et al.; it ranks the cubic anm pair wrongly at T=1024 and the tanh pair at T=256 where a canonical ANM (noise kernel) recovers both. The statistic is m*HSIC_b with m = min(T, 200) on a stride subsample. The value is defined only to ~1e-6 relative (one ulp of the fitted constant, BLAS thread count, SciPy build) and to the optimiser's end point (1.2% on iid_gaussian_T256).

metric_name_standard: conditional distribution similarity (CDS) statistic: spread across x-bins of the mean-centred, discretised conditional distributions p(y | x) (Fonollosa 2016/2019)
canonical_ref: Fonollosa 2016, arXiv:1601.06680 (book version: Cause Effect Pairs in Machine Learning, Springer 2019, pp. 339-347), §2.1 (discretisation into 2*maxdev*sfactor+1 segments of sigma/sfactor, truncation at maxdev*sigma; sfactor=3, maxdev=3 for "almost all measures") and §2.3 (CDS formula)
canonical_definition: CDS(X, Y) = sqrt( (1/M) * sum_{y=0}^{M-1} var_x( p_n(y | x) ) ), where p_n(y | x) is the conditional distribution of Y given each (discretised) value x, normalised to zero mean and then quantised as in §2.1; var_x is the sample variance over x. Lower CDS(X, Y) is taken as evidence for X -> Y (used as a classifier feature in both directions).
documented_definition: supplement §1.3.3, p.8: 'The conditional distribution similarity fit [27] is the standard deviation of the conditional probability distribution of y given x, where the distributions are estimated by discretizing the values.' keywords 'directed, nonlinear, unsigned'. GitBook causal-inference.md 'Conditional Distribution Similarity Fit' repeats the text.
delegate_lib: cdt==0.6.0 cdt.causality.pairwise.CDS().cds_score(x, y) with defaults ffactor=2, maxdev=3, minc=12 (numpy/pandas only)
implemented_as: A[i, j] = CDS().cds_score(x = z[i], y = z[j]) on z-scored data, one direction only. x is standardised (ddof=0), re-standardised on the samples with |x| < 3, multiplied by 2, rounded and clipped to [-6, 6] (13 bins of width 0.5 SD). For each x-bin with MORE than 12 samples: y values in the bin are centred on the bin mean and divided by the global std(y) (ddof=0), rounded*2 and clipped to [-6, 6], histogrammed over the 13 values -6..6 and normalised to a pmf. With P the (n_bins x 13) matrix of pmfs, columns are centred over bins and the result is np.std of all entries = sqrt( (1/13) sum_k var_x,ddof0(P[:, k]) ). Returns exactly 0 if no bin has > 12 samples (CDS.py:190-191), and exactly 0.0 when exactly one bin has > 12 samples (P is then 1 x 13, CDS.py:194 centring gives all zeros, np.std = 0.0 at CDS.py:195). When several qualifying bins have identical pmfs the result is 0 only up to rounding of the column mean: exactly 0.0 for 2 identical bins, but up to ~2e-17 for 3 or 7 identical bins with non-dyadic pmf entries (probe cleanup/cdt_pairwise/ident_bins.py). Probe: from-scratch numpy version matches to <= 1.4e-17 on 6 dataset/T combinations.

deviation_from_documented: (a) The supplement's 'standard deviation of the conditional probability distribution of y given x' reads as the SD of Y | X; the code returns the variability ACROSS x-bins of the shapes of the mean-centred conditional pmfs (a pooled SD of probabilities), as in Fonollosa §2.3. (b) Parameters (0.5-SD bins, 13 levels, truncation at 3 SD, minimum 13 samples per x-bin) and the exact 0 returned when at most one bin qualifies (or the 0 up to rounding when all qualifying pmfs coincide) are undocumented. (c) Direction meaning (lower = more consistent with i -> j) is undocumented; cdt's two-direction difference (CDS.py:131-141) is not used. (d) Documented cdt v0.5.23 vs installed 0.6.0 (already documented).
deviation_from_canonical: (1) ffactor=2 (13 levels) rather than the sfactor=3 (19 levels) that Fonollosa §2.1 states for 'almost all measures' (whether CDS was one of the exceptions in the original jarfo code is an open question). (2) var_x uses ddof=0 (np.std) whereas the paper says 'sample variance' (ambiguous). (3) Implementation details not in the paper: x is re-standardised on |x| < 3 before binning; x-bins with <= 12 samples are dropped; exact 0 is returned when no bin qualifies (CDS.py:190-191) and, through the centring, when exactly one bin qualifies, or up to rounding when all qualifying pmfs are identical (CDS.py:193-195); the paper does not define CDS for fewer than two x-values. (4) Only one direction is returned (the paper uses both directions as classifier features).
units_and_range: dimensionless (SD of probabilities); >= 0, bounded above by 0.5; exactly 0 when at most one x-bin has > 12 samples (no-bin branch CDS.py:190-191, possible only for T <= 156 = 13 x 12; single-bin branch CDS.py:193-195, possible at any T when one bin holds all but <= 144 samples); 0 up to rounding (exactly 0.0 for two bins, <= ~2e-17 for 3 or 7) when all qualifying bins have identical conditional pmfs. Observed: anm_T64 all 12 entries (process 0 has no qualifying bin, max count 12; processes 1-3 have exactly one, max counts 16, 16, 18); iid_gaussian_T64 8 of 20 entries (rows 0 and 2, exactly one qualifying bin each, max counts 16 and 13). Invariant to positive affine rescaling of either input (internal standardisation); asymmetric.
direction_convention: A[i, j] = CDS(x = process i, y = process j): variability of p(z_j | z_i-bin); LOWER means more consistent with i -> j (cdt docstring CDS.py:92-93). Code-derived; to be confirmed empirically on the anm dataset.

metric_name_standard: regression error based causal inference (RECI) score: mean squared error of regressing the min-max-scaled effect on the min-max-scaled cause
canonical_ref: Blobaum, Janzing, Washio, Shimizu & Scholkopf 2018, AISTATS (PMLR 84):900-909, §2.2 eq. (1) (E[(E - phi(C))^2] <= E[(C - psi(E))^2] in the causal direction, variables scaled to [0, 1]), §4-5 (fit both directions, compare MSE; function classes LOG, MON a*x^n + b with n in [2, 9], POLY degree 1-9, SVR, NN; random train/test splits, MSE averaged over runs)
canonical_definition: Rescale X and Y to [0, 1]; MSE_{X->Y} = E[(Y - phi(X))^2] with phi the (estimated) regression of Y on X, MSE_{Y->X} likewise; infer X -> Y if MSE_{X->Y} < MSE_{Y->X}.
documented_definition: supplement §1.3.4, p.8: 'an estimate of the causal effect of x -> y by quantifying the error in a regression of y on x with a monomial (power product) model. In the bivariate case, this statistic is the MSE of the linear regression of the cubic (plus constant) of x with y'; keywords 'directed, nonlinear, unsigned'. GitBook causal-inference.md 'Regression Error-Based Causal Inference' repeats the text.

metric_name_standard: information-geometric causal inference (IGCI) score with entropy estimator and Gaussian reference measure: difference of 1-spacing differential-entropy estimates of the standardised variables
canonical_ref: Daniusis, Janzing, Mooij, Zscheischler, Steudel, Zhang & Scholkopf 2010, UAI (arXiv:1203.3475), §2.3 (IGCI rule: infer X -> Y if C_{X->Y} < 0), §3.2 (Gaussian reference measure), §3.5 eq. (12) (Kraskov et al. 2004 1-spacing estimator S_hat = psi(m) - psi(1) + 1/(m-1) sum log|x_{i+1} - x_i|), with preprocessing to zero mean / unit variance so that C_{X->Y} = S(p_Y) - S(p_X); Janzing et al. 2012, Artificial Intelligence 182-183:1-31
canonical_definition: C_{X->Y} = S_hat(Y~) - S_hat(X~) with X~, Y~ standardised (Gaussian reference) and S_hat the eq. (12) estimator; infer X -> Y if C_{X->Y} < 0, Y -> X if > 0; antisymmetric: C_{Y->X} = -C_{X->Y}.
documented_definition: supplement §1.3.2, p.8: 'Information-geometric causal inference [26] is a method for inferring causal influence from x -> y for deterministic systems with invertible functions. The statistic is computed using cdt as the difference in differential entropies where the probability density is computed via nearest-neighbor estimators.' keywords 'directed, nonlinear, unsigned'. GitBook causal-inference.md calls it 'Information-Geometric Conditional Independence' (as does the class name/name attribute).

deviation_from_canonical: (1) Returns -C_{X->Y} (cdt sign), so the canonical decision 'X -> Y if C < 0' becomes 'i -> j if A[i, j] > 0'. (2) Otherwise matches eq. (12) with the Gaussian-reference preprocessing of §3.5; zero spacings are skipped while the divisor stays m-1 (paper silent: eq. (12) is undefined when a spacing is 0 because of log 0; the skip-with-divisor-m-1 rule is cdt's eval_entropy, IGCI.py:42-56. The earlier statement that this is 'the same as the original Matlab-style estimator' had no cited source and is withdrawn: no original Matlab code was consulted in this audit. On quantised data this choice decides the value; see the tie candidate). (3) Applied to noisy, non-invertible and autocorrelated data outside the method's deterministic-invertible assumption (property of the method, not a code deviation).
units_and_range: nats (difference of differential-entropy estimates of unit-variance variables); signed, unbounded in principle, observed -0.52..+0.52 on the continuous check data and -6.35..+6.35 on logistic_maps_T1024 (period-4 y with repeated values: zero spacings are skipped while the divisor stays m-1); exactly antisymmetric; invariant to positive affine rescaling of each input (tests/README.md: igci differs between n1d0 and n0d0 by at most 3e-15); entropy of a standardised variable is <= 0.5*log(2*pi*e), so A[i, j] > 0 means z_i is closer to Gaussian than z_j.
direction_convention: A[i, j] = S_hat(z_i) - S_hat(z_j) = -C_{i->j}; POSITIVE means i -> j under the IGCI rule, and A[j, i] = -A[i, j]. Code-derived; probe on inline synthetic X ~ U(0,1), Y = X^3: A[x, y] = 0.772 / 0.845 / 0.902 at T = 256 / 1024 / 4096 vs analytic -C^G = 0.883.

what_changed: Matches Daniusis et al. eq. (12) with the Gaussian reference measure up to the sign convention: A[i, j] = -C_{i->j} (positive = i -> j). The deciding agreement is the 22 exact runs against the independent _kernels_distance.igci_ref (no cdt/sklearn), max abs 3.0e-14; the analytic cubic check is statistical and its 20-seed means (0.8746 / 0.8742 / 0.8741) do not approach 0.8832 (finite-sample bias), so check_method is independent-impl. Score mapping: anchor 9's clause 'trivial documented convention (... sign of a symmetric quantity)' is applied by analogy. The quantity is antisymmetric, so negating it equals transposing it (A[i, j] = -C_{i->j} = C_{j->i}), and the orientation agrees with pyspi's directed convention (Directed.multivariate evaluates A[i, j] with process i as the first, source argument, and a positive A[i, j] means i -> j). The convention is documented only in the delegate, in cdt's docstring (IGCI.py:138 '>0 if a->b'), not in pyspi's supplement, config or GitBook. The output is signed and exactly antisymmetric but the class, config and supplement label it 'unsigned'. Zero spacings (tied data) are skipped with divisor m-1 (cdt eval_entropy; the paper is silent). The check data contain no ties (every exact-run dataset is continuous), so the tie rule was not compared against the reference in a manifest run; a scratch probe reproduces it to 8.4e-15 on an EEG window. Scope: on quantised recordings this rule dominates the value. metric_name_standard: Convergent cross mapping (CCM) cross-map skill rho(L) = corr(X_j, Xhat_j | M_{X_i}) summarised over library sizes L (mean, max) and the directional skill difference (diff)
canonical_ref: Sugihara G, May R, Ye H, Hsieh C-h, Deyle E, Fogarty M, Munch S (2012) Detecting causality in complex ecosystems. Science 338(6106):496-500, main text and Supplementary Materials (cross-map estimate, simplex weights, convergence criterion); simplex projection: Sugihara G & May RM (1990) Nature 344:734-741; E selection by simplex forecast skill: Sugihara & May 1990 and Chang, Ushio & Hsieh (2017) Ecol Res 32:785-796.
canonical_definition: Shadow manifold M_X = {x(t) = (X(t), X(t-tau), ..., X(t-(E-1)tau))}. For each t take the E+1 nearest library neighbours x(t_1..t_{E+1}) of x(t) (t itself excluded), u_i = exp(-d(x(t),x(t_i))/d(x(t),x(t_1))), w_i = u_i/sum u; cross-map estimate Yhat(t)|M_X = sum_i w_i Y(t_i); skill rho(L) = Pearson corr(Y, Yhat|M_X) for random libraries of length L. Y causes X ("X <- Y") is inferred when rho(Y|M_X) increases with L and converges; the two directions are compared. Convergence, not a summary of the curve, is the causal criterion.
documented_definition: supplement §1.3.5, p.8-9 (pack lines 381-413): "there is a causal influence from time series x → y if the Takens time-delay embedding of y can be used to predict the observations of x"; E-None: "we infer the embedding dimension to be the maximum of the two univariate delay embeddings that best predicted each time series"; "we use 21 uniformly sampled library sizes between this minimum and maximum"; "summary statistics of the mean (modifier mean) and the maximum (max) across the curves"; keywords list "unsigned". The supplement lists six ccm SPIs (no diff). GitBook spi-descriptions/causal-inference.md (Convergent Cross-Mapping) repeats this text and adds "mean (mean), maximum (max) and difference (diff) across the curves" without defining diff; it lists all nine identifiers.

The result is bitwise identical to causal.ccm.E-10 (probe on var2_bivariate T=256: "mean E-None==E-10: True", "diff E-None==E-10: True"). deviation_from_canonical: (1) E is fixed at 10 instead of chosen by simplex forecast skill. The documented rule (one E = max(E_i, E_j) for both directions) is attributed by the supplement (p.9) to the Sugihara 2012 Supplementary Materials and the pyEDM documentation, and pyEDM/cppEDM take one E per CCM call; whether each direction should instead use the E of the variable being embedded is an interpretation, not a sourced canonical rule (no Sugihara 2012 passage prescribing per-direction E was located). (2) Convergence, the CCM causal criterion, is replaced by the mean or max of rho over L (documented; the mean includes the small-L part of the curve). (3) diff is a pyspi-specific antisymmetric skill difference, not part of Sugihara 2012. (4) tau fixed at 1 sample, no exclusion radius beyond self (Sugihara 2012 has no Theiler window either; later EDM practice recommends one). (5) Otherwise the per-library cross-map (E+1 neighbours, exp(-d/d_min) weights, Pearson rho, random libraries) matches Sugihara 2012 / rEDM practice (Sugihara 2012 does not specify a tie rule; when the (E+1)-th neighbour distance is tied, cppEDM CCM keeps the first E+1 entries of std::sort by distance with no tie expansion (the expansion in Simplex.cc L93-157 is gated to Method::Simplex, EDM_Neighbors.cc L282), so the neighbours chosen among equal distances depend on the implementation-defined sort order; this affects values only when neighbour distances tie, e.g. the period-4 process of logistic_maps).
units_and_range: Dimensionless Pearson correlations. mean and max in [-1, 1] (negative values occur; cppEDM returns rho = 0, not NaN, when either vector has zero variance, Common.cc L205-207); diff in [-2, 2] and antisymmetric (diff = mean - mean^T). Diagonal: 0 from a direct .multivariate call (ccmf initialised to zeros), NaN after Calculator.compute. Whole matrix NaN when cppEDM throws (short series). Not symmetric for mean/max.
direction_convention: A[i,j] = summary over L of rho(x_j | M_{x_i}): skill of predicting process j from the delay embedding of process i (pyEDM column "proc_i:proc_j", causal.py:143). By Sugihara's criterion a large A[i,j] is evidence that j causes i (j -> i), the transpose of pyspi's generic Directed orientation A[i,j] = i -> j (base.py:91-93; TE infotheory.py:377-383). diff[i,j] = mean_L[rho(x_j|M_i) - rho(x_i|M_j)] > 0 means j -> i dominates. Probe (logistic_maps T=256, process 1 drives process 0, E=2): A_mean[0,1] = 0.7415 > A_mean[1,0] = 0.3226, diff[0,1] = +0.4188. Confirmed in the check stage (the probe quoted above ran on the old period-4 logistic_maps fixture): on logistic_maps_chaotic (x = process 0 drives y = process 1 only) ccm_E-1_diff gives diff[1,0] = +0.0360 (dir-diff, pass) and the swapped input (processes [1, 0]) gives diff[0,1] = +0.0360 (dir-diff-swap, pass); ccm_E-10 at T=1024 gives mean A[1,0] = 0.5921 vs A[0,1] = -0.0512, diff[1,0] = +0.6432 (stats3-E10, T=1024); the delegate kernel at E=2 (full library) gives 'y xmap x' = A[1,0] = 0.8824 vs A[0,1] = 0.2909. So A[i,j] = rho(x_j | M_{x_i}) and a large A[i,j] is evidence that j -> i (row = target), the transpose of the glossary convention (glossary-of-terms.md:25-27, rows = sources) and of TE/GC (base.pair_handling|var2_bivariate|1024|pipeline|calls-gc_gaussian: row = source).

metric_name_standard: Convergent cross mapping (CCM) cross-map skill rho(L) = corr(X_j, Xhat_j | M_{X_i}) summarised over library sizes L (mean, max) and the directional skill difference (diff)
canonical_ref: Sugihara G, May R, Ye H, Hsieh C-h, Deyle E, Fogarty M, Munch S (2012) Detecting causality in complex ecosystems. Science 338(6106):496-500, main text and Supplementary Materials (cross-map estimate, simplex weights, convergence criterion); simplex projection: Sugihara G & May RM (1990) Nature 344:734-741; E selection by simplex forecast skill: Sugihara & May 1990 and Chang, Ushio & Hsieh (2017) Ecol Res 32:785-796.
canonical_definition: Shadow manifold M_X = {x(t) = (X(t), X(t-tau), ..., X(t-(E-1)tau))}. For each t take the E+1 nearest library neighbours x(t_1..t_{E+1}) of x(t) (t itself excluded), u_i = exp(-d(x(t),x(t_i))/d(x(t),x(t_1))), w_i = u_i/sum u; cross-map estimate Yhat(t)|M_X = sum_i w_i Y(t_i); skill rho(L) = Pearson corr(Y, Yhat|M_X) for random libraries of length L. Y causes X ("X <- Y") is inferred when rho(Y|M_X) increases with L and converges; the two directions are compared. Convergence, not a summary of the curve, is the causal criterion.
documented_definition: supplement §1.3.5, p.8-9 (pack lines 381-413): "there is a causal influence from time series x → y if the Takens time-delay embedding of y can be used to predict the observations of x"; E-None: "we infer the embedding dimension to be the maximum of the two univariate delay embeddings that best predicted each time series"; "we use 21 uniformly sampled library sizes between this minimum and maximum"; "summary statistics of the mean (modifier mean) and the maximum (max) across the curves"; keywords list "unsigned". The supplement lists six ccm SPIs (no diff). GitBook spi-descriptions/causal-inference.md (Convergent Cross-Mapping) repeats this text and adds "mean (mean), maximum (max) and difference (diff) across the curves" without defining diff; it lists all nine identifiers.

implemented_as: Default pipeline z-scores each process. E=None: for each process, pyEDM.EmbedDimension (simplex, Tp=1, lib = pred = rows 10..N-10, E = 1..10) is run and embedding[i] = embed_df.max()["E"], the column maximum of E, which is always 10 (known bug 2), so E = 10 for every pair. Then for each unordered pair (i<j) one pyEDM.CCM call with E = max(E_i, E_j) = 10, tau = 1 sample, Tp = 0, knn = E+1 = 11 (exactly E+1: CCM does not expand ties, see below), no exclusion radius (self excluded), 100 random libraries per size drawn without replacement (seed 42), library sizes lowerE = 20 to upperE = floor((T-11)/10)*10 in steps floor((upperE-20)/21), first 22 sizes kept. Each library size gives the mean over 100 libraries of Pearson rho between observed and cross-mapped values over all prediction rows (rows 9..T-1). ccmf[i,j,:] = rho(x_j | M_{x_i})(L); ccmf[j,i,:] = rho(x_i | M_{x_j})(L). Statistics: mean = nanmean over the 22 L, max = nanmax over L, diff = nanmean over L of ccmf - ccmf^T. The result is bitwise identical to causal.ccm.E-10 (probe on var2_bivariate T=256: "mean E-None==E-10: True", "diff E-None==E-10: True"). Neighbour ties: cppEDM tie detection runs only when parameters.method == Method::Simplex (EDM_Neighbors.cc L282); CCM builds its Parameters with Method::CCM (API.cc L659) and reuses them unchanged in colToTarget/targetToCol (CCM.cc L21-26) and in the per-sample local SimplexClass (CCM.cc L342), so ties/anyTies stay false, the tie expansion in Simplex.cc L93-157 never runs, and exactly knn = E+1 neighbours are used: the first E+1 entries of std::sort by distance only (DistanceCompare, Common.cc L10-13; EDM_Neighbors.cc L226), whose order among equal distances is unspecified (std::sort is not stable). Exactly-zero distances still get weight 1 with all others at the 1e-6 floor (Simplex.cc L57-70). On logistic_maps the embedded process 1 (period-4 driver, 4 distinct values) has a tie at the (E+1)-th neighbour distance at every prediction row (probe fable_dt3/fm2.py, T=256, full library: 256 of 256 rows at E=1, 247 of 247 at E=10), so the whole ccmf[1,0] curve on that dataset depends on which equal-distance rows std::sort places first. deviation_from_canonical: (1) E is fixed at 10 instead of chosen by simplex forecast skill. The documented rule (one E = max(E_i, E_j) for both directions) is attributed by the supplement (p.9) to the Sugihara 2012 Supplementary Materials and the pyEDM documentation, and pyEDM/cppEDM take one E per CCM call; whether each direction should instead use the E of the variable being embedded is an interpretation, not a sourced canonical rule (no Sugihara 2012 passage prescribing per-direction E was located). (2) Convergence, the CCM causal criterion, is replaced by the mean or max of rho over L (documented; the mean includes the small-L part of the curve). (3) diff is a pyspi-specific antisymmetric skill difference, not part of Sugihara 2012. (4) tau fixed at 1 sample, no exclusion radius beyond self (Sugihara 2012 has no Theiler window either; later EDM practice recommends one). (5) Otherwise the per-library cross-map (E+1 neighbours, exp(-d/d_min) weights, Pearson rho, random libraries) matches Sugihara 2012 / rEDM practice (Sugihara 2012 does not specify a tie rule; when the (E+1)-th neighbour distance is tied, cppEDM CCM keeps the first E+1 entries of std::sort by distance with no tie expansion (the expansion in Simplex.cc L93-157 is gated to Method::Simplex, EDM_Neighbors.cc L282), so the neighbours chosen among equal distances depend on the implementation-defined sort order; this affects values only when neighbour distances tie, e.g. the period-4 process of logistic_maps).

direction_convention: A[i,j] = summary over L of rho(x_j | M_{x_i}): skill of predicting process j from the delay embedding of process i (pyEDM column "proc_i:proc_j", causal.py:143). By Sugihara's criterion a large A[i,j] is evidence that j causes i (j -> i), the transpose of pyspi's generic Directed orientation A[i,j] = i -> j (base.py:91-93; TE infotheory.py:377-383). diff[i,j] = mean_L[rho(x_j|M_i) - rho(x_i|M_j)] > 0 means j -> i dominates. metric_name_standard: Convergent cross mapping (CCM) cross-map skill rho(L) = corr(X_j, Xhat_j | M_{X_i}) summarised over library sizes L (mean, max) and the directional skill difference (diff)
canonical_ref: Sugihara G, May R, Ye H, Hsieh C-h, Deyle E, Fogarty M, Munch S (2012) Detecting causality in complex ecosystems. Science 338(6106):496-500, main text and Supplementary Materials (cross-map estimate, simplex weights, convergence criterion); simplex projection: Sugihara G & May RM (1990) Nature 344:734-741; E selection by simplex forecast skill: Sugihara & May 1990 and Chang, Ushio & Hsieh (2017) Ecol Res 32:785-796.
canonical_definition: Shadow manifold M_X = {x(t) = (X(t), X(t-tau), ..., X(t-(E-1)tau))}. For each t take the E+1 nearest library neighbours x(t_1..t_{E+1}) of x(t) (t itself excluded), u_i = exp(-d(x(t),x(t_i))/d(x(t),x(t_1))), w_i = u_i/sum u; cross-map estimate Yhat(t)|M_X = sum_i w_i Y(t_i); skill rho(L) = Pearson corr(Y, Yhat|M_X) for random libraries of length L. Y causes X ("X <- Y") is inferred when rho(Y|M_X) increases with L and converges; the two directions are compared. Convergence, not a summary of the curve, is the causal criterion.
documented_definition: supplement §1.3.5, p.8-9 (pack lines 381-413): "there is a causal influence from time series x → y if the Takens time-delay embedding of y can be used to predict the observations of x"; E-None: "we infer the embedding dimension to be the maximum of the two univariate delay embeddings that best predicted each time series"; "we use 21 uniformly sampled library sizes between this minimum and maximum"; "summary statistics of the mean (modifier mean) and the maximum (max) across the curves"; keywords list "unsigned". The supplement lists six ccm SPIs (no diff). GitBook spi-descriptions/causal-inference.md (Convergent Cross-Mapping) repeats this text and adds "mean (mean), maximum (max) and difference (diff) across the curves" without defining diff; it lists all nine identifiers.

implemented_as: Default pipeline z-scores each process. E=1 for both directions: the "embedding" is the scalar x_i(t) (no delay coordinates), knn = 2 (exactly E+1: CCM does not expand ties, see below), Tp = 0, no exclusion radius (self excluded). For each unordered pair one pyEDM.CCM call; library sizes lowerE = 10 to upperE = floor((T-2)/10)*10 in steps floor((upperE-10)/21), first 22 sizes kept; 100 random libraries per size without replacement (seed 42); per size the mean over libraries of Pearson rho between x_j(t) and its 2-nearest-neighbour exponentially weighted estimate from x_i over all T rows. ccmf[i,j,:] = rho(x_j | x_i)(L); mean / max / diff over the 22 sizes as for every ccm unit. With E=1 this is a nonparametric contemporaneous regression skill of x_j on x_i, not a state-space (Takens) reconstruction. Neighbour ties: cppEDM tie detection runs only when parameters.method == Method::Simplex (EDM_Neighbors.cc L282); CCM builds its Parameters with Method::CCM (API.cc L659) and reuses them unchanged in colToTarget/targetToCol (CCM.cc L21-26) and in the per-sample local SimplexClass (CCM.cc L342), so ties/anyTies stay false, the tie expansion in Simplex.cc L93-157 never runs, and exactly knn = E+1 neighbours are used: the first E+1 entries of std::sort by distance only (DistanceCompare, Common.cc L10-13; EDM_Neighbors.cc L226), whose order among equal distances is unspecified (std::sort is not stable). Exactly-zero distances still get weight 1 with all others at the 1e-6 floor (Simplex.cc L57-70). On logistic_maps the embedded process 1 (period-4 driver, 4 distinct values) has a tie at the (E+1)-th neighbour distance at every prediction row (probe fable_dt3/fm2.py, T=256, full library: 256 of 256 rows at E=1, 247 of 247 at E=10), so the whole ccmf[1,0] curve on that dataset depends on which equal-distance rows std::sort places first. deviation_from_documented: (1) 22 library sizes, not 21; truncated at T=64 (10..52 of 10..60). (2) diff undefined in the supplement (GitBook names it only); code: mean - mean^T. (3) Keywords unsigned vs Signed class. (4) Orientation candidate: A[i,j] is evidence for j -> i. (5) The documented description of CCM as using "the Takens time-delay embedding" does not hold for E=1, where no delay coordinate is used.
deviation_from_canonical: (1) E=1 is not a delay embedding: Takens' theorem needs E > 2d, so the cross map is a 2-nearest-neighbour regression of x_j(t) on x_i(t); it responds to static (instantaneous) functional dependence without any dynamics (from-scratch probe on iid x1 = x0^2 + noise: rho(x1|x0) = 0.972, rho(x0|x1) = -0.032). (2) Convergence criterion replaced by mean/max of rho over L (documented). (3) diff is pyspi-specific. (4) Per-library cross-map algorithm otherwise matches Sugihara 2012 (E+1 neighbours, exp(-d/d_min) weights, Pearson rho) (Sugihara 2012 does not specify a tie rule; when the (E+1)-th neighbour distance is tied, cppEDM CCM keeps the first E+1 entries of std::sort by distance with no tie expansion (the expansion in Simplex.cc L93-157 is gated to Method::Simplex, EDM_Neighbors.cc L282), so the neighbours chosen among equal distances depend on the implementation-defined sort order; this affects values only when neighbour distances tie, e.g. the period-4 process of logistic_maps).
units_and_range: Dimensionless Pearson correlations. mean and max in [-1, 1] (negative values occur; cppEDM returns rho = 0, not NaN, when either vector has zero variance, Common.cc L205-207); diff in [-2, 2] and antisymmetric (diff = mean - mean^T). Diagonal: 0 from a direct .multivariate call (ccmf initialised to zeros), NaN after Calculator.compute. Whole matrix NaN when cppEDM throws (short series). Not symmetric for mean/max.
direction_convention: A[i,j] = summary over L of rho(x_j | M_{x_i}): skill of predicting process j from the delay embedding of process i (pyEDM column "proc_i:proc_j", causal.py:143). metric_name_standard: Convergent cross mapping (CCM) cross-map skill rho(L) = corr(X_j, Xhat_j | M_{X_i}) summarised over library sizes L (mean, max) and the directional skill difference (diff)
canonical_ref: Sugihara G, May R, Ye H, Hsieh C-h, Deyle E, Fogarty M, Munch S (2012) Detecting causality in complex ecosystems. Science 338(6106):496-500, main text and Supplementary Materials (cross-map estimate, simplex weights, convergence criterion); simplex projection: Sugihara G & May RM (1990) Nature 344:734-741; E selection by simplex forecast skill: Sugihara & May 1990 and Chang, Ushio & Hsieh (2017) Ecol Res 32:785-796.
canonical_definition: Shadow manifold M_X = {x(t) = (X(t), X(t-tau), ..., X(t-(E-1)tau))}. For each t take the E+1 nearest library neighbours x(t_1..t_{E+1}) of x(t) (t itself excluded), u_i = exp(-d(x(t),x(t_i))/d(x(t),x(t_1))), w_i = u_i/sum u; cross-map estimate Yhat(t)|M_X = sum_i w_i Y(t_i); skill rho(L) = Pearson corr(Y, Yhat|M_X) for random libraries of length L. Y causes X ("X <- Y") is inferred when rho(Y|M_X) increases with L and converges; the two directions are compared. Convergence, not a summary of the curve, is the causal criterion.
documented_definition: supplement §1.3.5, p.8-9 (pack lines 381-413): "there is a causal influence from time series x → y if the Takens time-delay embedding of y can be used to predict the observations of x"; E-None: "we infer the embedding dimension to be the maximum of the two univariate delay embeddings that best predicted each time series"; "we use 21 uniformly sampled library sizes between this minimum and maximum"; "summary statistics of the mean (modifier mean) and the maximum (max) across the curves"; keywords list "unsigned". The supplement lists six ccm SPIs (no diff). GitBook spi-descriptions/causal-inference.md (Convergent Cross-Mapping) repeats this text and adds "mean (mean), maximum (max) and difference (diff) across the curves" without defining diff; it lists all nine identifiers.

implemented_as: Default pipeline z-scores each process. E=1 for both directions: the "embedding" is the scalar x_i(t) (no delay coordinates), knn = 2 (exactly E+1: CCM does not expand ties, see below), Tp = 0, no exclusion radius (self excluded). For each unordered pair one pyEDM.CCM call; library sizes lowerE = 10 to upperE = floor((T-2)/10)*10 in steps floor((upperE-10)/21), first 22 sizes kept; 100 random libraries per size without replacement (seed 42); per size the mean over libraries of Pearson rho between x_j(t) and its 2-nearest-neighbour exponentially weighted estimate from x_i over all T rows. ccmf[i,j,:] = rho(x_j | x_i)(L); mean / max / diff over the 22 sizes as for every ccm unit. With E=1 this is a nonparametric contemporaneous regression skill of x_j on x_i, not a state-space (Takens) reconstruction. Neighbour ties: cppEDM tie detection runs only when parameters.method == Method::Simplex (EDM_Neighbors.cc L282); CCM builds its Parameters with Method::CCM (API.cc L659) and reuses them unchanged in colToTarget/targetToCol (CCM.cc L21-26) and in the per-sample local SimplexClass (CCM.cc L342), so ties/anyTies stay false, the tie expansion in Simplex.cc L93-157 never runs, and exactly knn = E+1 neighbours are used: the first E+1 entries of std::sort by distance only (DistanceCompare, Common.cc L10-13; EDM_Neighbors.cc L226), whose order among equal distances is unspecified (std::sort is not stable). deviation_from_documented: (1) 22 library sizes, not 21; truncated at T=64 (10..52 of 10..60). (2) diff undefined in the supplement (GitBook names it only); code: mean - mean^T. (3) Keywords unsigned vs Signed class. (4) Orientation candidate: A[i,j] is evidence for j -> i. (5) The documented description of CCM as using "the Takens time-delay embedding" does not hold for E=1, where no delay coordinate is used.
deviation_from_canonical: (1) E=1 is not a delay embedding: Takens' theorem needs E > 2d, so the cross map is a 2-nearest-neighbour regression of x_j(t) on x_i(t); it responds to static (instantaneous) functional dependence without any dynamics (from-scratch probe on iid x1 = x0^2 + noise: rho(x1|x0) = 0.972, rho(x0|x1) = -0.032). (2) Convergence criterion replaced by mean/max of rho over L (documented). (3) diff is pyspi-specific. (4) Per-library cross-map algorithm otherwise matches Sugihara 2012 (E+1 neighbours, exp(-d/d_min) weights, Pearson rho) (Sugihara 2012 does not specify a tie rule; when the (E+1)-th neighbour distance is tied, cppEDM CCM keeps the first E+1 entries of std::sort by distance with no tie expansion (the expansion in Simplex.cc L93-157 is gated to Method::Simplex, EDM_Neighbors.cc L282), so the neighbours chosen among equal distances depend on the implementation-defined sort order; this affects values only when neighbour distances tie, e.g. the period-4 process of logistic_maps).

Diagonal: 0 from a direct .multivariate call (ccmf initialised to zeros), NaN after Calculator.compute. Whole matrix NaN when cppEDM throws (short series). Not symmetric for mean/max.
direction_convention: A[i,j] = summary over L of rho(x_j | M_{x_i}): skill of predicting process j from the delay embedding of process i (pyEDM column "proc_i:proc_j", causal.py:143). metric_name_standard: Convergent cross mapping (CCM) cross-map skill rho(L) = corr(X_j, Xhat_j | M_{X_i}) summarised over library sizes L (mean, max) and the directional skill difference (diff)
canonical_ref: Sugihara G, May R, Ye H, Hsieh C-h, Deyle E, Fogarty M, Munch S (2012) Detecting causality in complex ecosystems. Science 338(6106):496-500, main text and Supplementary Materials (cross-map estimate, simplex weights, convergence criterion); simplex projection: Sugihara G & May RM (1990) Nature 344:734-741; E selection by simplex forecast skill: Sugihara & May 1990 and Chang, Ushio & Hsieh (2017) Ecol Res 32:785-796.
canonical_definition: Shadow manifold M_X = {x(t) = (X(t), X(t-tau), ..., X(t-(E-1)tau))}. For each t take the E+1 nearest library neighbours x(t_1..t_{E+1}) of x(t) (t itself excluded), u_i = exp(-d(x(t),x(t_i))/d(x(t),x(t_1))), w_i = u_i/sum u; cross-map estimate Yhat(t)|M_X = sum_i w_i Y(t_i); skill rho(L) = Pearson corr(Y, Yhat|M_X) for random libraries of length L. Y causes X ("X <- Y") is inferred when rho(Y|M_X) increases with L and converges; the two directions are compared. Convergence, not a summary of the curve, is the causal criterion.

direction_convention: A[i,j] = summary over L of rho(x_j | M_{x_i}): skill of predicting process j from the delay embedding of process i (pyEDM column "proc_i:proc_j", causal.py:143). metric_name_standard: Convergent cross mapping (CCM) cross-map skill rho(L) = corr(X_j, Xhat_j | M_{X_i}) summarised over library sizes L (mean, max) and the directional skill difference (diff)
canonical_ref: Sugihara G, May R, Ye H, Hsieh C-h, Deyle E, Fogarty M, Munch S (2012) Detecting causality in complex ecosystems. Science 338(6106):496-500, main text and Supplementary Materials (cross-map estimate, simplex weights, convergence criterion); simplex projection: Sugihara G & May RM (1990) Nature 344:734-741; E selection by simplex forecast skill: Sugihara & May 1990 and Chang, Ushio & Hsieh (2017) Ecol Res 32:785-796.
canonical_definition: Shadow manifold M_X = {x(t) = (X(t), X(t-tau), ..., X(t-(E-1)tau))}. For each t take the E+1 nearest library neighbours x(t_1..t_{E+1}) of x(t) (t itself excluded), u_i = exp(-d(x(t),x(t_i))/d(x(t),x(t_1))), w_i = u_i/sum u; cross-map estimate Yhat(t)|M_X = sum_i w_i Y(t_i); skill rho(L) = Pearson corr(Y, Yhat|M_X) for random libraries of length L. Y causes X ("X <- Y") is inferred when rho(Y|M_X) increases with L and converges; the two directions are compared. Convergence, not a summary of the curve, is the causal criterion.
documented_definition: supplement §1.3.5, p.8-9 (pack lines 381-413): "there is a causal influence from time series x → y if the Takens time-delay embedding of y can be used to predict the observations of x"; E-None: "we infer the embedding dimension to be the maximum of the two univariate delay embeddings that best predicted each time series"; "we use 21 uniformly sampled library sizes between this minimum and maximum"; "summary statistics of the mean (modifier mean) and the maximum (max) across the curves"; keywords list "unsigned". The supplement lists six ccm SPIs (no diff). GitBook spi-descriptions/causal-inference.md (Convergent Cross-Mapping) repeats this text and adds "mean (mean), maximum (max) and difference (diff) across the curves" without defining diff; it lists all nine identifiers.

deviation_from_canonical: (1) Fixed E=10 and tau=1 for every dataset instead of a data-driven E/tau (Sugihara 2012 chose E by simplex projection). (2) Convergence criterion replaced by mean/max of rho over L (documented). (3) diff is pyspi-specific. (4) No exclusion radius beyond self. (5) Per-library cross-map algorithm otherwise matches Sugihara 2012 (Sugihara 2012 does not specify a tie rule; when the (E+1)-th neighbour distance is tied, cppEDM CCM keeps the first E+1 entries of std::sort by distance with no tie expansion (the expansion in Simplex.cc L93-157 is gated to Method::Simplex, EDM_Neighbors.cc L282), so the neighbours chosen among equal distances depend on the implementation-defined sort order; this affects values only when neighbour distances tie, e.g. the period-4 process of logistic_maps). direction_convention: A[i,j] = summary over L of rho(x_j | M_{x_i}): skill of predicting process j from the delay embedding of process i (pyEDM column "proc_i:proc_j", causal.py:143). metric_name_standard: Convergent cross mapping (CCM) cross-map skill rho(L) = corr(X_j, Xhat_j | M_{X_i}) summarised over library sizes L (mean, max) and the directional skill difference (diff)
canonical_ref: Sugihara G, May R, Ye H, Hsieh C-h, Deyle E, Fogarty M, Munch S (2012) Detecting causality in complex ecosystems. Science 338(6106):496-500, main text and Supplementary Materials (cross-map estimate, simplex weights, convergence criterion); simplex projection: Sugihara G & May RM (1990) Nature 344:734-741; E selection by simplex forecast skill: Sugihara & May 1990 and Chang, Ushio & Hsieh (2017) Ecol Res 32:785-796.
canonical_definition: Shadow manifold M_X = {x(t) = (X(t), X(t-tau), ..., X(t-(E-1)tau))}. For each t take the E+1 nearest library neighbours x(t_1..t_{E+1}) of x(t) (t itself excluded), u_i = exp(-d(x(t),x(t_i))/d(x(t),x(t_1))), w_i = u_i/sum u; cross-map estimate Yhat(t)|M_X = sum_i w_i Y(t_i); skill rho(L) = Pearson corr(Y, Yhat|M_X) for random libraries of length L. Y causes X ("X <- Y") is inferred when rho(Y|M_X) increases with L and converges; the two directions are compared. Convergence, not a summary of the curve, is the causal criterion.
documented_definition: supplement §1.3.5, p.8-9 (pack lines 381-413): "there is a causal influence from time series x → y if the Takens time-delay embedding of y can be used to predict the observations of x"; E-None: "we infer the embedding dimension to be the maximum of the two univariate delay embeddings that best predicted each time series"; "we use 21 uniformly sampled library sizes between this minimum and maximum"; "summary statistics of the mean (modifier mean) and the maximum (max) across the curves"; keywords list "unsigned". The supplement lists six ccm SPIs (no diff). GitBook spi-descriptions/causal-inference.md (Convergent Cross-Mapping) repeats this text and adds "mean (mean), maximum (max) and difference (diff) across the curves" without defining diff; it lists all nine identifiers.

deviation_from_documented: (1) 22 library sizes, not 21; truncated at T=64 (20..41 of 20..50) and T=256 (20..230 of 20..240). (2) diff undefined in the supplement; code: mean - mean^T. (3) Keywords unsigned vs Signed class. (4) Orientation candidate: A[i,j] is evidence for j -> i. (5) Fails (all-NaN in Calculator) for T <= 60.
deviation_from_canonical: (1) Fixed E=10 and tau=1 for every dataset instead of a data-driven E/tau (Sugihara 2012 chose E by simplex projection). (2) Convergence criterion replaced by mean/max of rho over L (documented). (3) diff is pyspi-specific. (4) No exclusion radius beyond self. (5) Per-library cross-map algorithm otherwise matches Sugihara 2012 (Sugihara 2012 does not specify a tie rule; when the (E+1)-th neighbour distance is tied, cppEDM CCM keeps the first E+1 entries of std::sort by distance with no tie expansion (the expansion in Simplex.cc L93-157 is gated to Method::Simplex, EDM_Neighbors.cc L282), so the neighbours chosen among equal distances depend on the implementation-defined sort order; this affects values only when neighbour distances tie, e.g. the period-4 process of logistic_maps). Behaviour note (not a code defect): on stochastic linear data CCM direction readings are unreliable; probe on var2_bivariate T=256 (0 -> 1) gives A_mean[0,1] = 0.3208 > A_mean[1,0] = 0.0774, which under the Sugihara reading points to 1 -> 0.
units_and_range: Dimensionless Pearson correlations. mean and max in [-1, 1] (negative values occur; cppEDM returns rho = 0, not NaN, when either vector has zero variance, Common.cc L205-207); diff in [-2, 2] and antisymmetric (diff = mean - mean^T). Diagonal: 0 from a direct .multivariate call (ccmf initialised to zeros), NaN after Calculator.compute. Whole matrix NaN when cppEDM throws (short series). Not symmetric for mean/max.
direction_convention: A[i,j] = summary over L of rho(x_j | M_{x_i}): skill of predicting process j from the delay embedding of process i (pyEDM column "proc_i:proc_j", causal.py:143). By Sugihara's criterion a large A[i,j] is evidence that j causes i (j -> i), the transpose of pyspi's generic Directed orientation A[i,j] = i -> j (base.py:91-93; TE infotheory.py:377-383). diff[i,j] = mean_L[rho(x_j|M_i) - rho(x_i|M_j)] > 0 means j -> i dominates. Probe (logistic_maps T=256, process 1 drives process 0, E=2): A_mean[0,1] = 0.7415 > A_mean[1,0] = 0.3226, diff[0,1] = +0.4188. Confirmed in the check stage (the probe quoted above ran on the old period-4 logistic_maps fixture): on logistic_maps_chaotic (x = process 0 drives y = process 1 only) ccm_E-1_diff gives diff[1,0] = +0.0360 (dir-diff, pass) and the swapped input (processes [1, 0]) gives diff[0,1] = +0.0360 (dir-diff-swap, pass); ccm_E-10 at T=1024 gives mean A[1,0] = 0.5921 vs A[0,1] = -0.0512, diff[1,0] = +0.6432 (stats3-E10, T=1024); the delegate kernel at E=2 (full library) gives 'y xmap x' = A[1,0] = 0.8824 vs A[0,1] = 0.2909. So A[i,j] = rho(x_j | M_{x_i}) and a large A[i,j] is evidence that j -> i (row = target), the transpose of the glossary convention (glossary-of-terms.md:25-27, rows = sources) and of TE/GC (base.pair_handling|var2_bivariate|1024|pipeline|calls-gc_gaussian: row = source).

metric_name_standard: Joint differential entropy H(X_i, X_j) of the paired samples, Kozachenko-Leonenko estimate
canonical_ref: Cover TM, Thomas JA (2006) Elements of Information Theory, 2nd ed., Wiley, §8.4 (joint differential entropy h(X,Y) = -∫ f(x,y) log f(x,y)); estimator: Kozachenko & Leonenko (1987) Probl. canonical_definition: H(X,Y) = -E[log f_{XY}(X,Y)] for the joint density of contemporaneous pairs (x_t, y_t); KL estimate -psi(1) + psi(N) + log(pi/4) + (2/N) sum_t log(2 rho_t) with rho_t the Euclidean NN distance in R^2.
documented_definition: Supplement §1.4.1, p.10 (supplement.txt:444; the pack lists 454): "The joint entropy [33] quantifies the uncertainty over the paired observations"; keywords "undirected, nonlinear, unsigned, bivariate, contemporaneous"; SPI 59 je_kozachenko. canonical_ref: Cover TM, Thomas JA (2006) Elements of Information Theory, 2nd ed., Wiley, Ch. 8 (Def. 8.1/8.4.1 joint differential entropy); estimator: Kantz H, Schreiber T (1997) Nonlinear Time Series Analysis, CUP (box-kernel / correlation-sum density p_r(x) = (1/N) sum_n Theta(r - ||x - x_n||_max)); resubstitution entropy estimator: Ahmad IA, Lin P-E (1976) IEEE Trans. metric_name_standard: Conditional differential entropy H(X_j | X_i) of contemporaneous samples, Kozachenko-Leonenko estimate (difference of two KL entropies)
canonical_ref: Cover TM, Thomas JA (2006) Elements of Information Theory, 2nd ed., §8.4 (h(X|Y) = h(X,Y) - h(Y)); estimator Kozachenko & Leonenko (1987); Kraskov et al. (2004) Phys Rev E 69:066138 Eq. (20), k=1
canonical_definition: H(Y|X) = -E[log f(Y|X)] = H(X,Y) - H(X), here with X = x_i, Y = x_j (contemporaneous pairs).
documented_definition: Supplement §1.4.2, p.10 (supplement.txt:451; the pack lists 461): "Conditional entropy [33] quantifies the uncertainty over the observations in y in the context of simultaneously observing x"; keywords "undirected, nonlinear, unsigned, bivariate, contemporaneous"; SPI 62 ce_kozachenko. GitBook information-theory.md lines 46-62 (same text).
delegate_lib: JIDT jar (labelled 1.6.1, post-tag build matching commit a9b6b3e77c) EntropyCalculatorMultiVariateKozachenko.computeAverageLocalOfObservations, d=2 and d=1
implemented_as: A[i,j] = H_KL(z_i, z_j) - H_KL(z_i), i.e. the entropy of process j conditioned on process i (contemporaneous). The joint entropy is shared/cached with je (data.joint_entropy) and the marginal is cached in data.entropy keyed by estimator. Each term is a separate KL estimate (independent nearest-neighbour searches in R^2 and R^1), so the KL biases do not cancel as they would in a KSG construction. Directed.multivariate fills all ordered pairs. All T samples are used; no Theiler window.

deviation_from_documented: (1) Keyword 'undirected' (supplement, GitBook line 48, config.yaml:413) vs the code's Directed class and label 'directed'. The value is asymmetric by construction; REVIEW M8 already notes the conditioning order. (2) Label 'linear' (infotheory.py:53-54) vs documented 'nonlinear'. The formula itself matches the prose (y given x, with x = row i and y = row j).
deviation_from_canonical: None in the formula (H(X_i,X_j) - H(X_i) = H(X_j|X_i) exactly; probe3 reproduces A[0,1] and A[1,0] with a from-scratch KL to <= 3.6e-15 with noise off). Estimator level: the difference of two independent KL estimates carries an O(1) small-sample bias that a KSG-style conditional estimator would partly cancel (the supplement itself says this). Noise and naive-distance effects are as in infotheory.est.kozachenko; at d <= 2 the naive defect is negligible (var2 T=4096: 1.409 vs ref 1.409, probe6).
units_and_range: Nats; real, unbounded, can be negative (differential conditional entropy). Goes strongly negative for near-functional relations (shared_envelope copy x2 = x0: ce = -17.03 at T=1024, probe7, noise/tie dominated). Labelled 'unsigned'. Asymmetric.
direction_convention: A[i,j] = H(x_j | x_i): row = conditioning variable, column = variable whose uncertainty is measured (infotheory.py:248 joint(i,j) - entropy(i)). metric_name_standard: Causally conditioned (block) entropy H(Y^n || X^n) with block length n = 5, Gaussian model
canonical_ref: Kramer G. 1998, PhD thesis 'Directed information for channels with feedback', ETH Zurich, eq. (3.x) causal conditioning H(Y^N||X^N) = sum_{n=1}^N H(Y_n | Y^{n-1}, X^n); Ziebart B.D., Bagnell J.A. & Dey A.K. 2010, ICML (maximum causal entropy); Amblard P.-O. & Michel O.J.J. 2011, J Comput Neurosci 30:7-16
canonical_definition: H(Y^N || X^N) = sum_{n=1}^{N} H(Y_n | Y_1..Y_{n-1}, X_1..X_n) (X up to and including time n)
documented_definition: supplement §1.4.7, p.11 (supplement.txt:513-524): 'Causally conditioned entropy [42-44] aims to measure the uncertainty remaining in time series y in the context of the entire (causal) past of both time series x and y. The measure is computed as a sum of conditional entropies (of y given both the past of x and the past of y) with increasing history lengths. ... for computational reasons, we restrict the history length to 10. This corresponds to the assumption that the joint process is, at maximum, a 10th-order Markov chain.' Keywords 'directed, nonlinear, unsigned, bivariate, time-dependent'. GitBook information-theory.md:24-42 same text.

metric_name_standard: Causally conditioned entropy H(Y^n || X^n) of target j given source i over a block of n = 5 samples (Kramer), box-kernel plug-in under stationarity, bits
canonical_ref: Kramer G (1998) Directed Information for Channels with Feedback, PhD thesis ETH Zurich (Hartung-Gorre), Def. of causally conditioned entropy H(Y^N||X^N) = sum_{n=1}^N H(Y_n | Y^{n-1}, X^n); Massey JL (1990) Proc. ISITA 'Causality, feedback and directed information'; Quinn CJ, Coleman TP, Kiyavash N, Hatsopoulos NG (2011) J Comput Neurosci 30:17-44
canonical_definition: H(Y^n || X^n) = sum_{m=1}^{n} H(Y_m | Y^{m-1}, X^m), where X^m includes the current X_m; under stationarity term m = H(Y_t | Y_{t-1..t-m+1}, X_{t..t-m+1})
documented_definition: supplement §1.4.7, p.11 (supplement.txt:513-525; pack lines 524-536): 'Causally conditioned entropy [42-44] aims to measure the uncertainty remaining in time series y in the context of the entire (causal) past of both time series x and y. The measure is computed as a sum of conditional entropies (of y given both the past of x and the past of y) with increasing history lengths ... for computational reasons, we restrict the history length to 10. This corresponds to the assumption that the joint process is, at maximum, a 10th-order Markov chain.' identifier 84 cce_kernel_W-0.5; keywords directed, nonlinear, unsigned, bivariate, time-dependent. metric_name_standard: Lagged conditional entropy H(Y_t | X_{t-1}) of the target given the source's previous value ('cross-map entropy' in pyspi), box-kernel plug-in, bits
canonical_ref: No canonical 'cross-map entropy' in the literature was found; the computed quantity is the conditional differential entropy h(Y_t | X_{t-1}) = h(Y_t) - I(X_{t-1}; Y_t) (Cover & Thomas 2006 Ch. 8). The name evokes convergent cross mapping (Sugihara G et al. 2012 Science 338:496), which is not what is computed.
canonical_definition: h(Y_t | X_{t-1}) = h(X_{t-1}, Y_t) - h(X_{t-1}); box-kernel plug-in on the T-1 aligned pairs
documented_definition: Not described in the supplement (no xme section in §1.4, supplement.txt:405-549; pack lines 414-561) nor in GitBook information-theory.md. metric_name_standard: Lagged conditional entropy of the target present given the source past (pyspi 'cross-map entropy', history_length=10; actually 9 source lags), Kozachenko-Leonenko estimate
canonical_ref: No published definition of 'cross-map entropy' found. Closest standard quantity: the conditional differential entropy of the target's present given the source's past, H(Y_t | X_{t-1},...,X_{t-k}) (Cover & Thomas 2006, Elements of Information Theory 2nd ed. §8.4; h(Y|X) = h(X,Y) - h(X)). The name echoes convergent cross mapping (Sugihara et al. 2012 Science 338:496-500), but no cross-mapping is performed. Estimator Kozachenko & Leonenko (1987); Kraskov et al. (2004) Eq. (20).
canonical_definition: Reading 'history length k' as the k most recent source samples: H(Y_t | X_{t-1..t-k}); for k=10, conditioning on x_{t-1},...,x_{t-10} (joint dimension 11).
documented_definition: No supplement section (supplement.txt has no 'xme', 'cross-map entropy' or 'crossmap' entry). GitBook table-of-spis.md line 73 only lists 'Cross-Map Entropy', base identifier xme, with xme_kozachenko_k1 and xme_kozachenko_k10; information-theory.md has no xme section. Class name 'Cross-map entropy' (infotheory.py:396); config.yaml:439-446 labels 'unsigned, directed, time-dependent, bivariate'. The documented meaning of history_length is therefore only implicit in the identifier suffix _k1/_k10.

metric_name_standard: Lagged conditional entropy of the target present given the source past (pyspi 'cross-map entropy', history_length=10; actually 9 source lags), Kozachenko-Leonenko estimate
canonical_ref: No published definition of 'cross-map entropy' found. Closest standard quantity: the conditional differential entropy of the target's present given the source's past, H(Y_t | X_{t-1},...,X_{t-k}) (Cover & Thomas 2006, Elements of Information Theory 2nd ed. §8.4; h(Y|X) = h(X,Y) - h(X)). The name echoes convergent cross mapping (Sugihara et al. 2012 Science 338:496-500), but no cross-mapping is performed. Estimator Kozachenko & Leonenko (1987); Kraskov et al. (2004) Eq. (20).
canonical_definition: Reading 'history length k' as the k most recent source samples: H(Y_t | X_{t-1..t-k}); for k=10, conditioning on x_{t-1},...,x_{t-10} (joint dimension 11).
documented_definition: No supplement section (supplement.txt has no 'xme', 'cross-map entropy' or 'crossmap' entry). GitBook table-of-spis.md line 73 only lists 'Cross-Map Entropy', base identifier xme, with xme_kozachenko_k1 and xme_kozachenko_k10; information-theory.md has no xme section. Class name 'Cross-map entropy' (infotheory.py:396); config.yaml:439-446 labels 'unsigned, directed, time-dependent, bivariate'. The documented meaning of history_length is therefore only implicit in the identifier suffix _k1/_k10.

metric_name_standard: Directed information I(X^n -> Y^n) (Massey), block length n = 5, Gaussian model (pyspi variant)
canonical_ref: Massey J. 1990, Proc. Int. Symp. Inf. Theory Appl. (ISITA), 'Causality, feedback and directed information', eq. (6)-(7); Kramer G. 1998 PhD thesis ETH Zurich (I(X^N->Y^N) = H(Y^N) - H(Y^N||X^N)); Amblard & Michel 2011, J Comput Neurosci 30:7-16
canonical_definition: I(X^N -> Y^N) = sum_{n=1}^{N} I(X^n; Y_n | Y^{n-1}) = H(Y^N) - H(Y^N || X^N), with H(Y^N) = sum_n H(Y_n | Y^{n-1})
documented_definition: supplement §1.4.8, p.11-12 (supplement.txt:526-537): 'Directed information [42, 45] is a measure of information flow from a source time series x to a target time series y that is related to transfer entropy, but has no time lag between source and target [46, App. C]. The directed information can be computed as a difference between the conditional entropy of y given its own past, and causally conditioned entropy [42-44]. For the same reasons as for causally conditioned entropy, we restrict its computation up to a history length of 10.' Keywords 'directed, nonlinear, unsigned, bivariate, time-dependent'. GitBook information-theory.md:68-86 same text.

implemented_as: A[i,j] = sum_{m=1}^{5} H(Y^m)/m - cce(i,j), where H(Y^m) is the Gaussian entropy of the m-dimensional delay vector of x_j (T-m+1 samples, z-scored, ddof=1) and cce(i,j) is the CausalEntropy value (5-term sum, shared cache). The first term is a sum of block-entropy-per-symbol estimates, not H(Y^5) = sum_m H(Y_m | Y^{m-1}). Since H(Y^m)/m >= H(Y_m|Y^{m-1}) for every m, the code value exceeds Massey's DI by sum_{m=1}^{5} H(Y^m)/m - H(Y^5) >= 0, a quantity that depends only on the target's autocorrelation (for an AR(1) target with coefficient phi it equals 0.6417*(-ln(1-phi^2)) nats).

metric_name_standard: Directed information I(X^n -> Y^n) (Massey), block length n = 5, Gaussian model (pyspi variant)
canonical_ref: Massey J. 1990, Proc. Int. Symp. Inf. Theory Appl. (ISITA), 'Causality, feedback and directed information', eq. (6)-(7); Kramer G. 1998 PhD thesis ETH Zurich (I(X^N->Y^N) = H(Y^N) - H(Y^N||X^N)); Amblard & Michel 2011, J Comput Neurosci 30:7-16
canonical_definition: I(X^N -> Y^N) = sum_{n=1}^{N} I(X^n; Y_n | Y^{n-1}) = H(Y^N) - H(Y^N || X^N), with H(Y^N) = sum_n H(Y_n | Y^{n-1})
documented_definition: supplement §1.4.8, p.11-12 (supplement.txt:526-537): 'Directed information [42, 45] is a measure of information flow from a source time series x to a target time series y that is related to transfer entropy, but has no time lag between source and target [46, App. C]. The directed information can be computed as a difference between the conditional entropy of y given its own past, and causally conditioned entropy [42-44]. For the same reasons as for causally conditioned entropy, we restrict its computation up to a history length of 10.' Keywords 'directed, nonlinear, unsigned, bivariate, time-dependent'. GitBook information-theory.md:68-86 same text.

implemented_as: A[i,j] = sum_{m=1}^{5} H(Y^m)/m - cce(i,j), where H(Y^m) is the Gaussian entropy of the m-dimensional delay vector of x_j (T-m+1 samples, z-scored, ddof=1) and cce(i,j) is the CausalEntropy value (5-term sum, shared cache). The first term is a sum of block-entropy-per-symbol estimates, not H(Y^5) = sum_m H(Y_m | Y^{m-1}). Since H(Y^m)/m >= H(Y_m|Y^{m-1}) for every m, the code value exceeds Massey's DI by sum_{m=1}^{5} H(Y^m)/m - H(Y^5) >= 0, a quantity that depends only on the target's autocorrelation (for an AR(1) target with coefficient phi it equals 0.6417*(-ln(1-phi^2)) nats).

metric_name_standard: Directed information I(X^n -> Y^n) (Massey), intended as H(Y^n) - H(Y^n || X^n) with n=5; pyspi replaces H(Y^n) by a sum of normalised block entropies
canonical_ref: Massey JL (1990) "Causality, feedback and directed information", Proc. Int. Symp. Inf. Theory Appl. (ISITA-90), pp. 303-305: I(X^N -> Y^N) = sum_{n=1}^N I(X^n; Y_n | Y^{n-1}); Kramer G (1998) PhD thesis ETH Zurich: I(X^N -> Y^N) = H(Y^N) - H(Y^N || X^N); Amblard & Michel (2011) J Comput Neurosci 30:7-16. Estimator Kozachenko & Leonenko (1987); Kraskov et al. (2004) Eq. (20).
canonical_definition: DI_n = H(Y^n) - H(Y^n || X^n) = sum_{i=1}^n [H(Y_i | Y^{i-1}) - H(Y_i | Y^{i-1}, X^i)] >= 0, where H(Y^n) = sum_i H(Y_i | Y^{i-1}) is the n-block joint entropy of the target. It is zero when X and Y are independent.
documented_definition: Supplement §1.4.8, p.11 (supplement.txt:526; the pack lists 537): "a measure of information flow from a source time series x to a target time series y that is related to transfer entropy, but has no time lag between source and target ... can be computed as a difference between the conditional entropy of y given its own past, and causally conditioned entropy ... we restrict its computation up to a history length of 10"; keywords "directed, nonlinear, unsigned, bivariate, time-dependent"; SPI 86 di_kozachenko. GitBook information-theory.md lines 68-84 (same text). Docstring infotheory.py:505 "Compute directed information from i to j".

deviation_from_documented: (1) History length 5 instead of the documented 10. (2) The documented construction ('conditional entropy of y given its own past' minus CCE) corresponds to H(Y^n) = sum_k H(Y_k | Y^{k-1}). The code instead uses sum_k H(Y^k)/k, which is a different quantity. (3) Label 'linear' vs documented 'nonlinear'.
deviation_from_canonical: The target term differs from Massey/Kramer. For a stationary target with block entropies H_k, sum_{k=1}^n H_k/k >= H_n (H_k/k is non-increasing), with equality only for a serially independent target. pyspi DI = canonical DI + B, with B = sum_k H_k/k - H_n >= 0. B is not zero under independence of X and Y when Y is autocorrelated. For a Gaussian AR(1) target with coefficient phi, B = (H_5harmonic - 1) * (-0.5 log(1 - phi^2)) = 1.2833 * (-0.5 log(1-phi^2)): 0.185 nat (phi=0.5), 1.066 nat (phi=0.9). The gap di_pyspi - [H_KL(Y^5) - CCE] is, sample by sample, the KL plug-in of B (sum_k H_KL(Y^k)/k - H_KL(Y^5) on the same estimates; probe8 agreement <= 2.7e-4 nat, the residual being the 1e-8 noise). At T=1024 one realisation of that KL gap is noisy and seed-dependent: probe8, 10 seeds of independent AR(1) pairs, mean (sd, range) 0.040 (0.046, -0.039..0.116) at phi=0, 0.200 (0.069, 0.096..0.318) at phi=0.5, 1.036 (0.148, 0.881..1.414) at phi=0.9; the single probe4 draws were 0.034, 0.322 and 1.111. The Gaussian plug-in of B on the same targets (0.5 log det of the sample k-lag covariances) is tighter: 0.001 (0.001), 0.190 (0.020), 1.082 (0.081), close to the population B. Composition as coded is reproduced by a from-scratch KL to <= 1.4e-14 with noise off (probe3). At T >= 2005 the JIDT naive-distance defect corrupts the CCE term (probe6 T=4096 iid_gaussian: 2.614 vs reference 0.028; var2_bivariate 2.409 vs 0.574).
units_and_range: Nats; real, can be negative in estimates (probe7: delayed_noise reverse cells to -2.34; iid_gaussian T=64 down to -1.72), and strongly positive under independence when the target is autocorrelated (bias B). Canonical DI is >= 0. Labelled 'unsigned'. Asymmetric. Includes zero-lag coupling: X^i contains x_t, so instantaneous correlation contributes in both directions.
direction_convention: A[i,j] = DI from source i to target j (infotheory.py:505-510; target term uses z_j). var2_bivariate (x0 -> x1) T=1024: A[0,1]=0.614 > A[1,0]=0.134. delayed_noise (x0 leads x1 by 1): A[0,1]=5.76 > A[1,0]=-2.34 (probe7). gauss_ar1_pair (A[0,1]=0.3: x1 -> x0 stronger than x0 -> x1, 0.2): A[1,0]=0.767 > A[0,1]=0.49 (probe7).
