deviation_from_documented: (1) 'unsigned' keyword/label vs signed antisymmetric output (A[j,i] = -A[i,j]; already REVIEW M6). (2) 'bivariate' keyword vs implementation: the Benjamini-Hochberg threshold is computed over all channel pairs jointly, so a pair's delay (and whether it is NaN) depends on which other channels are in the dataset (probe: var2_bivariate T=256 full band pair alone -0.4725, same pair plus 5 iid channels NaN; narrowband_f0-0.1 T=256 full band -0.0277 vs -0.9866; gauss_ar1_pair T=1024 full band -1.793 vs NaN). (3) 'statistically significant coherence values' is implemented as: one-sided Fisher-z test with bias 1/8, BH-FDR 0.05 over all frequencies x pairs, then only the LARGEST contiguous significant run, decimated to every s-th bin, minimum 3 points; none of these rules is documented. (4) Frequency grid/endpoints as for PSI: n_fft/2 bins (not 125 bins from 4/T), strict endpoints so f = 0.25 is in neither half band and DC is excluded. (5) Missing outputs are frequent and undocumented: all-NaN pairs whenever no run of >= 3 'independent' significant bins exists (probe NaN fractions: iid_gaussian 20/20 for most T and bands, var2_bivariate 2/2 for the high band at T >= 256, narrowband_f0-0.25 6/6 at T >= 1024, logistic_maps 2/2 everywhere); bands with zero bins raise ValueError (whole matrix NaN) and bands with one bin give all-NaN (EEG bands 0.5-2, 2-4, 4-6 /1024 at T=512 and T=1024).
deviation_from_canonical: Core estimator (OLS slope of unwrapped coherency phase vs frequency over significant frequencies, divided by 2 pi) matches the canonical group-delay idea; intercept is free. Differences: significance is FDR-controlled across all pairs of the dataset (a pair's estimate depends on unrelated channels); only the largest contiguous significant cluster is used; the 'independent frequency' spacing is band-relative ((fmax-fmin)/50 rounded up to bins) rather than the multitaper resolution 2W = 6/T, so at T = 64 adjacent, strongly correlated bins count as independent (s = 1 < 6) and iid_gaussian yields spurious finite delays (probe T=64 full band: A[0,2] = 0.716, A[2,3] = -0.744), while at large T the spacing exceeds the coherence bandwidth of narrowband couplings so they never reach 3 points (narrowband_f0-0.25 all NaN at T >= 1024); phase is unwrapped across the whole in-band grid before masking (check stage: this does NOT change the slope, because the kept points lie in one contiguous significant run and a grid unwrap equals the run's own unwrap up to a constant 2 pi k absorbed by the free intercept; max difference 2.8e-14 over 125 replica runs); regression is unweighted (no coherence weighting). Gotman's exact selection and weighting rules are not re-checked (open question).
units_and_range: Samples (fs = 1; cycles/sample frequency axis), signed, unbounded in principle (|delay| limited in practice by the phase slope over the band); antisymmetric (A[j,i] = -A[i,j] exactly, probe max|A + A.T| = 0 when finite); NaN on the diagonal and for every pair without a qualifying significant run; whole matrix NaN when the band has no bins (exception).
direction_convention: S_ij = X_i X_j^*; if x_j(t) = x_i(t - tau) then arg C_ij(f) = +2 pi f tau, slope = 2 pi tau and A[i,j] = +tau. Probe delayed_noise T=256 band 0-0.25 (x0 leads x1, x2, x3 by 1, 3, 5): A[0,1] = +1.033, A[0,2] = +3.008, A[0,3] = +5.081, A[1,2] = +1.973, A[2,3] = +2.075, A[1,0] = -1.033. So A[i,j] > 0 means row i leads column j by A[i,j] samples. For var2_bivariate (X -> Y) the population group delay from the true spectrum is +1.13 samples (A[0,1] > 0, X leads); pyspi's A[0,1] = -0.47 at T=256 full band is a finite-sample artefact of the significance selection, not a property of group delay (check stage, popgd runs). Workflow 4b challenge probe (scratchpad wf4b_mid-eeg/gd_localslope.py): on the 7-bin run pyspi kept at T = 256 (f = 0.176-0.199) the true VAR coherency phase has local slope +1.53 samples (whole band +1.13), while the replica gives -0.4725 (full band) and -0.5550 (low band), so the negative sign is not a local property of the true phase.

what_changed: The estimator core (OLS slope of the unwrapped coherency phase, delay = slope/2 pi, A[j,i] = -A[i,j]) is the canonical group delay and is exact on pure delays, but which bins enter is decided by library machinery that neither the supplement nor Gotman 1983 (as cited) specifies: a per-bin Fisher-z test with only 5 tapers (power does not grow with T), Benjamini-Hochberg pooled over all channel pairs (a pair's delay changes or becomes NaN when unrelated channels are added), only the largest contiguous run, and decimation by the band-relative step ceil(((fmax-fmin)/50) n_fft) instead of the multitaper bandwidth (spurious delays on white noise at T=64 and in EEG bands at T=1024; narrowband couplings never reach 3 points at large T). Result: frequent NaN, unstable or wrong-sign delays for moderately coherent couplings (var2_bivariate). Signed and antisymmetric despite the 'unsigned' label (REVIEW M6). EEG consequence (elaborates the all-NaN cases of REVIEW M6): the retained selection holds 10 gd bands with edges at k/2048 cycles/sample; at the workflow window T = 1024 (2048 Hz, 0.5 s) the 0.5-2, 2-4 and 4-6 /1024 bands (1-4, 4-8 and 8-12 Hz) hold one bin each under the strict endpoint rule and are all-NaN by construction (spectral.gd|*|eeg:* runs), and at T = 512 they hold no bin (analytic bin count), so the delegate raises ValueError and the Calculator returns an all-NaN matrix (as observed at T = 256). Rubric anchor 6 (group-delay significance machinery).

metric_name_standard: nonparametric (Wilson-factorisation) spectral Granger causality, Geweke frequency-domain causality f_{j->i}(f), pairwise bivariate, summarised by mean or max over a frequency band
canonical_ref: Geweke J. 1982, J. Am. Stat. Assoc. 77(378):304-313 (frequency-domain decomposition of linear feedback; the f_{y->x}(lambda) formula, and (1/2pi) integral of f_{y->x} = F_{y->x} under his regularity condition); nonparametric estimation: Dhamala, Rangarajan & Ding 2008, Phys. Rev. Lett. 100:018701 and NeuroImage 41:354-362 (spectral matrix from Fourier/multitaper transforms, factorised by Wilson 1972, SIAM J. Appl. Math. 23:420-426). Equation numbers not re-checked against the papers (from memory; formula also in Ding, Chen & Bressler 2006, Handbook of Time Series Analysis, ch. 17).
canonical_definition: S(f) = psi(f) psi(f)^H (minimum-phase Wilson factor), Sigma = psi_0 psi_0^T, H(f) = psi(f) psi_0^{-1}; f_{y->x}(f) = ln( S_xx(f) / [ S_xx(f) - (Sigma_yy - Sigma_xy^2/Sigma_xx) |H_xy(f)|^2 ] ) >= 0, with S estimated consistently (spectral smoothing / tapers or trials growing with the data). Band summary (mean/max over a band) is a pyspi construction; the mean over the full band [-1/2, 1/2] approximates the time-domain Geweke F_{y->x}.
documented_definition: supplement §1.5.12, p.17 (supplement.txt lines 809-818: heading 809, quoted text 811-818): "Spectral Granger causality [40] is the frequency domain equivalent to Granger causality, computed via the spectral transfer matrix and noise covariance that are estimated using either a parametric (VAR model) approach [41] or nonparametric (spectral factorization) approach [57, 58]. We implement the nonparametric form from the Spectral Connectivity Toolbox [56] and the parametric implementation from v0.9 of NiTime [74]. The VAR model is estimated via least squares using the same order for both processes, where the order is either inferred (denoted by modifier order-None) or fixed. We infer a VAR model order from the Bayesian information criterion (with a maximum lag of 50, implemented in the NiTime toolkit), as well as choosing fixed orders of one (denoted by order-1) and 20 (order-20)." Keywords: "directed, linear, unsigned, bivariate, frequency-dependent". Band rule, supplement §1.5, p.12 (supplement.txt heading line 570, quoted text lines 589-599): "We use 125 uniformly sampled bins across the entire frequency range, f in [f0, fs/2] ... f0 = 4/T ... fmin-0_fmax-0-5: the full-frequency range, f in [0, fs/2]; fmin-0_fmax-0-25: f in [0, fs/4]; fmin-0-25_fmax-0-5: f in [fs/4, fs/2]"; summary = mean or max over the band. Same text on GitBook spectral.md:350-358 (Spectral Granger Causality). Matrix convention for directed SPIs, GitBook glossary-of-terms.md:27: "entry calc.table[...][0,1] will be the directed information from process 0 to process 1. The rows in this table reflect the sources while the columns reflect the targets." Refs: [40] Granger 1969 Econometrica 37:424; [41] Geweke 1982 JASA 77:304; [56] spectral_connectivity (Denovellis et al.); [57,58] Dhamala, Rangarajan & Ding 2008 NeuroImage 41:354 and PRL 100:018701; [74] Rokem et al. NiTime.

implemented_as: Input z-scored per channel (ddof=1; optional detrend). Whole (T x P) array transformed once by a single-window multitaper DFT: NW=3, 5 DPSS tapers, constant detrend, n_fft = next_fast_len(T) = T (no zero padding), fs=1; cross-spectral matrix = mean over the 5 tapers (one trial). For each unordered pair the 2x2 two-sided CSM is Wilson-factorised (tol 1e-8, <= 60 iterations, warning only), Sigma and H derived from the factor, and predictive_power[k,l] = ln S_kk - ln(S_kk - (Sigma_ll - Sigma_kl^2/Sigma_kk)|H_kl|^2) = Geweke causality FROM l TO k, with S_kk the multitaper auto-spectrum; values <= 0 and logs of negative intrinsic power become NaN. Frequencies k/T for k = 0..T/2-1 (Nyquist dropped). pyspi forces fmin <= 0 to 1e-5 (excludes DC), keeps fmin <= f <= fmax (both inclusive; 0.25 bin in both half-bands), takes np.nanmean or np.nanmax over the kept bins per cell, NaNs cells with > 50% NaN bins, and returns A[a, b] = summary of predictive_power[a, b] = GC from b to a. Pairwise bivariate (no conditioning on third processes).

deviation_from_documented: (1) Direction: documented matrix convention is rows = sources, columns = targets (glossary-of-terms.md:27); implemented A[i, j] = GC from j to i (target-by-source). Probe var2_bivariate (true 0 -> 1 only): T=4096 A[0,1]=0.1231, A[1,0]=0.4024; delayed_noise T=1024 (x0 leads): column 0 of rows 1-3 = 2.57, 2.56, 2.75 while row 0 = 0.11-0.13. (2) Frequency grid: documented "125 uniformly sampled bins across f in [f0, fs/2], f0 = 4/T"; implemented T/2 - 1 bins k/T, k = 1..T/2-1 for the full band (31 at T=64, 127 at T=256, 2047 at T=4096; probe), DC excluded by the fmin override, Nyquist excluded by the library slice (the Nyquist drop is already documented: DEPENDENCY_COMPATIBILITY_REVIEW.md, REVIEW M4). (3) Identifiers with "fmin-0" run with fmin = 1e-5 (spectral.py:343-345), so the documented band [0, fs/2] actually excludes the DC bin. (4) "values <= 0 -> NaN" and the >50%-NaN cell rule are undocumented; NaN bins are silently dropped from the mean/max (nanmean/nanmax). (5) Not documented: when the Cholesky initialisation fails (e.g. two identical channels) the run raises AttributeError and the whole matrix is NaN in the Calculator (probe shared_envelope T=256, x2 == x0).
deviation_from_canonical: Formula per frequency matches Geweke 1982 / Dhamala 2008 (rotated noise variance, |H_xy|^2), and the kernel reproduces Sigma to 1e-6 on an exact VAR spectrum (probe: Wilson on the exact two-sided var2 spectrum, reconstruction rel. error 3e-9, Sigma_hat = Sigma). Value-changing estimator choices: spectral estimate from a single window with only 5 tapers (fixed NW=3) whatever T, so the per-frequency estimate has ~10 degrees of freedom and its positive bias does not shrink with T (probe iid_gaussian null: full-band mean 0.146/0.106 at T=256, 0.127/0.121 at T=4096; with NW=10 (19 tapers) 0.025, NW=40 (78 tapers) 0.0044 at T=4096); no zero padding (n_fft = T), and the Wilson factor of the rough single-window estimate does not reproduce S (probe: max |psi psi^H - S|/max|S| 3e-3 to 0.38 across datasets, with NaN bins and "Maximum iterations reached" on logistic_maps T>=1024 and trending T=256/1024), while S_kk in the formula is the raw multitaper auto-spectrum, so S and the factor disagree. Pairwise bivariate, not conditional (canonical for a bivariate definition). Band mean/max is a pyspi construction (no canonical summary); the mean over (0, 1/2) excluding DC and Nyquist approximates, but is not, the time-domain F.
units_and_range: nats (natural log), per-frequency >= 0 in theory; output >= 0 or NaN (non-positive bins are NaN, then dropped); unbounded above; finite-sample null level about 0.1-0.15 nats with the default 5 tapers. Directed, asymmetric. Diagonal NaN.
direction_convention: A[i, j] = spectral GC from process j (source, column) to process i (target, row), i.e. TARGET-by-SOURCE, the transpose of the documented sources-in-rows convention (GitBook glossary-of-terms.md:27) and of other pyspi directed SPIs (e.g. infotheory.py:274 src, targ = data[[i, j]]). score_rubric_note: Anchor 7 names the expectation over 5 tapers. The band bias is about 0.125 nats and does not fall with T (conv 0.128/0.126/0.125).
what_changed: The per-frequency quantity is Geweke's (1982) spectral GC from the Wilson factors of the multitaper CSM (Dhamala, Rangarajan & Ding 2008), reproduced fp-exactly from scratch and on an exact spectrum. The value-changing difference from the canonical consistent estimator is the spectral estimate: one window, NW = 3, 5 tapers whatever T, about 10 degrees of freedom per bin, so the band statistic carries a positive bias of about 0.125 nats that does not decrease with T (conv runs; the bias falls to 0.023 / 0.005 with 19 / 78 tapers). Rubric anchor 7 ('expectation over 5 tapers'): matches the supplement's 'nonparametric form from the Spectral Connectivity Toolbox' but differs from the canonical estimator in a value-changing way. Also: A[i, j] = GC j -> i (row = target), the transpose of the glossary convention; bins k/T with DC excluded by the fmin override and Nyquist dropped (not the documented 125 bins); NaN bins (values <= 0, including every bin of an exactly zero GC) are dropped by nanmean/nanmax; a duplicated channel either aborts the whole SPI with AttributeError (numpy >= 2.4 as checked: minimum_phase_decomposition.py:48) or, depending on round-off, returns finite values for the copy pair.

A batch must keep (b) as a whole-SPI failure or record the change. The random start from the global numpy RNG (minimum_phase_decomposition.py:54-63), which in a batched call would hit every pair, is reachable only under a numpy that still has the deprecated numpy.linalg.linalg shim (numpy < 2.4 as checked: 2.2.6 and 2.3.3 resolve xp.linalg.linalg.LinAlgError with a DeprecationWarning, 2.4.6 and 2.5.4 raise AttributeError) or a spectral_connectivity release whose handler catches xp.linalg.LinAlgError; that rng-stream risk is conditional on such a numpy or library version and does not apply in this environment (pyproject.toml pins numpy>=2.5.4,<2.6)

metric_name_standard: parametric (VAR) spectral Granger causality with BIC-selected order (nitime), Geweke f_{j->i}(f), pairwise bivariate, band mean or max
canonical_ref: Geweke J. 1982, J. Am. Stat. Assoc. 77(378):304-313 (frequency-domain causality f_{y->x}(lambda) from a bivariate VAR); VAR estimation: OLS or Yule-Walker/Whittle (Whittle 1963 Biometrika 50:129-134; LWR recursion Morf, Vieira & Kailath 1978 Ann. Statist. 6:643-648; Lutkepohl 2005, New Introduction to Multiple Time Series Analysis, ch. 3); order selection: Schwarz 1978 Ann. Statist. 6:461-464, VAR form Lutkepohl 2005 §4.3 (global minimum over 0..p_max); Ding, Chen & Bressler 2006 (q-bio/0608035) eq. (51) as cited by nitime. Equation/section numbers not re-checked against the texts (from memory).
canonical_definition: Fit x_t = sum_{k=1}^{p} A_k x_{t-k} + e_t (p selected by BIC, global minimum), Sigma = Cov(e); H(f) = (I - sum_k A_k e^{-i 2 pi f k})^{-1}, S = H Sigma H^H; f_{y->x}(f) = ln( S_xx(f) / [ S_xx(f) - (Sigma_yy - Sigma_xy^2/Sigma_xx) |H_xy(f)|^2 ] ) >= 0. Band mean/max is a pyspi construction; the full-band mean approximates the time-domain Geweke F_{y->x} = ln(Sigma_xx^restricted / Sigma_xx).
documented_definition: supplement §1.5.12, p.17 (supplement.txt lines 809-818: heading 809, quoted text 811-818): "Spectral Granger causality [40] is the frequency domain equivalent to Granger causality, computed via the spectral transfer matrix and noise covariance that are estimated using either a parametric (VAR model) approach [41] or nonparametric (spectral factorization) approach [57, 58]. We implement the nonparametric form from the Spectral Connectivity Toolbox [56] and the parametric implementation from v0.9 of NiTime [74]. The VAR model is estimated via least squares using the same order for both processes, where the order is either inferred (denoted by modifier order-None) or fixed. We infer a VAR model order from the Bayesian information criterion (with a maximum lag of 50, implemented in the NiTime toolkit), as well as choosing fixed orders of one (denoted by order-1) and 20 (order-20)." Keywords: "directed, linear, unsigned, bivariate, frequency-dependent". Band rule, supplement §1.5, p.12 (supplement.txt heading line 570, quoted text lines 589-599): "We use 125 uniformly sampled bins across the entire frequency range, f in [f0, fs/2] ... f0 = 4/T ... fmin-0_fmax-0-5: the full-frequency range, f in [0, fs/2]; fmin-0_fmax-0-25: f in [0, fs/4]; fmin-0-25_fmax-0-5: f in [fs/4, fs/2]"; summary = mean or max over the band. Same text on GitBook spectral.md:350-358 (Spectral Granger Causality). Matrix convention for directed SPIs, GitBook glossary-of-terms.md:27: "entry calc.table[...][0,1] will be the directed information from process 0 to process 1. The rows in this table reflect the sources while the columns reflect the targets." Refs: [40] Granger 1969 Econometrica 37:424; [41] Geweke 1982 JASA 77:304; [56] spectral_connectivity (Denovellis et al.); [57,58] Dhamala, Rangarajan & Ding 2008 NeuroImage 41:354 and PRL 100:018701; [74] Rokem et al. NiTime.

implemented_as: Input z-scored per channel (ddof=1; optional detrend). For each pair (i<j) the order is chosen by nitime: for lag = 1..49 fit VAR(lag-1) by LWR on the N-k autocovariances, BIC = 2 ln det(ecov) + 8 m ln(2T)/(2T), stop at the first increase and keep the previous order (orders 0..48 fitted but only 0..47 returnable (check stage: the last fitted order is never returned, a BIC still decreasing at order 48 raises ValueError); order 0 gives GC identically 0); if no increase occurs (including when BIC is NaN because det(ecov) <= 0) nitime raises ValueError (see the error path below). From (a, ecov) nitime evaluates H on omega_k = pi k/513 (scipy freqz, Nyquist excluded) and Geweke f_{x->y}, f_{y->x} on that grid, labelled with get_freqs = k/1024 (k = 0..512, label 0.5 at the last point). pyspi builds F[a,b] = GC a -> b, then transposes so cache[0,f,a,b] = GC b -> a; keeps labels 1e-5 <= f <= fmax (DC excluded by the fmin override, both ends inclusive), np.nanmean/np.nanmax per cell, NaN where > 50% of bins are NaN; any ValueError (BIC non-termination, singular LWR matrix) reaches the handler at spectral.py:438-440, whose warnings.warn(err) at :439 raises TypeError under the message-regex warnings filters numpy installs on import, so a direct multivariate() call raises TypeError and Calculator.compute sets the whole table to NaN (calculator.py:336-337); the intended all-NaN return at :440 happens only under catch_warnings(record=True)+simplefilter("always") or resetwarnings(). A[i, j] = band summary of GC from j to i. No mean removal inside nitime (relies on z-scoring).

metric_name_standard: parametric (VAR) spectral Granger causality with BIC-selected order (nitime), Geweke f_{j->i}(f), pairwise bivariate, band mean or max
canonical_ref: Geweke J. 1982, J. Am. Stat. Assoc. 77(378):304-313 (frequency-domain causality f_{y->x}(lambda) from a bivariate VAR); VAR estimation: OLS or Yule-Walker/Whittle (Whittle 1963 Biometrika 50:129-134; LWR recursion Morf, Vieira & Kailath 1978 Ann. Statist. 6:643-648; Lutkepohl 2005, New Introduction to Multiple Time Series Analysis, ch. 3); order selection: Schwarz 1978 Ann. Statist. 6:461-464, VAR form Lutkepohl 2005 §4.3 (global minimum over 0..p_max); Ding, Chen & Bressler 2006 (q-bio/0608035) eq. (51) as cited by nitime. Equation/section numbers not re-checked against the texts (from memory).
canonical_definition: Fit x_t = sum_{k=1}^{p} A_k x_{t-k} + e_t (p selected by BIC, global minimum), Sigma = Cov(e); H(f) = (I - sum_k A_k e^{-i 2 pi f k})^{-1}, S = H Sigma H^H; f_{y->x}(f) = ln( S_xx(f) / [ S_xx(f) - (Sigma_yy - Sigma_xy^2/Sigma_xx) |H_xy(f)|^2 ] ) >= 0. Band mean/max is a pyspi construction; the full-band mean approximates the time-domain Geweke F_{y->x} = ln(Sigma_xx^restricted / Sigma_xx).
documented_definition: supplement §1.5.12, p.17 (supplement.txt lines 809-818: heading 809, quoted text 811-818): "Spectral Granger causality [40] is the frequency domain equivalent to Granger causality, computed via the spectral transfer matrix and noise covariance that are estimated using either a parametric (VAR model) approach [41] or nonparametric (spectral factorization) approach [57, 58]. We implement the nonparametric form from the Spectral Connectivity Toolbox [56] and the parametric implementation from v0.9 of NiTime [74]. The VAR model is estimated via least squares using the same order for both processes, where the order is either inferred (denoted by modifier order-None) or fixed. We infer a VAR model order from the Bayesian information criterion (with a maximum lag of 50, implemented in the NiTime toolkit), as well as choosing fixed orders of one (denoted by order-1) and 20 (order-20)." Keywords: "directed, linear, unsigned, bivariate, frequency-dependent". deviation_from_canonical: Per-frequency formula is Geweke 1982 (nitime autoregressive.py:485-509, standard rotated-noise form). Value-changing differences: VAR coefficients from LWR on the N-k-divisor, non-demeaned autocovariances instead of OLS or the positive-definite biased (divisor N) Yule-Walker; evaluation grid off by a factor 1024/1026 relative to its labels; pairwise bivariate VAR. Order selection is not standard BIC: (a) first local minimum instead of global minimum over 0..p_max, (b) penalty with Ntotal = 2T (n_process * T) gives 2 p^2 m ln(2T)/(2T), about half the standard VAR Schwarz penalty (Lutkepohl 2005 SC(m) = ln det Sigma_m + m K^2 ln T / T, doubled: 2 p^2 m ln T / T); nitime deviates from its own stated definition here: the bayesian_information_criterion docstring (.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/nitime/utils.py:2348-2358, "an implementation of equation (51) in Ding et al. (2006)") defines N_total as "the number of time-points", i.e. T, while granger.py:38 passes Ntotal = n_process * x1.shape[-1] = 2T; how Ding et al. 2006 eq. (51) itself counts channels is a secondary question (not re-checked against the paper). Order 0 is admissible and yields GC = 0 exactly. Probe delayed_noise (x0 leads by 1, 3, 5): T >= 256 every pair with relative delay >= 2 gets order 0 and A = 0 exactly; only x0 -> x1 is detected (A[1,0] = 4.71 at T=1024). Band mean/max is a pyspi construction.

score_rubric_note: Anchor 6: the LWR fit and nitime's first-local-minimum BIC (order 0 allowed) depart from both the supplement and the Schwarz rule. On delayed_noise the orders are (1,0,0,0,0,0) vs (1,3,5,2,4,2).
what_changed: Formula (Geweke 1982 rotated-noise spectral GC) and implementation are fp-exact against an independent re-implementation, and on VAR data the unit converges to the population value. It deviates from both the supplement and the canonical method in interpretable ways: the VAR is fitted by the LWR (Whittle) recursion on non-demeaned N-k-divisor autocovariances, not least squares (small at T=1024: <= 0.0066); the order is the FIRST local minimum of nitime's BIC over orders 0..48 (returnable 0..47), with order 0 allowed, so lagged couplings whose first lag gives no gain are set to exactly 0 (delayed_noise: 5 of 6 links), and when the criterion turns NaN (N-k autocovariances with det <= 0) the loop never stops and the whole SPI fails through a handler that itself raises TypeError (narrowband, logistic_maps, shared_envelope, delayed_noise T=64). The BIC penalty uses Ntot = 2T where nitime's own docstring defines T; on borderline VAR(2) draws this selects a higher order than the Ntot = T rule on 42/200 draws (none of the 11 suite datasets is affected). Rubric anchor 6 (deviates from both in an interpretable way; 'LWR instead of OLS' alone would be 7). Also: A[i, j] = GC j -> i (row = target, transpose of the glossary); 513-point freqz grid labelled k/1024 but evaluated at k/1026 (<= 6e-4 on band statistics); not offset invariant with normalise=False.

metric_name_standard: parametric (VAR) spectral Granger causality with BIC-selected order (nitime), Geweke f_{j->i}(f), pairwise bivariate, band mean or max
canonical_ref: Geweke J. 1982, J. Am. Stat. Assoc. 77(378):304-313 (frequency-domain causality f_{y->x}(lambda) from a bivariate VAR); VAR estimation: OLS or Yule-Walker/Whittle (Whittle 1963 Biometrika 50:129-134; LWR recursion Morf, Vieira & Kailath 1978 Ann. Statist. 6:643-648; Lutkepohl 2005, New Introduction to Multiple Time Series Analysis, ch. 3); order selection: Schwarz 1978 Ann. Statist. 6:461-464, VAR form Lutkepohl 2005 §4.3 (global minimum over 0..p_max); Ding, Chen & Bressler 2006 (q-bio/0608035) eq. (51) as cited by nitime. Equation/section numbers not re-checked against the texts (from memory).
canonical_definition: Fit x_t = sum_{k=1}^{p} A_k x_{t-k} + e_t (p selected by BIC, global minimum), Sigma = Cov(e); H(f) = (I - sum_k A_k e^{-i 2 pi f k})^{-1}, S = H Sigma H^H; f_{y->x}(f) = ln( S_xx(f) / [ S_xx(f) - (Sigma_yy - Sigma_xy^2/Sigma_xx) |H_xy(f)|^2 ] ) >= 0. Band mean/max is a pyspi construction; the full-band mean approximates the time-domain Geweke F_{y->x} = ln(Sigma_xx^restricted / Sigma_xx).
documented_definition: supplement §1.5.12, p.17 (supplement.txt lines 809-818: heading 809, quoted text 811-818): "Spectral Granger causality [40] is the frequency domain equivalent to Granger causality, computed via the spectral transfer matrix and noise covariance that are estimated using either a parametric (VAR model) approach [41] or nonparametric (spectral factorization) approach [57, 58]. We implement the nonparametric form from the Spectral Connectivity Toolbox [56] and the parametric implementation from v0.9 of NiTime [74]. The VAR model is estimated via least squares using the same order for both processes, where the order is either inferred (denoted by modifier order-None) or fixed. We infer a VAR model order from the Bayesian information criterion (with a maximum lag of 50, implemented in the NiTime toolkit), as well as choosing fixed orders of one (denoted by order-1) and 20 (order-20)." Keywords: "directed, linear, unsigned, bivariate, frequency-dependent". Band rule, supplement §1.5, p.12 (supplement.txt heading line 570, quoted text lines 589-599): "We use 125 uniformly sampled bins across the entire frequency range, f in [f0, fs/2] ... f0 = 4/T ... fmin-0_fmax-0-5: the full-frequency range, f in [0, fs/2]; fmin-0_fmax-0-25: f in [0, fs/4]; fmin-0-25_fmax-0-5: f in [fs/4, fs/2]"; summary = mean or max over the band. Same text on GitBook spectral.md:350-358 (Spectral Granger Causality). Matrix convention for directed SPIs, GitBook glossary-of-terms.md:27: "entry calc.table[...][0,1] will be the directed information from process 0 to process 1. The rows in this table reflect the sources while the columns reflect the targets." Refs: [40] Granger 1969 Econometrica 37:424; [41] Geweke 1982 JASA 77:304; [56] spectral_connectivity (Denovellis et al.); [57,58] Dhamala, Rangarajan & Ding 2008 NeuroImage 41:354 and PRL 100:018701; [74] Rokem et al. NiTime.

From (a, ecov) nitime evaluates H on omega_k = pi k/513 (scipy freqz, Nyquist excluded) and Geweke f_{x->y}, f_{y->x} on that grid, labelled with get_freqs = k/1024 (k = 0..512, label 0.5 at the last point). pyspi builds F[a,b] = GC a -> b, then transposes so cache[0,f,a,b] = GC b -> a; keeps labels 1e-5 <= f <= fmax (DC excluded by the fmin override, both ends inclusive), np.nanmean/np.nanmax per cell, NaN where > 50% of bins are NaN; any ValueError (BIC non-termination, singular LWR matrix) reaches the handler at spectral.py:438-440, whose warnings.warn(err) at :439 raises TypeError under the message-regex warnings filters numpy installs on import, so a direct multivariate() call raises TypeError and Calculator.compute sets the whole table to NaN (calculator.py:336-337); the intended all-NaN return at :440 happens only under catch_warnings(record=True)+simplefilter("always") or resetwarnings(). (3) "parametric implementation from v0.9 of NiTime": installed nitime 0.12.1. (4) Frequency grid: documented 125 bins on [4/T, fs/2]; implemented 513 freqz points omega_k = pi k/513 (f = k/1026) labelled k/1024, so the label 0.5 is the point 0.49903 and the label 0.25 is 0.24951 (probe). (5) Identifiers "fmin-0" run with fmin = 1e-5, which drops only the DC point. (6) "maximum lag of 50": the search fits orders 0..48 (range(1, 50) with P = lag - 1) and can return only 0..47 and stops at the FIRST local minimum of BIC; if BIC never increases the run fails (nitime ValueError; pyspi handler raises TypeError, so a direct call raises and the Calculator table is all NaN) instead of using the maximum order. (7) Documented "unsigned" but negative values occur when the LWR noise covariance is not positive definite (see units_and_range).
deviation_from_canonical: Per-frequency formula is Geweke 1982 (nitime autoregressive.py:485-509, standard rotated-noise form). Value-changing differences: VAR coefficients from LWR on the N-k-divisor, non-demeaned autocovariances instead of OLS or the positive-definite biased (divisor N) Yule-Walker; evaluation grid off by a factor 1024/1026 relative to its labels; pairwise bivariate VAR. Order selection is not standard BIC: (a) first local minimum instead of global minimum over 0..p_max, (b) penalty with Ntotal = 2T (n_process * T) gives 2 p^2 m ln(2T)/(2T), about half the standard VAR Schwarz penalty (Lutkepohl 2005 SC(m) = ln det Sigma_m + m K^2 ln T / T, doubled: 2 p^2 m ln T / T); nitime deviates from its own stated definition here: the bayesian_information_criterion docstring (.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/nitime/utils.py:2348-2358, "an implementation of equation (51) in Ding et al. (2006)") defines N_total as "the number of time-points", i.e. T, while granger.py:38 passes Ntotal = n_process * x1.shape[-1] = 2T; how Ding et al. 2006 eq. (51) itself counts channels is a secondary question (not re-checked against the paper). Order 0 is admissible and yields GC = 0 exactly. Probe delayed_noise (x0 leads by 1, 3, 5): T >= 256 every pair with relative delay >= 2 gets order 0 and A = 0 exactly; only x0 -> x1 is detected (A[1,0] = 4.71 at T=1024). Band mean/max is a pyspi construction.
units_and_range: nats; canonical spectral GC is >= 0, but here the parametric values are not clipped: negative values and NaN (log of a negative ratio) occur when the LWR noise covariance is indefinite (gamma - upsilon^2/sigma < 0 or sigma < 0). Exactly 0 when BIC selects order 0 (iid_gaussian at all T). canonical_definition: Fit x_t = sum_{k=1}^{p} A_k x_{t-k} + e_t (p = 1), Sigma = Cov(e); H(f) = (I - sum_k A_k e^{-i 2 pi f k})^{-1}, S = H Sigma H^H; f_{y->x}(f) = ln( S_xx(f) / [ S_xx(f) - (Sigma_yy - Sigma_xy^2/Sigma_xx) |H_xy(f)|^2 ] ) >= 0. Band mean/max is a pyspi construction; the full-band mean approximates the time-domain Geweke F_{y->x} = ln(Sigma_xx^restricted / Sigma_xx).
documented_definition: supplement §1.5.12, p.17 (supplement.txt lines 809-818: heading 809, quoted text 811-818): "Spectral Granger causality [40] is the frequency domain equivalent to Granger causality, computed via the spectral transfer matrix and noise covariance that are estimated using either a parametric (VAR model) approach [41] or nonparametric (spectral factorization) approach [57, 58]. We implement the nonparametric form from the Spectral Connectivity Toolbox [56] and the parametric implementation from v0.9 of NiTime [74]. The VAR model is estimated via least squares using the same order for both processes, where the order is either inferred (denoted by modifier order-None) or fixed. We infer a VAR model order from the Bayesian information criterion (with a maximum lag of 50, implemented in the NiTime toolkit), as well as choosing fixed orders of one (denoted by order-1) and 20 (order-20)." Keywords: "directed, linear, unsigned, bivariate, frequency-dependent". Band rule, supplement §1.5, p.12 (supplement.txt heading line 570, quoted text lines 589-599): "We use 125 uniformly sampled bins across the entire frequency range, f in [f0, fs/2] ... f0 = 4/T ... fmin-0_fmax-0-5: the full-frequency range, f in [0, fs/2]; fmin-0_fmax-0-25: f in [0, fs/4]; fmin-0-25_fmax-0-5: f in [fs/4, fs/2]"; summary = mean or max over the band. Same text on GitBook spectral.md:350-358 (Spectral Granger Causality). Matrix convention for directed SPIs, GitBook glossary-of-terms.md:27: "entry calc.table[...][0,1] will be the directed information from process 0 to process 1. The rows in this table reflect the sources while the columns reflect the targets." Refs: [40] Granger 1969 Econometrica 37:424; [41] Geweke 1982 JASA 77:304; [56] spectral_connectivity (Denovellis et al.); [57,58] Dhamala, Rangarajan & Ding 2008 NeuroImage 41:354 and PRL 100:018701; [74] Rokem et al. metric_name_standard: parametric (VAR(20)) spectral Granger causality (nitime), Geweke f_{j->i}(f), pairwise bivariate, band mean or max
canonical_ref: Geweke J. 1982, J. Am. Stat. Assoc. 77(378):304-313 (frequency-domain causality f_{y->x}(lambda) from a bivariate VAR); VAR estimation: OLS or Yule-Walker/Whittle (Whittle 1963 Biometrika 50:129-134; LWR recursion Morf, Vieira & Kailath 1978 Ann. Statist. 6:643-648; Lutkepohl 2005, New Introduction to Multiple Time Series Analysis, ch. 3). Equation/section numbers not re-checked against the texts (from memory).
canonical_definition: Fit x_t = sum_{k=1}^{p} A_k x_{t-k} + e_t (p = 20), Sigma = Cov(e); H(f) = (I - sum_k A_k e^{-i 2 pi f k})^{-1}, S = H Sigma H^H; f_{y->x}(f) = ln( S_xx(f) / [ S_xx(f) - (Sigma_yy - Sigma_xy^2/Sigma_xx) |H_xy(f)|^2 ] ) >= 0. Band mean/max is a pyspi construction; the full-band mean approximates the time-domain Geweke F_{y->x} = ln(Sigma_xx^restricted / Sigma_xx).
documented_definition: supplement §1.5.12, p.17 (supplement.txt lines 809-818: heading 809, quoted text 811-818): "Spectral Granger causality [40] is the frequency domain equivalent to Granger causality, computed via the spectral transfer matrix and noise covariance that are estimated using either a parametric (VAR model) approach [41] or nonparametric (spectral factorization) approach [57, 58]. We implement the nonparametric form from the Spectral Connectivity Toolbox [56] and the parametric implementation from v0.9 of NiTime [74]. The VAR model is estimated via least squares using the same order for both processes, where the order is either inferred (denoted by modifier order-None) or fixed. We infer a VAR model order from the Bayesian information criterion (with a maximum lag of 50, implemented in the NiTime toolkit), as well as choosing fixed orders of one (denoted by order-1) and 20 (order-20)." Keywords: "directed, linear, unsigned, bivariate, frequency-dependent". deviation_from_canonical: Per-frequency formula is Geweke 1982 (nitime autoregressive.py:485-509, standard rotated-noise form). Value-changing differences: VAR coefficients from LWR on the N-k-divisor, non-demeaned autocovariances instead of OLS or the positive-definite biased (divisor N) Yule-Walker; evaluation grid off by a factor 1024/1026 relative to its labels; pairwise bivariate VAR. Fixed order 20 on short series (T = 64: 2 x 2 x 20 = 80 coefficients from 64 samples) makes the N-k-divisor LWR fit ill-conditioned: non-positive-definite noise covariance, negative and NaN per-frequency values. Band mean/max is a pyspi construction.

metric_name_standard: parametric (VAR(20)) spectral Granger causality (nitime), Geweke f_{j->i}(f), pairwise bivariate, band mean or max
canonical_ref: Geweke J. 1982, J. Am. Stat. Assoc. 77(378):304-313 (frequency-domain causality f_{y->x}(lambda) from a bivariate VAR); VAR estimation: OLS or Yule-Walker/Whittle (Whittle 1963 Biometrika 50:129-134; LWR recursion Morf, Vieira & Kailath 1978 Ann. Statist. 6:643-648; Lutkepohl 2005, New Introduction to Multiple Time Series Analysis, ch. 3). Equation/section numbers not re-checked against the texts (from memory).
canonical_definition: Fit x_t = sum_{k=1}^{p} A_k x_{t-k} + e_t (p = 20), Sigma = Cov(e); H(f) = (I - sum_k A_k e^{-i 2 pi f k})^{-1}, S = H Sigma H^H; f_{y->x}(f) = ln( S_xx(f) / [ S_xx(f) - (Sigma_yy - Sigma_xy^2/Sigma_xx) |H_xy(f)|^2 ] ) >= 0. Band mean/max is a pyspi construction; the full-band mean approximates the time-domain Geweke F_{y->x} = ln(Sigma_xx^restricted / Sigma_xx).
documented_definition: supplement §1.5.12, p.17 (supplement.txt lines 809-818: heading 809, quoted text 811-818): "Spectral Granger causality [40] is the frequency domain equivalent to Granger causality, computed via the spectral transfer matrix and noise covariance that are estimated using either a parametric (VAR model) approach [41] or nonparametric (spectral factorization) approach [57, 58]. We implement the nonparametric form from the Spectral Connectivity Toolbox [56] and the parametric implementation from v0.9 of NiTime [74]. The VAR model is estimated via least squares using the same order for both processes, where the order is either inferred (denoted by modifier order-None) or fixed. We infer a VAR model order from the Bayesian information criterion (with a maximum lag of 50, implemented in the NiTime toolkit), as well as choosing fixed orders of one (denoted by order-1) and 20 (order-20)." Keywords: "directed, linear, unsigned, bivariate, frequency-dependent". Band rule, supplement §1.5, p.12 (supplement.txt heading line 570, quoted text lines 589-599): "We use 125 uniformly sampled bins across the entire frequency range, f in [f0, fs/2] ... f0 = 4/T ... fmin-0_fmax-0-5: the full-frequency range, f in [0, fs/2]; fmin-0_fmax-0-25: f in [0, fs/4]; fmin-0-25_fmax-0-5: f in [fs/4, fs/2]"; summary = mean or max over the band. Same text on GitBook spectral.md:350-358 (Spectral Granger Causality). Matrix convention for directed SPIs, GitBook glossary-of-terms.md:27: "entry calc.table[...][0,1] will be the directed information from process 0 to process 1. The rows in this table reflect the sources while the columns reflect the targets." Refs: [40] Granger 1969 Econometrica 37:424; [41] Geweke 1982 JASA 77:304; [56] spectral_connectivity (Denovellis et al.); [57,58] Dhamala, Rangarajan & Ding 2008 NeuroImage 41:354 and PRL 100:018701; [74] Rokem et al. NiTime.

For each pair (i<j) nitime fits a bivariate VAR(20) by the LWR (block Yule-Walker/Whittle) recursion on autocovariances with divisor N-k and no demeaning; no order selection. From (a, ecov) nitime evaluates H on omega_k = pi k/513 (scipy freqz, Nyquist excluded) and Geweke f_{x->y}, f_{y->x} on that grid, labelled with get_freqs = k/1024 (k = 0..512, label 0.5 at the last point). pyspi builds F[a,b] = GC a -> b, then transposes so cache[0,f,a,b] = GC b -> a; keeps labels 1e-5 <= f <= fmax (DC excluded by the fmin override, both ends inclusive), np.nanmean/np.nanmax per cell, NaN where > 50% of bins are NaN; any ValueError (e.g. singular LWR matrix) reaches the handler at spectral.py:438-440, whose warnings.warn(err) at :439 raises TypeError under the message-regex warnings filters numpy installs on import, so a direct multivariate() call raises TypeError and Calculator.compute sets the whole table to NaN (calculator.py:336-337); the intended all-NaN return at :440 happens only under catch_warnings(record=True)+simplefilter("always") or resetwarnings(). deviation_from_canonical: Per-frequency formula is Geweke 1982 (nitime autoregressive.py:485-509, standard rotated-noise form). Value-changing differences: VAR coefficients from LWR on the N-k-divisor, non-demeaned autocovariances instead of OLS or the positive-definite biased (divisor N) Yule-Walker; evaluation grid off by a factor 1024/1026 relative to its labels; pairwise bivariate VAR. Fixed order 20 on short series (T = 64: 2 x 2 x 20 = 80 coefficients from 64 samples) makes the N-k-divisor LWR fit ill-conditioned: non-positive-definite noise covariance, negative and NaN per-frequency values. Band mean/max is a pyspi construction.
units_and_range: nats; canonical spectral GC is >= 0, but here the parametric values are not clipped: negative values and NaN (log of a negative ratio) occur when the LWR noise covariance is indefinite (gamma - upsilon^2/sigma < 0 or sigma < 0). direction_convention: A[i, j] = spectral GC from process j (source, column) to process i (target, row), i.e. TARGET-by-SOURCE, the transpose of the documented sources-in-rows convention (GitBook glossary-of-terms.md:27) and of other pyspi directed SPIs (e.g. infotheory.py:274 src, targ = data[[i, j]]). metric_name_standard: phase slope index (PSI, Nolte et al. 2008), here a single-epoch, time-resolved Morlet-wavelet variant summarised by mean or max over a set of time samples
canonical_ref: Nolte G, Ziehe A, Nikulin VV, Schloegl A, Kraemer N, Brismar T, Mueller K-R (2008), Robustly estimating the flow direction of information in complex physical systems, Phys. Rev. Lett. 100, 234101; arXiv:0712.2352. Equation numbers as in the arXiv:0712.2352 text: eq. 3 (raw PSI, Psi_tilde_ij = Im sum_{f in F} C_ij*(f) C_ij(f+delta_f)), eq. 4 (coherency C_ij = S_ij/sqrt(S_ii S_jj)), eq. 5 (equivalent weighted sum of sines with weights alpha_ij(f) = |C_ij(f)|, the 'weighted by the coherence' form), eq. 6 (normalisation Psi = Psi_tilde/std(Psi_tilde), std estimated by the jackknife over epochs); direction convention from eq. 2 and the text after it: S_12 = <y1 y2*>, a positive slope means y1 -> y2. Coherency C_ij(f) = S_ij(f)/sqrt(S_ii(f) S_jj(f)) with S an expectation (segment/epoch average) of the cross-spectrum (Nolte et al. 2004, Clin. Neurophysiol. 115:2292). Morlet wavelet transform: Grossmann & Morlet 1984; Tallon-Baudry et al. 1997 J. Neurosci. 17:722 (normalisation used by MNE). Note that unsmoothed, single-realisation wavelet coherency has unit modulus (Torrence & Webster 1999 J. Climate 12:2679, smoothing required). The Nolte 2008 equation numbers were checked against the arXiv:0712.2352 text; the other citation details are from memory and were not checked against copies.
canonical_definition: Psi_tilde_ij = Im( sum_{f in F} C_ij*(f) C_ij(f + delta_f) ), adjacent frequencies of the analysis grid within band F, C_ij the (expected) coherency; (Nolte eq. 3); normalised Psi = Psi_tilde / std(Psi_tilde) with a jackknife std (eq. 6). Antisymmetric: Psi_ji = -Psi_ij. Positive Psi_ij (with S_ij = E[x_i x_j*]) means i leads j (i is the sender). No canonical time-resolved single-trial version exists; time-resolved PSI requires coherency estimated across trials/epochs or with smoothing.
documented_definition: supplement §1.5.4, p.14 (heading at supplement.txt file line 644; the briefing pack numbered it 658): "The phase slope index (PSI) [62] is a directed measure of information flow computed using the complex-valued coherency ... evaluates the consistency of the changes in phase differences across a pre-specified frequency range, weighted by the coherence ... The time-frequency decomposition is given by a Morlet wavelet, with spectral densities indexed by a time-frequency tuple ... we take the average (denoted by the mean modifier) or the maximum (max) PSI across all time points. We use the same pre-specified frequency ranges as outlined at the beginning of this section (i.e., low, high or full)"; keywords "directed, linear/nonlinear, unsigned, bivariate, frequency-dependent and time-frequency dependent". Band rule from supplement §1.5, p.12-13 (heading at file line 570, band bullets at lines 595-599; the briefing pack gives §1.5 as lines 582-613): fmin-0_fmax-0-5 = f in [0, fs/2], fmin-0_fmax-0-25 = [0, fs/4], fmin-0-25_fmax-0-5 = [fs/4, fs/2], fs = 1. GitBook spectral.md:322-346 (Phase Slope Index) repeats the same text. [62] = Nolte et al. 2008.

implemented_as: Input z-scored per channel (ddof=1; optional detrend first). The whole (N,T) dataset is passed as ONE epoch (1,N,T). MNE builds 10 complex Morlet wavelets at f = linspace(0.2, 0.5, 10) (step 1/30, n_cycles = 7 default, zero_mean=True, sigma_t = 7/(2 pi f), support +-5 sigma_t, lengths 55..23 samples), computes the CWT by FFT linear convolution with zero padding, mode 'same' (T samples per frequency). For each lower-triangle pair (seed i > target j) the single-epoch coherency C(f,t) = W_i W_j* / (|W_i| |W_j|) has unit modulus, so PSI(t) = Im sum_{k=0..8} C*(f_k,t) C(f_{k+1},t) = sum_k sin(dphi(f_{k+1},t) - dphi(f_k,t)) with dphi = phase_i - phase_j: a sum of 9 unweighted adjacent-frequency phase-difference increments, one band (all 10 frequencies), shape (N,N,1,T). The f = 0.5 (Nyquist) wavelet is purely real, so dphi(0.5,t) is 0 or pi. pyspi then takes freq = freqs_computed[0] (the 10 wavelet frequencies), freq_id = indices with fmin <= f <= fmax, and indexes the LAST (time) axis with these frequency indices: full band -> time samples t = 0..9, low band [0,0.25] -> t = 0,1, high band [0.25,0.5] -> t = 2..9. Statistic = np.nanmean or np.nanmax (signed) over axes (band, selected time). Lower triangle copied to upper (symmetric matrix), diagonal NaN. mt_adaptive=True is passed but unused in cwt mode. For T < 25 the default fmin = 5/T drops wavelet frequencies and the index mapping shifts (T=20: 8 frequencies, low band empty -> NaN).

deviation_from_canonical: (a) Coherency is not an expectation: one epoch and no time/frequency smoothing, so |C| = 1 and PSI(t) = sum of sines of adjacent phase-difference increments (probe: mne PSI equals sum sin(diff dphi) to 2.2e-15). Canonical PSI requires coherency averaged over segments/trials. (b) No normalisation by the jackknife std (raw Psi_tilde; MNE also returns raw, common practice). (c) The adjacent-frequency kernel itself matches Nolte eq. 3 (unlike the multitaper all-pairs variant, REVIEW M5), on a 10-point Morlet grid with step 1/30 and the Nyquist frequency included; the Nyquist wavelet is real so its phase difference is 0 or pi and the last increment is not a phase slope. (d) Aggregation over time samples 0..9 at the signal start (zero-padding edge) instead of a time-averaged or band-limited quantity; observed effect: sign of pyspi output disagrees with the true lead/lag on delayed_noise and var2_bivariate (see candidates). (e) Canonical PSI is antisymmetric; output is symmetrised. (f) max is the signed maximum, not a canonical summary.
units_and_range: Dimensionless raw PSI per time point in [-9, 9] (9 adjacent pairs of unit-modulus coherency); mean/max over 2..10 time samples, so the output range is [-9, 9]; signed, can be negative (despite 'unsigned' label). NaN if a band selects no sample (T < 25 low band) or for constant input. Symmetric matrix by construction; diagonal NaN.
direction_convention: MNE (docstring effective.py:52-53, and csd = seed * conj(target) at epochs.py:652): PSI for (seed, target) is positive when the seed leads. Seeds are rows of tril_indices (i > j), so the raw dense value psi[i, j] (i > j) is positive when the higher-index channel i leads j. pyspi copies it to the upper triangle: A[i,j] = A[j,i] = PSI(max(i,j) -> min(i,j)). Probe (time samples 30..T-30, delayed_noise where x0 leads x1, x2, x3): psi[i,j] < 0 for every pair at every T (the higher index lags); var2_bivariate (x0 -> x1): psi[1,0] central mean -0.39/-0.39/-0.24/-0.18 at T = 64/256/1024/4096. The pyspi output itself (first-10-sample window) does not preserve this sign reliably (see candidates). Confirmed in the check stage for the library step (raw psi[i, j] for i > j is negative on every delayed_noise pair, rawpsi runs; the intended smoothed-coherency PSI has the truth sign on 100% of pairs, int runs); see direction_observed for what the stored value carries.

score_rubric_note: Wrong-axis clause: frequency indices select time samples 0..9 (full), 0..1 (low) and 2..9 (high). In the tsel probe, changes outside the selection are 0.0.
what_changed: Rubric anchor 0 (wrong axis indexed; already documented as the wavelet PSI axis selection, EEG_OPTIMIZATION_NOTES.md §review / KNOWN_ISSUES). All six identifiers store the mean or signed max of the same full-band (0.2-0.5, 10 Morlet frequencies) single-epoch PSI(t) over the first 10 (full), 2 (low) or 8 (high) TIME samples, because the frequency indices are applied to the time axis; the band never restricts frequencies. On the kernel path and the default (no-detrend) pipeline path the temporal content of input samples t >= 37 cannot reach the stored value (winperm-tail change 0.0; kernel-path tail perturbations <= 1.2e-13); on the default pipeline path those samples act only through the per-channel z-score mean (the SD is a positive rescaling that PSI ignores), and a tail offset of +0.5 moves the stored values by up to 3.13 because the zero-mean Morlet transform of a constant is not zero inside the zero-padded edge window (tailpert). With detrend (pipeline-detrend) this horizon does not hold: the fitted line is a time-weighted sum of the tail, so the time order of the tail reaches the stored value (wavelet.psi|delayed_noise|1024|pipeline-detrend|tailpert: rescaling x[:, 37:] about its own mean changes it by 0.087; the review probe review_detrend_rev.py shows the same for a time reversal of x[:, 37:]). On top of that: one epoch gives unit-modulus coherency, so PSI(t) is a sum of 9 unweighted sines (no coherence weighting, the documented and canonical weighting is absent); the 0.5 wavelet is real, so the last increment is a 0/pi phase; the antisymmetric quantity is mirrored into a symmetric matrix whose sign follows channel order; labels say undirected/unsigned for a signed, directed quantity. Consequences measured: sign agreement with the true lead/lag 0.10-0.50 per identifier while the intended quantity scores 1.0 on the full and high variants and 0.86 on mean-low and max-low (ref_intended_whole_agree over the same 72 dir runs; 0.0 on logistic_maps_chaotic T64, 0.33 on var2_chain T64) and a numpy Welch PSI scores 1.0 (delayed_noise welch runs); null spread constant in T (SD about 1.28) instead of shrinking like the all-time mean (0.32 -> 0.06). The replica reproduces the computation to 1e-12, so the code does what the trace says; the stored number does not describe the documented or canonical PSI.

metric_name_standard: in-sample (training) mean squared error of a ridge regression (alpha = 1, unpenalised intercept) of y = x_j on x = x_i; on z-scored data a monotone transform of the squared Pearson correlation
canonical_ref: Hoerl & Kennard 1970, Technometrics 12(1):55-67, ridge estimator beta*(k) = (X'X + kI)^-1 X'y (section 2); scikit-learn objective ||y - Xw||^2_2 + alpha ||w||^2_2 with centred X, y (sklearn/linear_model/_ridge.py Ridge docstring, the delegate's own statement); Hastie, Tibshirani & Friedman 2009, The Elements of Statistical Learning, 2nd ed., Springer, section 3.4.1 Ridge Regression (intercept left out of the penalty; inputs centred and beta_0 estimated by ybar) is the independent source for the unpenalised-intercept and centring convention (ESL section and wording from memory, not re-checked against the book). Hoerl & Kennard work with X'X in correlation form, so their k is on a different scale from sklearn's alpha on ddof=1 z-scores (see what_changed).
canonical_definition: w = sum(xc*yc) / (sum(xc^2) + alpha), b = ybar - w*xbar, MSE = (1/T) sum (y_t - b - w x_t)^2; for z-scored (ddof=1) inputs with alpha = 1: w = r (T-1)/T and MSE = ((T-1)/T) * (1 - r^2 (T-1)(T+1)/T^2)
documented_definition: supplement §1.6.1, p.18 (supplement.txt lines 856-868; the briefing pack gives 874-887, which is off by 18 lines): "we use a number of linear models and record the mean squared error (MSE) of a regression of y on x. The following models (with the default parameters) from scikit-learn [2] are included: stochastic gradient descent regression with a squared loss (ordinary least squares fit) function (denoted by modifier SGDRegressor); Ridge regression, which uses l2-norm regularization (Ride); the Elastic-Net model [76, 77], which uses both l1 and l2-norm regularization (ElasticNet); and the Bayesian Ridge regressor uses a gamma distribution prior (with lambda1 = lambda2 = 1e-6) for the l2-norm regularizor in Ridge regression (BayesianRidge). This yields four SPIs: 215. lmfit_SGDRegressor 216. lmfit_Ridge 217. lmfit_ElasticNet 218. lmfit_BayesianRidge"; keywords "directed, linear, unsigned, bivariate, contemporaneous"; rationale "Linear regression is commonly used for establishing independence through model fits (e.g., see additive noise models in Sec. 1.3.1)". deviation_from_documented: (a) The supplement and GitBook name the modifier "Ride" (typo for Ridge). (b) "With the default parameters": pyspi passes random_state=42, which is inert for the cholesky solver (no numeric effect). (c) The documented keyword "directed" is not borne out under the default z-scoring: the value depends only on r_ij and T, so A is symmetric (see candidates). (d) The documentation does not state that the MSE is in-sample (no train/test split), nor that lower = stronger dependence. Otherwise the documented "MSE of a regression of y on x" with l2 regularisation matches the code.
deviation_from_canonical: none for the estimator: the fit is exactly the Hoerl-Kennard ridge estimator with k = alpha = 1 on centred data with an unpenalised intercept. The SPI is the in-sample MSE of that fit, a pyspi construction; on z-scored data it is the closed-form ((T-1)/T)(1 - r^2 (T^2-1)/T^2), i.e. an affine, decreasing function of r^2 whose shrinkage term (T^2-1)/T^2 vanishes as T grows. The fixed alpha = 1 is scale dependent: its relative strength is 1/(T-1) for z-scored data but changes with the raw scale when normalise=False.
units_and_range: units of the target variance (dimensionless after z-scoring); unsigned, >= 0; on z-scored data in [(T-1)/T^3, (T-1)/T): (T-1)/T^3 for identical series (probe shared_envelope pair (0,2): 2.403e-04 at T=64, 5.959e-08 at T=4096) and close to (T-1)/T for r = 0; symmetric (A = A.T to 7.8e-16) under default preprocessing; asymmetric with normalise=False (A[i, j] scales with var(x_j)); constant processes (zscore division by zero) were not probed.
direction_convention: A[i, j] = in-sample MSE of the linear prediction of process j (target, column) from process i (predictor, row), per misc.py:122-126; LOWER = j better linearly predicted from i. Code-derived; with the default z-scoring the matrix is symmetric (see units_and_range), so the direction is only empirically identifiable with normalise=False, where column j scales with var(x_j) (probe on scaled_offset_T1024: column means of A track std_j^2 = 0.0395, 4.058, 24.78, 97.89).

what_changed: Estimator: nothing; the alpha = 1 Hoerl-Kennard ridge fit with an unpenalised intercept is reproduced to floating point. The SPI is the in-sample MSE of that fit; on z-scored data it equals ((T-1)/T)(1 - r^2 (T^2-1)/T^2) on all 84 dataset/T combinations, i.e. an affine, decreasing function of r^2, and it is symmetric. Documentation-level only: modifier typo "Ride"; the "directed" keyword is not borne out under the default z-scoring. Hyperparameter scale (a convention fixed by the documented 'default parameters', not a deviation; score unaffected): alpha = 1 acts on ddof=1 z-scores with X'X = T-1, so w = r(T-1)/T, whereas the same k on Hoerl-Kennard correlation-form X (X'X = 1) would give w = r/2; on raw data (normalise=False) the relative strength changes with scale.

metric_name_standard: in-sample (training) mean squared error of a ridge regression (alpha = 1, unpenalised intercept) of y = x_j on x = x_i; on z-scored data a monotone transform of the squared Pearson correlation
canonical_ref: Hoerl & Kennard 1970, Technometrics 12(1):55-67, ridge estimator beta*(k) = (X'X + kI)^-1 X'y (section 2); scikit-learn objective ||y - Xw||^2_2 + alpha ||w||^2_2 with centred X, y (sklearn/linear_model/_ridge.py Ridge docstring, the delegate's own statement); Hastie, Tibshirani & Friedman 2009, The Elements of Statistical Learning, 2nd ed., Springer, section 3.4.1 Ridge Regression (intercept left out of the penalty; inputs centred and beta_0 estimated by ybar) is the independent source for the unpenalised-intercept and centring convention (ESL section and wording from memory, not re-checked against the book). Hoerl & Kennard work with X'X in correlation form, so their k is on a different scale from sklearn's alpha on ddof=1 z-scores (see what_changed).
canonical_definition: w = sum(xc*yc) / (sum(xc^2) + alpha), b = ybar - w*xbar, MSE = (1/T) sum (y_t - b - w x_t)^2; for z-scored (ddof=1) inputs with alpha = 1: w = r (T-1)/T and MSE = ((T-1)/T) * (1 - r^2 (T-1)(T+1)/T^2)

deviation_from_documented: (a) The supplement and GitBook name the modifier "Ride" (typo for Ridge). (b) "With the default parameters": pyspi passes random_state=42, which is inert for the cholesky solver (no numeric effect). (c) The documented keyword "directed" is not borne out under the default z-scoring: the value depends only on r_ij and T, so A is symmetric (see candidates). (d) The documentation does not state that the MSE is in-sample (no train/test split), nor that lower = stronger dependence. Otherwise the documented "MSE of a regression of y on x" with l2 regularisation matches the code.
deviation_from_canonical: none for the estimator: the fit is exactly the Hoerl-Kennard ridge estimator with k = alpha = 1 on centred data with an unpenalised intercept. The SPI is the in-sample MSE of that fit, a pyspi construction; on z-scored data it is the closed-form ((T-1)/T)(1 - r^2 (T^2-1)/T^2), i.e. an affine, decreasing function of r^2 whose shrinkage term (T^2-1)/T^2 vanishes as T grows. The fixed alpha = 1 is scale dependent: its relative strength is 1/(T-1) for z-scored data but changes with the raw scale when normalise=False.
units_and_range: units of the target variance (dimensionless after z-scoring); unsigned, >= 0; on z-scored data in [(T-1)/T^3, (T-1)/T): (T-1)/T^3 for identical series (probe shared_envelope pair (0,2): 2.403e-04 at T=64, 5.959e-08 at T=4096) and close to (T-1)/T for r = 0; symmetric (A = A.T to 7.8e-16) under default preprocessing; asymmetric with normalise=False (A[i, j] scales with var(x_j)); constant processes (zscore division by zero) were not probed.
direction_convention: A[i, j] = in-sample MSE of the linear prediction of process j (target, column) from process i (predictor, row), per misc.py:122-126; LOWER = j better linearly predicted from i. Code-derived; with the default z-scoring the matrix is symmetric (see units_and_range), so the direction is only empirically identifiable with normalise=False, where column j scales with var(x_j) (probe on scaled_offset_T1024: column means of A track std_j^2 = 0.0395, 4.058, 24.78, 97.89).

what_changed: Estimator: nothing; the alpha = 1 Hoerl-Kennard ridge fit with an unpenalised intercept is reproduced to floating point. Hyperparameter scale (a convention fixed by the documented 'default parameters', not a deviation; score unaffected): alpha = 1 acts on ddof=1 z-scores with X'X = T-1, so w = r(T-1)/T, whereas the same k on Hoerl-Kennard correlation-form X (X'X = 1) would give w = r/2; on raw data (normalise=False) the relative strength changes with scale.

metric_name_standard: in-sample mean squared error of a lasso regression (alpha = 1, sklearn scaling 1/(2T)) of y = x_j on x = x_i
canonical_ref: Tibshirani 1996, J. R. Stat. Soc. B 58(1):267-288, lasso estimator and its soft-threshold solution for orthonormal design (section 2.2); scikit-learn objective (1/(2 n_samples)) ||y - Xw||^2_2 + alpha ||w||_1 (sklearn/linear_model/_coordinate_descent.py:1334); coordinate descent: Friedman, Hastie & Tibshirani 2010, J Stat Softw 33(1)
canonical_definition: single centred predictor: w = S(sum(xc*yc)/T, alpha) / (sum(xc^2)/T) with S(u, a) = sign(u) max(|u| - a, 0); b = ybar - w xbar; MSE = (1/T) sum (y - b - w x)^2. For z-scored (ddof=1) inputs and alpha = 1: |sum(xc*yc)/T| = |r|(T-1)/T < 1 always, so w = 0 and MSE = (T-1)/T for every pair
documented_definition: Not documented. supplement §1.6.1, p.18 (supplement.txt lines 856-868; the briefing pack gives 874-887, which is off by 18 lines): "we use a number of linear models and record the mean squared error (MSE) of a regression of y on x. The following models (with the default parameters) from scikit-learn [2] are included: stochastic gradient descent regression with a squared loss (ordinary least squares fit) function (denoted by modifier SGDRegressor); Ridge regression, which uses l2-norm regularization (Ride); the Elastic-Net model [76, 77], which uses both l1 and l2-norm regularization (ElasticNet); and the Bayesian Ridge regressor uses a gamma distribution prior (with lambda1 = lambda2 = 1e-6) for the l2-norm regularizor in Ridge regression (BayesianRidge). This yields four SPIs: 215. lmfit_SGDRegressor 216. lmfit_Ridge 217. lmfit_ElasticNet 218. lmfit_BayesianRidge"; keywords "directed, linear, unsigned, bivariate, contemporaneous"; rationale "Linear regression is commonly used for establishing independence through model fits (e.g., see additive noise models in Sec. 1.3.1)". GitBook spi-descriptions/miscellaneous.md "Linear Model Fit" repeats the text verbatim (including the typo "Ride") and lists the same four identifiers. The supplement says "This yields four SPIs" and neither it nor the GitBook mentions Lasso or lmfit_Lasso; the identifier exists only through pyspi/config.yaml:1275.

deviation_from_documented: (a) The SPI is undocumented: supplement §1.6.1 lists four lmfit SPIs (215-218) and the GitBook four identifiers; lmfit_Lasso is a fifth produced by config.yaml:1275. (b) If read against the family description ("record the MSE of a regression of y on x"), the regression is degenerate: the coefficient is always exactly 0 on default-preprocessed data, so the output is the constant (T-1)/T and does not depend on the data at all. (c) "directed" label: trivially symmetric (constant).
deviation_from_canonical: The estimator itself is the canonical lasso (sklearn scaling, unpenalised intercept), which the checks reproduce; the deviation is in the choice alpha = 1: with sklearn's 1/(2T) scaling the threshold for a nonzero coefficient on one standardised predictor is |r|(T-1)/T > 1, which is impossible, so the fitted model is always the intercept-only model and the SPI is the constant ((T-1)/T). With normalise=False the coefficient is nonzero only when the biased covariance |cov0(x_i, x_j)| > 1, which makes the SPI depend on the absolute scale of the raw data.
units_and_range: units of the target variance; on z-scored data exactly (T-1)/T for every off-diagonal entry (0.984375 at T=64 ... 0.999755859375 at T=4096), symmetric, no information; with normalise=False equals var0(x_j) unless |cov0(x_i, x_j)| > 1 (probe scaled_offset_T1024 raw: column values 0.0395, 4.058, 24.78, 97.89 = var0 of the target, except A[2,3] = 35.675 vs 97.894 and A[3,2] = 9.0302 vs 24.779 where |cov0| > 1); unsigned, >= 0.
direction_convention: A[i, j] = in-sample MSE of the linear prediction of process j (target, column) from process i (predictor, row), per misc.py:122-126; LOWER = j better linearly predicted from i. Code-derived; with the default z-scoring the matrix is symmetric (see units_and_range), so the direction is only empirically identifiable with normalise=False, where column j scales with var(x_j) (probe on scaled_offset_T1024: column means of A track std_j^2 = 0.0395, 4.058, 24.78, 97.89).

metric_name_standard: in-sample mean squared error of a lasso regression (alpha = 1, sklearn scaling 1/(2T)) of y = x_j on x = x_i
canonical_ref: Tibshirani 1996, J. R. Stat. Soc. B 58(1):267-288, lasso estimator and its soft-threshold solution for orthonormal design (section 2.2); scikit-learn objective (1/(2 n_samples)) ||y - Xw||^2_2 + alpha ||w||_1 (sklearn/linear_model/_coordinate_descent.py:1334); coordinate descent: Friedman, Hastie & Tibshirani 2010, J Stat Softw 33(1)
canonical_definition: single centred predictor: w = S(sum(xc*yc)/T, alpha) / (sum(xc^2)/T) with S(u, a) = sign(u) max(|u| - a, 0); b = ybar - w xbar; MSE = (1/T) sum (y - b - w x)^2. For z-scored (ddof=1) inputs and alpha = 1: |sum(xc*yc)/T| = |r|(T-1)/T < 1 always, so w = 0 and MSE = (T-1)/T for every pair

The following models (with the default parameters) from scikit-learn [2] are included: stochastic gradient descent regression with a squared loss (ordinary least squares fit) function (denoted by modifier SGDRegressor); Ridge regression, which uses l2-norm regularization (Ride); the Elastic-Net model [76, 77], which uses both l1 and l2-norm regularization (ElasticNet); and the Bayesian Ridge regressor uses a gamma distribution prior (with lambda1 = lambda2 = 1e-6) for the l2-norm regularizor in Ridge regression (BayesianRidge). This yields four SPIs: 215. lmfit_SGDRegressor 216. lmfit_Ridge 217. lmfit_ElasticNet 218. lmfit_BayesianRidge"; keywords "directed, linear, unsigned, bivariate, contemporaneous"; rationale "Linear regression is commonly used for establishing independence through model fits (e.g., see additive noise models in Sec. 1.3.1)". GitBook spi-descriptions/miscellaneous.md "Linear Model Fit" repeats the text verbatim (including the typo "Ride") and lists the same four identifiers. deviation_from_documented: (a) The SPI is undocumented: supplement §1.6.1 lists four lmfit SPIs (215-218) and the GitBook four identifiers; lmfit_Lasso is a fifth produced by config.yaml:1275. (b) If read against the family description ("record the MSE of a regression of y on x"), the regression is degenerate: the coefficient is always exactly 0 on default-preprocessed data, so the output is the constant (T-1)/T and does not depend on the data at all. (c) "directed" label: trivially symmetric (constant).
deviation_from_canonical: The estimator itself is the canonical lasso (sklearn scaling, unpenalised intercept), which the checks reproduce; the deviation is in the choice alpha = 1: with sklearn's 1/(2T) scaling the threshold for a nonzero coefficient on one standardised predictor is |r|(T-1)/T > 1, which is impossible, so the fitted model is always the intercept-only model and the SPI is the constant ((T-1)/T). With normalise=False the coefficient is nonzero only when the biased covariance |cov0(x_i, x_j)| > 1, which makes the SPI depend on the absolute scale of the raw data.
units_and_range: units of the target variance; on z-scored data exactly (T-1)/T for every off-diagonal entry (0.984375 at T=64 ... 0.999755859375 at T=4096), symmetric, no information; with normalise=False equals var0(x_j) unless |cov0(x_i, x_j)| > 1 (probe scaled_offset_T1024 raw: column values 0.0395, 4.058, 24.78, 97.89 = var0 of the target, except A[2,3] = 35.675 vs 97.894 and A[3,2] = 9.0302 vs 24.779 where |cov0| > 1); unsigned, >= 0.
direction_convention: A[i, j] = in-sample MSE of the linear prediction of process j (target, column) from process i (predictor, row), per misc.py:122-126; LOWER = j better linearly predicted from i. Code-derived; with the default z-scoring the matrix is symmetric (see units_and_range), so the direction is only empirically identifiable with normalise=False, where column j scales with var(x_j) (probe on scaled_offset_T1024: column means of A track std_j^2 = 0.0395, 4.058, 24.78, 97.89).

what_changed: The lasso estimator is sklearn's penalised form of Tibshirani 1996 and agrees with the analytic soft-threshold solution, but with alpha = 1 and sklearn's 1/(2T) loss scaling the coefficient of a standardised predictor is zero whenever |r|(T-1)/T <= 1, which always holds; coordinate descent exits at iteration 0 and the prediction is the target mean, so the SPI is the data-independent constant (T-1)/T on every dataset, at every T and under detrending. The SPI is also absent from the supplement ("four SPIs") and the GitBook. On raw (normalise=False) data it fits only pairs with |cov0| > 1. As a practical consequence for the EEG data, lmfit_Lasso is in the retained EEG-185 set (audit/env/retained_metrics.txt:82), and on the EEG workflow preprocessing (detrend then z-score) it is the same constant (T-1)/T (the 12 pipeline-detrend constant runs pass with the 84 pipeline runs, 96/96, max_abs 3.55e-15), so it stores no information.

For Lasso the default-path value is the constant (T-1)/T, so no orientation is visible at all.

metric_name_standard: in-sample mean squared error of a linear least-squares fit of y = x_j on x = x_i obtained by stochastic gradient descent (sklearn SGDRegressor defaults: squared loss, l2 penalty alpha = 1e-4, invscaling learning rate); an approximation to the OLS residual variance (T-1)/T (1 - r^2)
canonical_ref: Target quantity: ordinary least squares residual mean square (Legendre 1805 / Gauss 1809; any regression text, e.g. Seber & Lee 2003, Linear Regression Analysis, ch. 3); optimiser: Robbins & Monro 1951, Ann. Math. Stat. 22(3):400-407; Bottou 2010, Proc. COMPSTAT, "Large-scale machine learning with stochastic gradient descent" (sklearn user guide reference)
canonical_definition: OLS: w = sum(xc*yc)/sum(xc^2), b = ybar - w xbar, MSE = (1/T) sum (y - b - w x)^2 = ((T-1)/T)(1 - r^2) for z-scored inputs; SGD minimises (1/T) sum 0.5 (y_t - w x_t - b)^2 + 0.5 alpha w^2 (alpha = 1e-4) by per-sample updates and only approximates this minimiser

The following models (with the default parameters) from scikit-learn [2] are included: stochastic gradient descent regression with a squared loss (ordinary least squares fit) function (denoted by modifier SGDRegressor); Ridge regression, which uses l2-norm regularization (Ride); the Elastic-Net model [76, 77], which uses both l1 and l2-norm regularization (ElasticNet); and the Bayesian Ridge regressor uses a gamma distribution prior (with lambda1 = lambda2 = 1e-6) for the l2-norm regularizor in Ridge regression (BayesianRidge). This yields four SPIs: 215. lmfit_SGDRegressor 216. lmfit_Ridge 217. lmfit_ElasticNet 218. lmfit_BayesianRidge"; keywords "directed, linear, unsigned, bivariate, contemporaneous"; rationale "Linear regression is commonly used for establishing independence through model fits (e.g., see additive noise models in Sec. 1.3.1)". metric_name_standard: in-sample mean squared error of a linear least-squares fit of y = x_j on x = x_i obtained by stochastic gradient descent (sklearn SGDRegressor defaults: squared loss, l2 penalty alpha = 1e-4, invscaling learning rate); an approximation to the OLS residual variance (T-1)/T (1 - r^2)
canonical_ref: Target quantity: ordinary least squares residual mean square (Legendre 1805 / Gauss 1809; any regression text, e.g. Seber & Lee 2003, Linear Regression Analysis, ch. 3); optimiser: Robbins & Monro 1951, Ann. Math. Stat. 22(3):400-407; Bottou 2010, Proc. COMPSTAT, "Large-scale machine learning with stochastic gradient descent" (sklearn user guide reference)
canonical_definition: OLS: w = sum(xc*yc)/sum(xc^2), b = ybar - w xbar, MSE = (1/T) sum (y - b - w x)^2 = ((T-1)/T)(1 - r^2) for z-scored inputs; SGD minimises (1/T) sum 0.5 (y_t - w x_t - b)^2 + 0.5 alpha w^2 (alpha = 1e-4) by per-sample updates and only approximates this minimiser

The following models (with the default parameters) from scikit-learn [2] are included: stochastic gradient descent regression with a squared loss (ordinary least squares fit) function (denoted by modifier SGDRegressor); Ridge regression, which uses l2-norm regularization (Ride); the Elastic-Net model [76, 77], which uses both l1 and l2-norm regularization (ElasticNet); and the Bayesian Ridge regressor uses a gamma distribution prior (with lambda1 = lambda2 = 1e-6) for the l2-norm regularizor in Ridge regression (BayesianRidge). This yields four SPIs: 215. lmfit_SGDRegressor 216. lmfit_Ridge 217. lmfit_ElasticNet 218. lmfit_BayesianRidge"; keywords "directed, linear, unsigned, bivariate, contemporaneous"; rationale "Linear regression is commonly used for establishing independence through model fits (e.g., see additive noise models in Sec. 1.3.1)". deviation_from_canonical: The canonical quantity behind the documented description is the OLS residual mean square ((T-1)/T)(1 - r^2) on z-scored data; the code returns the in-sample MSE of a stopped SGD iterate, which is >= the OLS value by an optimiser-dependent excess (probe: up to 2.93e-3 at T=64 on cointegrated, 5.8e-4 at T=4096) that does not vanish with T because the stopping rule (tol = 1e-3 on the running epoch objective, 5 epochs) stops after ~7 epochs at large T with a step size eta0/t^0.25 still around 0.01/(7T)^0.25 ~ 1e-3. metric_name_standard: in-sample mean squared error of an elastic-net regression (sklearn alpha = 1, l1_ratio = 0.5, i.e. naive elastic net with lambda1 = 0.5 and lambda2 = 0.5 on the 1/(2T) loss scale) of y = x_j on x = x_i
canonical_ref: Zou & Hastie 2005, J. R. Stat. Soc. B 67(2):301-320 (naive elastic net, eq. 3; their recommended estimator rescales by (1 + lambda2), section 3.2); coordinate descent solution: Friedman, Hastie & Tibshirani 2010, J Stat Softw 33(1):1-22 (supplement ref [76]); scikit-learn objective (1/(2T)) ||y - Xw||^2 + alpha l1_ratio ||w||_1 + 0.5 alpha (1 - l1_ratio) ||w||^2 (_coordinate_descent.py:884-894)
canonical_definition: single centred predictor: w = S(sum(xc*yc)/T, alpha*l1_ratio) / (sum(xc^2)/T + alpha*(1 - l1_ratio)); MSE = (1/T) sum (y - b - w x)^2. For z-scored inputs with c = (T-1)/T: w = sign(r) max(|r| c - 0.5, 0) / (c + 0.5) and MSE = c (1 - 2 w r + w^2); the exact minimiser has w = 0 and MSE = (T-1)/T only for |r| <= 0.5 T/(T-1). This is the exact minimiser; sklearn's stopped solver returns w = 0 over a wider band (see implemented_as).
documented_definition: supplement §1.6.1, p.18 (supplement.txt lines 856-868; the briefing pack gives 874-887, which is off by 18 lines): "we use a number of linear models and record the mean squared error (MSE) of a regression of y on x. The following models (with the default parameters) from scikit-learn [2] are included: stochastic gradient descent regression with a squared loss (ordinary least squares fit) function (denoted by modifier SGDRegressor); Ridge regression, which uses l2-norm regularization (Ride); the Elastic-Net model [76, 77], which uses both l1 and l2-norm regularization (ElasticNet); and the Bayesian Ridge regressor uses a gamma distribution prior (with lambda1 = lambda2 = 1e-6) for the l2-norm regularizor in Ridge regression (BayesianRidge). This yields four SPIs: 215. lmfit_SGDRegressor 216. lmfit_Ridge 217. lmfit_ElasticNet 218. lmfit_BayesianRidge"; keywords "directed, linear, unsigned, bivariate, contemporaneous"; rationale "Linear regression is commonly used for establishing independence through model fits (e.g., see additive noise models in Sec. 1.3.1)". GitBook spi-descriptions/miscellaneous.md "Linear Model Fit" repeats the text verbatim (including the typo "Ride") and lists the same four identifiers.

implemented_as: A[i, j] = in-sample MSE of the sklearn ElasticNet(alpha=1.0, l1_ratio=0.5, fit_intercept=True, max_iter=1000, tol=1e-4, selection="cyclic", random_state=42) fit of z_j on z_i. Coordinate descent starts at w = 0 and first evaluates the duality gap there (_cd_fast.pyx:391-400). With one z-scored feature, l1_reg = 0.5 T and s = x.y = r (T-1), that gap is 0.5 y.y (1 - min(1, 0.5 T/|s|))^2 (dual_gap_formulation_A, _cd_fast.pyx:138-159), and the solver returns w = 0 with n_iter_ 0 whenever it is <= tol*y.y = 1e-4 (T-1), i.e. whenever |r| <= 0.5 T/((T-1)(1 - sqrt(2e-4))) (0.51522 at T=64, 0.50916 at 256, 0.50767 at 1024, 0.50730 at 4096). Otherwise one cyclic update reaches the closed form above and the next gap check stops (n_iter_ 2). So pyspi returns (T-1)/T for |r| up to that tol bound, which is wider than the exact-minimiser threshold 0.5 T/(T-1) (0.50794 / 0.50196 / 0.50049 / 0.50012); in the band between them the exact minimiser has w between 0 and ~0.0048 and an MSE up to ~4.8e-3 below (T-1)/T, so the SPI jumps by ~4.8e-3 at the tol bound. deviation_from_documented: (a) Documented as "the Elastic-Net model [76, 77], which uses both l1 and l2-norm regularization" with default parameters: matches the code (alpha=1, l1_ratio=0.5); but ref [77] (Andersen et al., interior-point methods for cone programming) is not the algorithm used (coordinate descent, ref [76]). (b) Not stated: with these defaults the l1 threshold plus the solver's tol-based initial exit zero the coefficient for every pair with |r| <= ~0.51 (0.5 T/((T-1)(1 - sqrt(2e-4)))), so the SPI is the constant (T-1)/T for weak and moderate dependence. (c) "directed": symmetric on z-scored data.
deviation_from_canonical: The estimator is the naive elastic net of Zou & Hastie 2005 (no (1 + lambda2) rescaling of the coefficients, which Zou & Hastie recommend to undo double shrinkage), in sklearn's 1/(2T) loss scaling. It equals the exact minimiser except in a band just above the l1 threshold: sklearn's initial duality-gap exit (tol = 1e-4 relative to y.y) returns w = 0 for 0.5 T/(T-1) < |r| <= 0.5 T/((T-1)(1 - sqrt(2e-4))) where the exact minimiser has w > 0, an MSE overstatement of up to ~4.8e-3 (probe max 3.50e-3 on the audit datasets). The SPI (in-sample MSE at a fixed, large penalty) is a pyspi construction: it saturates at (T-1)/T for |r| up to ~0.51, jumps by ~4.8e-3 at that bound, and cannot fall below ~4/9 even for identical series, so it is a heavily censored, monotone (non-increasing in |r|) function of |r| with one jump discontinuity.
units_and_range: units of the target variance; on z-scored data in [~0.444, (T-1)/T]: (T-1)/T for |r| <= 0.5 T/((T-1)(1 - sqrt(2e-4))) (0.5152 at T=64, 0.5073 at T=4096; the exact-minimiser threshold 0.5 T/(T-1) is lower), then a jump down by ~4.8e-3 and a decrease to c (1 - w)^2 ~ 4/9 at |r| = 1 (probe shared_envelope identical pair 0.4468 at T=64); symmetric under default preprocessing; asymmetric and scale dependent with normalise=False; unsigned, >= 0.

metric_name_standard: in-sample mean squared error of an elastic-net regression (sklearn alpha = 1, l1_ratio = 0.5, i.e. naive elastic net with lambda1 = 0.5 and lambda2 = 0.5 on the 1/(2T) loss scale) of y = x_j on x = x_i
canonical_ref: Zou & Hastie 2005, J. R. Stat. Soc. B 67(2):301-320 (naive elastic net, eq. 3; their recommended estimator rescales by (1 + lambda2), section 3.2); coordinate descent solution: Friedman, Hastie & Tibshirani 2010, J Stat Softw 33(1):1-22 (supplement ref [76]); scikit-learn objective (1/(2T)) ||y - Xw||^2 + alpha l1_ratio ||w||_1 + 0.5 alpha (1 - l1_ratio) ||w||^2 (_coordinate_descent.py:884-894)
canonical_definition: single centred predictor: w = S(sum(xc*yc)/T, alpha*l1_ratio) / (sum(xc^2)/T + alpha*(1 - l1_ratio)); MSE = (1/T) sum (y - b - w x)^2. For z-scored inputs with c = (T-1)/T: w = sign(r) max(|r| c - 0.5, 0) / (c + 0.5) and MSE = c (1 - 2 w r + w^2); the exact minimiser has w = 0 and MSE = (T-1)/T only for |r| <= 0.5 T/(T-1). This is the exact minimiser; sklearn's stopped solver returns w = 0 over a wider band (see implemented_as).
