implemented_as: A[i, j] = in-sample MSE of the sklearn ElasticNet(alpha=1.0, l1_ratio=0.5, fit_intercept=True, max_iter=1000, tol=1e-4, selection="cyclic", random_state=42) fit of z_j on z_i. Coordinate descent starts at w = 0 and first evaluates the duality gap there (_cd_fast.pyx:391-400). With one z-scored feature, l1_reg = 0.5 T and s = x.y = r (T-1), that gap is 0.5 y.y (1 - min(1, 0.5 T/|s|))^2 (dual_gap_formulation_A, _cd_fast.pyx:138-159), and the solver returns w = 0 with n_iter_ 0 whenever it is <= tol*y.y = 1e-4 (T-1), i.e. whenever |r| <= 0.5 T/((T-1)(1 - sqrt(2e-4))) (0.51522 at T=64, 0.50916 at 256, 0.50767 at 1024, 0.50730 at 4096). Otherwise one cyclic update reaches the closed form above and the next gap check stops (n_iter_ 2). So pyspi returns (T-1)/T for |r| up to that tol bound, which is wider than the exact-minimiser threshold 0.5 T/(T-1) (0.50794 / 0.50196 / 0.50049 / 0.50012); in the band between them the exact minimiser has w between 0 and ~0.0048 and an MSE up to ~4.8e-3 below (T-1)/T, so the SPI jumps by ~4.8e-3 at the tol bound. Probe (lmfit_fix/fix1.py, 14 datasets x 4 T, 552 ordered pairs): max |A - closed form| = 3.50e-3 (6 pairs fall in the band, e.g. sparse_precision T=64 pair (1,0) r=0.5130: closed form 0.981006, pyspi 0.984375 = 63/64); max |A - closed form with the modelled tol exit| = 2.8e-16. Synthetic sweep (fix2.py, r step 1e-5 around the bound) places sklearn's switch from w = 0 to w != 0 at the modelled bound (1 boundary point of 1604 misclassified, at T=4096). Consequences on z-scored data: every pair with |r| <= ~0.51 gets the constant (T-1)/T (probe: iid_gaussian, delayed_noise, nonlinear_dependence all constant; bivariate_gaussian rho=0.3 pair constant); a perfectly dependent pair (r = 1) gives c (1 - w)^2 with w = (c - 0.5)/(c + 0.5) -> about 4/9 (probe shared_envelope identical pair: 0.4468 at T=64, 0.4445 at T=4096). random_state is inert (selection="cyclic").

deviation_from_documented: (a) Documented as "the Elastic-Net model [76, 77], which uses both l1 and l2-norm regularization" with default parameters: matches the code (alpha=1, l1_ratio=0.5); but ref [77] (Andersen et al., interior-point methods for cone programming) is not the algorithm used (coordinate descent, ref [76]). (b) Not stated: with these defaults the l1 threshold plus the solver's tol-based initial exit zero the coefficient for every pair with |r| <= ~0.51 (0.5 T/((T-1)(1 - sqrt(2e-4)))), so the SPI is the constant (T-1)/T for weak and moderate dependence. (c) "directed": symmetric on z-scored data.
deviation_from_canonical: The estimator is the naive elastic net of Zou & Hastie 2005 (no (1 + lambda2) rescaling of the coefficients, which Zou & Hastie recommend to undo double shrinkage), in sklearn's 1/(2T) loss scaling. It equals the exact minimiser except in a band just above the l1 threshold: sklearn's initial duality-gap exit (tol = 1e-4 relative to y.y) returns w = 0 for 0.5 T/(T-1) < |r| <= 0.5 T/((T-1)(1 - sqrt(2e-4))) where the exact minimiser has w > 0, an MSE overstatement of up to ~4.8e-3 (probe max 3.50e-3 on the audit datasets). The SPI (in-sample MSE at a fixed, large penalty) is a pyspi construction: it saturates at (T-1)/T for |r| up to ~0.51, jumps by ~4.8e-3 at that bound, and cannot fall below ~4/9 even for identical series, so it is a heavily censored, monotone (non-increasing in |r|) function of |r| with one jump discontinuity.
units_and_range: units of the target variance; on z-scored data in [~0.444, (T-1)/T]: (T-1)/T for |r| <= 0.5 T/((T-1)(1 - sqrt(2e-4))) (0.5152 at T=64, 0.5073 at T=4096; the exact-minimiser threshold 0.5 T/(T-1) is lower), then a jump down by ~4.8e-3 and a decrease to c (1 - w)^2 ~ 4/9 at |r| = 1 (probe shared_envelope identical pair 0.4468 at T=64); symmetric under default preprocessing; asymmetric and scale dependent with normalise=False; unsigned, >= 0.
direction_convention: A[i, j] = in-sample MSE of the linear prediction of process j (target, column) from process i (predictor, row), per misc.py:122-126; LOWER = j better linearly predicted from i. Code-derived; with the default z-scoring the matrix is symmetric (see units_and_range), so the direction is only empirically identifiable with normalise=False, where column j scales with var(x_j) (probe on scaled_offset_T1024: column means of A track std_j^2 = 0.0395, 4.058, 24.78, 97.89).

metric_name_standard: in-sample mean squared error of the posterior-mean fit of Bayesian ridge regression (evidence / type-II maximum-likelihood estimates of noise precision alpha and weight precision lambda, Gamma(1e-6, 1e-6) hyperpriors) of y = x_j on x = x_i
canonical_ref: MacKay 1992, Neural Computation 4(3):415-447 ("Bayesian interpolation"), evidence fixed-point updates gamma = sum alpha e/(lambda + alpha e), lambda = gamma/||w||^2, alpha = (N - gamma)/SSE (section 4); Tipping 2001, J. Mach. Learn. Res. 1:211-244 (Gamma hyperpriors, eqs. for the updates with a, b terms); both cited in sklearn/linear_model/_bayes.py:154-160
canonical_definition: w = (X^T X + (lambda/alpha) I)^-1 X^T y with (alpha, lambda) at the fixed point of gamma = alpha*e/(lambda + alpha*e), lambda = (gamma + 2 l1)/(w^2 + 2 l2), alpha = (T - gamma + 2 a1)/(SSE + 2 a2), e = sum(xc^2); MSE = (1/T) sum (y - b - w x)^2
documented_definition: supplement §1.6.1, p.18 (supplement.txt lines 856-868; the briefing pack gives 874-887, which is off by 18 lines): "we use a number of linear models and record the mean squared error (MSE) of a regression of y on x. The following models (with the default parameters) from scikit-learn [2] are included: stochastic gradient descent regression with a squared loss (ordinary least squares fit) function (denoted by modifier SGDRegressor); Ridge regression, which uses l2-norm regularization (Ride); the Elastic-Net model [76, 77], which uses both l1 and l2-norm regularization (ElasticNet); and the Bayesian Ridge regressor uses a gamma distribution prior (with lambda1 = lambda2 = 1e-6) for the l2-norm regularizor in Ridge regression (BayesianRidge). This yields four SPIs: 215. lmfit_SGDRegressor 216. lmfit_Ridge 217. lmfit_ElasticNet 218. lmfit_BayesianRidge"; keywords "directed, linear, unsigned, bivariate, contemporaneous"; rationale "Linear regression is commonly used for establishing independence through model fits (e.g., see additive noise models in Sec. 1.3.1)". GitBook spi-descriptions/miscellaneous.md "Linear Model Fit" repeats the text verbatim (including the typo "Ride") and lists the same four identifiers.

deviation_from_documented: (a) The documentation mentions only the weight-precision hyperprior "(with lambda1 = lambda2 = 1e-6)"; the noise-precision prior alpha_1 = alpha_2 = 1e-6 and the evidence (type-II ML) estimation of both precisions are not described, so readers cannot tell that the effective penalty is data dependent (lambda/alpha ~ 0.48 in the probe, versus Ridge's fixed 1). (b) "directed": symmetric on z-scored data. (c) In-sample MSE and "lower = stronger" not stated.
deviation_from_canonical: none for the estimator: sklearn implements the MacKay 1992 fixed-point updates with Tipping 2001 Gamma hyperpriors (shape/rate 1e-6) on centred data with an unpenalised intercept. The stopping rule (sum|delta w| < 1e-3) is loose, so the returned (alpha, lambda) are a near fixed point; check stage: the MSE differs from the MSE at the evidence maximiser by up to 8.5e-4 at T=64 and 1.0e-5 at T=4096 (misc.lmfit.BayesianRidge|*|pipeline|evidence), and the stop makes the SPI non-monotone in |r| by up to 1.4e-5. The SPI (in-sample MSE of the posterior mean) is a pyspi construction; on z-scored data it is a function of (r, T) only.
units_and_range: units of the target variance; on z-scored data in (0, (T-1)/T]: about 1e-19..1e-26 for identical series (probe shared_envelope), close to the OLS value (T-1)/T (1 - r^2) for strong dependence and approaching (T-1)/T for r ~ 0 (lambda grows as w -> 0); symmetric (<= 7.8e-16) under default preprocessing; asymmetric with normalise=False; unsigned, >= 0.
direction_convention: A[i, j] = in-sample MSE of the linear prediction of process j (target, column) from process i (predictor, row), per misc.py:122-126; LOWER = j better linearly predicted from i. Code-derived; with the default z-scoring the matrix is symmetric (see units_and_range), so the direction is only empirically identifiable with normalise=False, where column j scales with var(x_j) (probe on scaled_offset_T1024: column means of A track std_j^2 = 0.0395, 4.058, 24.78, 97.89).

what_changed: Estimator: sklearn's evidence recursion is reproduced to floating point, including the iteration count. The stopping rule (sum|delta w| < 1e-3) leaves (alpha, lambda) short of the evidence maximiser, so the MSE differs from the MSE at the maximiser by up to 8.5e-4 at T=64 and 1.0e-5 at T=4096. That is far below the sampling spread of the null MSE (about sqrt(2)/T), so it is a sklearn-default convention rather than a different quantity. The same stop makes the SPI slightly non-monotone in |r| (by up to 1.4e-5). The documentation mentions only lambda_1 = lambda_2 = 1e-6 and not the alpha hyperprior or the evidence estimation; the matrix is symmetric under the default preprocessing.

canonical_ref: MacKay 1992, Neural Computation 4(3):415-447 ("Bayesian interpolation"), evidence fixed-point updates gamma = sum alpha e/(lambda + alpha e), lambda = gamma/||w||^2, alpha = (N - gamma)/SSE (section 4); Tipping 2001, J. Mach. Learn. Res. 1:211-244 (Gamma hyperpriors, eqs. for the updates with a, b terms); both cited in sklearn/linear_model/_bayes.py:154-160
canonical_definition: w = (X^T X + (lambda/alpha) I)^-1 X^T y with (alpha, lambda) at the fixed point of gamma = alpha*e/(lambda + alpha*e), lambda = (gamma + 2 l1)/(w^2 + 2 l2), alpha = (T - gamma + 2 a1)/(SSE + 2 a2), e = sum(xc^2); MSE = (1/T) sum (y - b - w x)^2

deviation_from_canonical: none for the estimator: sklearn implements the MacKay 1992 fixed-point updates with Tipping 2001 Gamma hyperpriors (shape/rate 1e-6) on centred data with an unpenalised intercept. metric_name_standard: in-sample mean squared residual of the posterior mean of a Gaussian-process regression of y on x with a dot-product (linear) covariance, constant and white-noise terms, hyperparameters chosen by type-II maximum likelihood; equivalently the training MSE of a Bayesian linear regression of y on x with an N(0, 1) slope prior
canonical_ref: Williams & Rasmussen 1996, NIPS 8:514-520 (supplement ref [78], cited as 1995); Rasmussen & Williams 2006, Gaussian Processes for Machine Learning, MIT Press: Alg. 2.1 (p.19, posterior mean f_bar = K_*^T (K + sigma_n^2 I)^-1 y), §2.1 eqs. 2.8-2.11 (weight-space Bayesian linear regression, posterior mean w_bar = sigma_n^-2 A^-1 X y with A = sigma_n^-2 X X^T + Sigma_p^-1), §4.2.2 (dot-product covariance k = sigma_0^2 + x.x'), §5.4.1 eqs. 5.8-5.9 (log marginal likelihood and its gradient, ML-II). There is no canonical pairwise "GP fit MSE" statistic; the canonical object is the GP posterior mean and its residual.
canonical_definition: With k(x, x') = c + sigma_0^2 + x x' and noise variance s chosen by maximising log p(y | x, theta), the posterior mean is f_bar = K_f (K_f + s I)^-1 y; the score would be (1/T) sum_t (y_t - f_bar_t)^2. For one input this is Bayesian linear regression: slope posterior mean b = x'y / (x'x + s) (unit slope prior), intercept prior variance c + sigma_0^2.
documented_definition: supplement §1.6.2, p.18: 'we also use Gaussian process [78] model fits as a nonparametric measure of influence of x on y. Here, we use a combination of kernels (with parameters chosen from default settings) from the scikit-learn package [2] and compute the MSE of their fit. The fits are computed for the dot-product kernel with inhomogenity parameter sigma_0 = 1 (DotProduct) ... Each of these kernels are separately combined with the constant kernel (with a constant of 1.0) and the white kernel (with a noise level of 1)'; keywords 'directed, nonlinear, unsigned, bivariate, contemporaneous'. implemented_as: A[i, j] = mean((f_bar - z_j)^2) where f_bar is the GP posterior mean at the training inputs z_i (in-sample, not held out), on z-scored (ddof=1) data. Kernel = ConstantKernel(1.0) + WhiteKernel(1.0) + DotProduct(sigma_0=1.0), each with bounds (1e-5, 1e5); the documented values 1.0 are only the L-BFGS-B starting point theta = (0, 0, 0) in log space. One optimiser run, n_restarts_optimizer=0, alpha = 1e-10 jitter, normalize_y=False, random_state=None (unused). The white term enters K(X, X) for the likelihood and the solve but not K(X_test, X_train) (kernels.py:1419 returns zeros), so the prediction is the de-noised posterior mean, not an interpolant. Because z-scored inputs and targets have zero mean and x'x = y'y = T - 1, the constant and sigma_0 terms do not affect the prediction and are driven to their 1e-5 lower bounds (probe: fitted '0.00316**2 + WhiteKernel(noise_level=0.91) + DotProduct(sigma_0=1e-05)' on bivariate_gaussian_T256 0->1), leaving one effective hyperparameter s. The result equals the closed form mean((z_j - b z_i)^2) with b = z_i'z_j / (z_i'z_i + s) to <= 3e-14 relative (4 probes), i.e. approximately ((T-1)/T)(1 - r_ij^2) (max relative difference 6.2e-5 at T=64, 3.8e-6 at T=256 over 18 datasets). Fit warnings (bound ConvergenceWarnings) are suppressed by pyspi.

deviation_from_documented: (a) The documented values (sigma_0 = 1, constant 1.0, noise level 1) are only the starting point; all three hyperparameters are re-estimated per pair by maximising the log marginal likelihood within [1e-5, 1e5]. Fitted values differ from the documented ones: constant and sigma_0 sit at the 1e-5 lower bound in every probe and the noise level is about 1 - r^2 (e.g. 0.91, 0.326, 0.093). (b) Documented as 'nonparametric' and keyword 'nonlinear' (also class label, misc.py:132): the dot-product kernel GP is Bayesian linear regression (R&W §2.1), so the fit is linear and the value is a function of Pearson r and T only (candidate below). (c) Documented as 'directed': the value is symmetric to <= 8.1e-15 absolute on every probed dataset, so the direction is nominal under default preprocessing. (d) 'MSE of their fit' is the in-sample (training) MSE of the posterior mean, which the text implies but does not state.
deviation_from_canonical: (1) The constant and sigma_0 terms are redundant (both add a constant to the covariance), so the model has two non-identifiable hyperparameters. Under z-scoring both are irrelevant and go to the lower bound. (2) The slope prior variance is fixed at 1 (no amplitude hyperparameter), so the slope is ridge-shrunk by (T-1)/(T-1+s); the shrinkage is O(1/T) and invisible at T >= 64. (3) The score is the training MSE of the posterior mean, not a held-out or leave-one-out predictive error (R&W §5.4.2) and not a likelihood. Within the GP framework the computation is otherwise standard: the MSE of an own posterior mean at the fitted hyperparameters reproduces sklearn's MSE to <= 1.9e-15 absolute (the posterior-mean vectors themselves agree elementwise to <= 1.1e-13; 24 DotProduct pairs).
units_and_range: squared units of the target (SD^2 after z-scoring); >= 0; under default z-scoring about ((T-1)/T)(1 - r^2), so in [0, (T-1)/T] (observed 1.5e-15 for the bit-identical copy pair in shared_envelope to 0.996 for independent pairs at T=256); scale-dependent when normalise=False (scaled_offset_T256 raw: 0.036 to 97.3); symmetric in practice (|A - A^T| <= 8.1e-15); NaN matrix if the Cholesky fails.

score_rubric_note: Anchor 10's second clause fails. The supplement gives fixed hyperparameters (sigma_0 = 1, constant 1, noise 1) and calls the fit nonparametric. The code fits all three by ML-II, and the model is Bayesian linear regression. Holding the hyperparameters fixed changes the value by up to 1.5e-4 at T=64. The numeric half holds: 2.4e-9 relative against the independent blr_ml2 optimum (8/8 pipeline runs). No anchor-9 clause names this deviation.
what_changed: The estimator matches canonical GP regression with ML-II hyperparameters. With Constant + White + DotProduct, the GP is Bayesian linear regression, and pyspi's value is the in-sample MSE of the posterior mean at the type-II ML hyperparameters. The deciding reference is independent: on the default (z-scored) path pyspi equals an independent global ML-II optimum (blr_ml2, numpy/scipy only, no sklearn) to <= 2.4e-9 relative (8/8 pipeline scratch runs). The analytic ridge form (ridgecf) and the own Cholesky posterior (posterior, postmean) reproduce pyspi to <= 2.0e-13, but they take sklearn's fitted theta, so they check the posterior algebra and not the hyperparameter fit; the analytic closed form ((T-1)/T)(1 - r^2) agrees only to <= 6.1e-5 (T=64). Score mapping: on the default path the numeric half of anchor 10 is met (2.4e-9 <= 1e-8 relative against an independent reference) and its second half, 'matches the pyspi supplement description', fails, because the supplement misdescribes the computation (§1.6.2; (a) and (b) below). None of the anchor-9 clauses names this case literally: it is not a trivial value convention (squared vs not, ddof, log base, sign), not a tolerance set by estimator variance, and not a MATLAB/author reference. The README has no anchor for 'canonical computation reproduced, supplement wrong'; 9 is the nearest-anchor reading (README "Score columns: original, rubric reading, adjusted") for that case (the highest score below the one anchor-10 condition that fails), applied the same way to misc.coint.johansen_order-0_* and distance.hhg. (a) The documented values sigma_0 = 1, constant 1 and noise 1 are only starting points and are fitted. Holding them fixed changes the value by <= 9.2e-6 at T=256 and <= 1.5e-4 at T=64 on bivariate_gaussian (fixedhp runs); the fixed version is the ridge (alpha = 1) fit. The two versions separate only on correlated pairs: the fitted noise level is about 1 - r^2, which is close to the documented 1 when r is near 0. On near-independent pairs the fixed version agrees with pyspi to 1.5e-10 relative (nonlinear_dependence T256, all |r| <= 0.05), inside rtol 1e-8; correlated pairs separate it by 4.7e-4 (bivariate_gaussian T64), 1.5e-4 (anm T256) and 7.4e-6 (EEG 001_Baseline, 3 channels, T256) (scratch probe wf4b2_high-optimiser-other/p_gpfit.py). The fixedhp runs use bivariate_gaussian, whose pair correlations run from 0.06 to 0.83 at T64 (|r| 0.058-0.827) and from 0.02 to 0.82 at T256 (|r| 0.018-0.821); both datasets contain strongly correlated pairs, so they do separate the two versions. (b) The labels nonlinear and directed, and the word 'nonparametric', do not describe the computation. The value is ((T-1)/T)(1 - r^2) to <= 6.1e-5 relative, symmetric to <= 8.1e-15, and blind to x1 = x0^2 (0.995776 both ways). Other recorded deviations: (1) On raw (normalise=False) data, sklearn's single L-BFGS-B start stops on the factr test along the flat c + sigma_0^2 direction, up to 7.5e-5 below the ML-II maximum, which moves the value by <= 1.35e-4 relative. This is an optimiser tolerance on a non-default path; it does not arise under the default z-scoring, where c and sigma_0 do not affect the prediction. (2) The score is an in-sample error, not a predictive error. The earlier score of 7 rested on reading anchor 7 as a cap for optimiser units; the README has no such cap. Rubric reading is nearest-anchor 9 here and for misc.coint.johansen_order-0_*, but anchor 9 for distance.hhg, whose tie rounding sits under anchor 9's estimator-variance clause (distance.hhg score_rubric_note); the nearest-anchor wording above does not extend to distance.hhg.

metric_name_standard: in-sample mean squared residual of the posterior mean of a Gaussian-process regression of y on x with a dot-product (linear) covariance, constant and white-noise terms, hyperparameters chosen by type-II maximum likelihood; equivalently the training MSE of a Bayesian linear regression of y on x with an N(0, 1) slope prior
canonical_ref: Williams & Rasmussen 1996, NIPS 8:514-520 (supplement ref [78], cited as 1995); Rasmussen & Williams 2006, Gaussian Processes for Machine Learning, MIT Press: Alg. 2.1 (p.19, posterior mean f_bar = K_*^T (K + sigma_n^2 I)^-1 y), §2.1 eqs. 2.8-2.11 (weight-space Bayesian linear regression, posterior mean w_bar = sigma_n^-2 A^-1 X y with A = sigma_n^-2 X X^T + Sigma_p^-1), §4.2.2 (dot-product covariance k = sigma_0^2 + x.x'), §5.4.1 eqs. 5.8-5.9 (log marginal likelihood and its gradient, ML-II). There is no canonical pairwise "GP fit MSE" statistic; the canonical object is the GP posterior mean and its residual.
canonical_definition: With k(x, x') = c + sigma_0^2 + x x' and noise variance s chosen by maximising log p(y | x, theta), the posterior mean is f_bar = K_f (K_f + s I)^-1 y; the score would be (1/T) sum_t (y_t - f_bar_t)^2. For one input this is Bayesian linear regression: slope posterior mean b = x'y / (x'x + s) (unit slope prior), intercept prior variance c + sigma_0^2.
documented_definition: supplement §1.6.2, p.18: 'we also use Gaussian process [78] model fits as a nonparametric measure of influence of x on y. Here, we use a combination of kernels (with parameters chosen from default settings) from the scikit-learn package [2] and compute the MSE of their fit. The fits are computed for the dot-product kernel with inhomogenity parameter sigma_0 = 1 (DotProduct) ... Each of these kernels are separately combined with the constant kernel (with a constant of 1.0) and the white kernel (with a noise level of 1)'; keywords 'directed, nonlinear, unsigned, bivariate, contemporaneous'. GitBook spi-descriptions/miscellaneous.md lines 46-63 repeat the text verbatim and cite Williams & Rasmussen (WilRas96.pdf).
delegate_lib: scikit-learn==1.9.1 sklearn.gaussian_process.GaussianProcessRegressor.fit/predict with kernel ConstantKernel() + WhiteKernel() + DotProduct(); hyperparameters by scipy==1.17.1 scipy.optimize.minimize(method='L-BFGS-B'); score by sklearn.metrics.mean_squared_error
implemented_as: A[i, j] = mean((f_bar - z_j)^2) where f_bar is the GP posterior mean at the training inputs z_i (in-sample, not held out), on z-scored (ddof=1) data. Kernel = ConstantKernel(1.0) + WhiteKernel(1.0) + DotProduct(sigma_0=1.0), each with bounds (1e-5, 1e5); the documented values 1.0 are only the L-BFGS-B starting point theta = (0, 0, 0) in log space. One optimiser run, n_restarts_optimizer=0, alpha = 1e-10 jitter, normalize_y=False, random_state=None (unused). The white term enters K(X, X) for the likelihood and the solve but not K(X_test, X_train) (kernels.py:1419 returns zeros), so the prediction is the de-noised posterior mean, not an interpolant. Because z-scored inputs and targets have zero mean and x'x = y'y = T - 1, the constant and sigma_0 terms do not affect the prediction and are driven to their 1e-5 lower bounds (probe: fitted '0.00316**2 + WhiteKernel(noise_level=0.91) + DotProduct(sigma_0=1e-05)' on bivariate_gaussian_T256 0->1), leaving one effective hyperparameter s. The result equals the closed form mean((z_j - b z_i)^2) with b = z_i'z_j / (z_i'z_i + s) to <= 3e-14 relative (4 probes), i.e. approximately ((T-1)/T)(1 - r_ij^2) (max relative difference 6.2e-5 at T=64, 3.8e-6 at T=256 over 18 datasets). Fit warnings (bound ConvergenceWarnings) are suppressed by pyspi.

deviation_from_documented: (a) The documented values (sigma_0 = 1, constant 1.0, noise level 1) are only the starting point; all three hyperparameters are re-estimated per pair by maximising the log marginal likelihood within [1e-5, 1e5]. Fitted values differ from the documented ones: constant and sigma_0 sit at the 1e-5 lower bound in every probe and the noise level is about 1 - r^2 (e.g. 0.91, 0.326, 0.093). (b) Documented as 'nonparametric' and keyword 'nonlinear' (also class label, misc.py:132): the dot-product kernel GP is Bayesian linear regression (R&W §2.1), so the fit is linear and the value is a function of Pearson r and T only (candidate below). (c) Documented as 'directed': the value is symmetric to <= 8.1e-15 absolute on every probed dataset, so the direction is nominal under default preprocessing. (d) 'MSE of their fit' is the in-sample (training) MSE of the posterior mean, which the text implies but does not state.
deviation_from_canonical: (1) The constant and sigma_0 terms are redundant (both add a constant to the covariance), so the model has two non-identifiable hyperparameters. Under z-scoring both are irrelevant and go to the lower bound. (2) The slope prior variance is fixed at 1 (no amplitude hyperparameter), so the slope is ridge-shrunk by (T-1)/(T-1+s); the shrinkage is O(1/T) and invisible at T >= 64. (3) The score is the training MSE of the posterior mean, not a held-out or leave-one-out predictive error (R&W §5.4.2) and not a likelihood. Within the GP framework the computation is otherwise standard: the MSE of an own posterior mean at the fitted hyperparameters reproduces sklearn's MSE to <= 1.9e-15 absolute (the posterior-mean vectors themselves agree elementwise to <= 1.1e-13; 24 DotProduct pairs).
units_and_range: squared units of the target (SD^2 after z-scoring); >= 0; under default z-scoring about ((T-1)/T)(1 - r^2), so in [0, (T-1)/T] (observed 1.5e-15 for the bit-identical copy pair in shared_envelope to 0.996 for independent pairs at T=256); scale-dependent when normalise=False (scaled_offset_T256 raw: 0.036 to 97.3); symmetric in practice (|A - A^T| <= 8.1e-15); NaN matrix if the Cholesky fails.
direction_convention: A[i, j] = MSE of predicting process j (target, np.ravel(z[j])) from process i (input, z[i]), from misc.py:145-147 and base.py:91-93. Lower means i linearly predicts j better. For this kernel A[i, j] = A[j, i] to rounding under default preprocessing, so the convention is not observable from the values under z-scoring; confirmed in the check stage on raw data (misc.gpfit.DotProduct|scaled_offset|256|kernel|direction: A[i, j] scales with var(x_j)).

score_rubric_note: Anchor 10's second clause fails. The supplement gives fixed hyperparameters (sigma_0 = 1, constant 1, noise 1) and calls the fit nonparametric. The code fits all three by ML-II, and the model is Bayesian linear regression. Holding the hyperparameters fixed changes the value by up to 1.5e-4 at T=64. The numeric half holds: 2.4e-9 relative against the independent blr_ml2 optimum (8/8 pipeline runs). No anchor-9 clause names this deviation.
what_changed: The estimator matches canonical GP regression with ML-II hyperparameters. With Constant + White + DotProduct, the GP is Bayesian linear regression, and pyspi's value is the in-sample MSE of the posterior mean at the type-II ML hyperparameters. The deciding reference is independent: on the default (z-scored) path pyspi equals an independent global ML-II optimum (blr_ml2, numpy/scipy only, no sklearn) to <= 2.4e-9 relative (8/8 pipeline scratch runs). The analytic ridge form (ridgecf) and the own Cholesky posterior (posterior, postmean) reproduce pyspi to <= 2.0e-13, but they take sklearn's fitted theta, so they check the posterior algebra and not the hyperparameter fit; the analytic closed form ((T-1)/T)(1 - r^2) agrees only to <= 6.1e-5 (T=64). Score mapping: on the default path the numeric half of anchor 10 is met (2.4e-9 <= 1e-8 relative against an independent reference) and its second half, 'matches the pyspi supplement description', fails, because the supplement misdescribes the computation (§1.6.2; (a) and (b) below). None of the anchor-9 clauses names this case literally: it is not a trivial value convention (squared vs not, ddof, log base, sign), not a tolerance set by estimator variance, and not a MATLAB/author reference. The README has no anchor for 'canonical computation reproduced, supplement wrong'; 9 is the nearest-anchor reading (README "Score columns: original, rubric reading, adjusted") for that case (the highest score below the one anchor-10 condition that fails), applied the same way to misc.coint.johansen_order-0_* and distance.hhg. (a) The documented values sigma_0 = 1, constant 1 and noise 1 are only starting points and are fitted. Holding them fixed changes the value by <= 9.2e-6 at T=256 and <= 1.5e-4 at T=64 on bivariate_gaussian (fixedhp runs); the fixed version is the ridge (alpha = 1) fit. The two versions separate only on correlated pairs: the fitted noise level is about 1 - r^2, which is close to the documented 1 when r is near 0. On near-independent pairs the fixed version agrees with pyspi to 1.5e-10 relative (nonlinear_dependence T256, all |r| <= 0.05), inside rtol 1e-8; correlated pairs separate it by 4.7e-4 (bivariate_gaussian T64), 1.5e-4 (anm T256) and 7.4e-6 (EEG 001_Baseline, 3 channels, T256) (scratch probe wf4b2_high-optimiser-other/p_gpfit.py). The fixedhp runs use bivariate_gaussian, whose pair correlations run from 0.06 to 0.83 at T64 (|r| 0.058-0.827) and from 0.02 to 0.82 at T256 (|r| 0.018-0.821); both datasets contain strongly correlated pairs, so they do separate the two versions. (b) The labels nonlinear and directed, and the word 'nonparametric', do not describe the computation. The value is ((T-1)/T)(1 - r^2) to <= 6.1e-5 relative, symmetric to <= 8.1e-15, and blind to x1 = x0^2 (0.995776 both ways). Other recorded deviations: (1) On raw (normalise=False) data, sklearn's single L-BFGS-B start stops on the factr test along the flat c + sigma_0^2 direction, up to 7.5e-5 below the ML-II maximum, which moves the value by <= 1.35e-4 relative. This is an optimiser tolerance on a non-default path; it does not arise under the default z-scoring, where c and sigma_0 do not affect the prediction. (2) The score is an in-sample error, not a predictive error. The earlier score of 7 rested on reading anchor 7 as a cap for optimiser units; the README has no such cap. Rubric reading is nearest-anchor 9 here and for misc.coint.johansen_order-0_*, but anchor 9 for distance.hhg, whose tie rounding sits under anchor 9's estimator-variance clause (distance.hhg score_rubric_note); the nearest-anchor wording above does not extend to distance.hhg.

metric_name_standard: in-sample mean squared residual of the posterior mean of a Gaussian-process regression of y on x with a squared-exponential (RBF) covariance plus constant and white-noise terms, hyperparameters chosen by type-II maximum likelihood (single L-BFGS-B start)
canonical_ref: Williams & Rasmussen 1996, NIPS 8:514-520 (supplement ref [78], cited as 1995); Rasmussen & Williams 2006, Gaussian Processes for Machine Learning, MIT Press: Alg. 2.1 (p.19, posterior mean f_bar = K_*^T (K + sigma_n^2 I)^-1 y), eq. 2.31 (SE covariance with signal variance, k_y = sigma_f^2 exp(-(x - x')^2 / (2 l^2)) + sigma_n^2 delta), eq. 4.9 (SE kernel), §5.4.1 eqs. 5.8-5.9 (log marginal likelihood, ML-II, gradient; notes that multiple local optima exist and correspond to different interpretations of the data), §5.4.2 eq. 5.12 (leave-one-out predictive residual). There is no canonical pairwise "GP fit MSE" statistic; the canonical object is the GP posterior mean and its residual.
canonical_definition: With k(x, x') = c + sigma_f^2 exp(-(x - x')^2 / (2 l^2)) and noise variance s chosen by maximising log p(y | x, theta) (the global maximum, in practice approximated by several starts), the posterior mean is f_bar = K_f (K_f + s I)^-1 y; the score would be (1/T) sum_t (y_t - f_bar_t)^2, or the leave-one-out version r_t = [K^-1 y]_t / [K^-1]_tt if a predictive error is wanted.
documented_definition: supplement §1.6.2, p.18: 'we also use Gaussian process [78] model fits as a nonparametric measure of influence of x on y. Here, we use a combination of kernels (with parameters chosen from default settings) from the scikit-learn package [2] and compute the MSE of their fit. The fits are computed for ... the radial basis function (RBF) kernel with length scale l = 1 (RBF). Each of these kernels are separately combined with the constant kernel (with a constant of 1.0) and the white kernel (with a noise level of 1)'; keywords 'directed, nonlinear, unsigned, bivariate, contemporaneous'. GitBook spi-descriptions/miscellaneous.md lines 46-63 repeat the text verbatim and cite Williams & Rasmussen (WilRas96.pdf).
delegate_lib: scikit-learn==1.9.1 sklearn.gaussian_process.GaussianProcessRegressor.fit/predict with kernel ConstantKernel() + WhiteKernel() + RBF(); hyperparameters by scipy==1.17.1 scipy.optimize.minimize(method='L-BFGS-B'); score by sklearn.metrics.mean_squared_error
implemented_as: A[i, j] = mean((f_bar - z_j)^2) where f_bar is the GP posterior mean at the training inputs z_i (in-sample, not held out), on z-scored (ddof=1) data. Kernel = ConstantKernel(1.0) + WhiteKernel(1.0) + RBF(length_scale=1.0), k(x, x') = c + w delta + exp(-(x - x')^2 / (2 l^2)): the RBF amplitude is FIXED at 1 (the constant is added, not multiplied), so there is no signal-variance hyperparameter. c, w, l have bounds (1e-5, 1e5); the documented values 1.0 are only the L-BFGS-B starting point theta = (0, 0, 0) in log space. One optimiser run (n_restarts_optimizer=0), alpha = 1e-10 jitter, normalize_y=False, random_state=None (unused). The white term enters K(X, X) but not K(X_test, X_train) (kernels.py:1419), so the prediction is the de-noised posterior mean; an RBF with l below the input spacing, however, has Gram ~ I and is counted as signal, so the posterior mean then interpolates y. Probes: independent pairs give l -> 2e3..1e5 (upper bound 1e5), w ~ 1, A = (T-1)/T to 6 digits (0.996094 at T=256, 0.984375 at T=64); Gaussian pairs give l ~ 2-5 and A within 6.3e-2 relative of ((T-1)/T)(1 - r^2) at T=256; pyspi's own value equals the MSE of a from-scratch posterior mean at sklearn's fitted hyperparameters to <= 1.9e-15 absolute (the posterior-mean vectors themselves differ elementwise by up to 4.3e-13, np.linalg.solve vs sklearn's Cholesky; 24 RBF pairs). Fit warnings are suppressed by pyspi.

deviation_from_documented: (a) The documented values (l = 1, constant 1.0, noise level 1) are only the starting point; all three hyperparameters are re-estimated per pair by maximising the log marginal likelihood within [1e-5, 1e5]. Fitted values range from l = 1e-5 to 1e5, c mostly at its 1e-5 lower bound, w from 1e-5 to 1. (b) 'MSE of their fit' is the in-sample (training) MSE of the posterior mean; with a flexible kernel this can be ~0 without any predictive skill (candidate below). (c) The values depend on which local optimum the single start reaches, which the documentation does not mention.
deviation_from_canonical: (1) No signal-variance hyperparameter: the RBF amplitude is fixed at 1 (R&W eq. 2.31 has sigma_f^2), because the constant kernel is added rather than multiplied. For z-scored data with no dependence the model cannot switch the RBF off; it can only make it a constant (l -> upper bound, acting as a random intercept) or a unit-variance white-noise-like term (l -> below the input spacing). The two modes have similar likelihood but opposite predictions (candidate below). (2) Hyperparameters from one L-BFGS-B start, not the ML-II maximum; probes find the single start below the best multi-start likelihood (iid_gaussian_T256 0->1: -365.5228 vs -362.6346). (3) Score is the training MSE of the posterior mean, not a held-out or leave-one-out predictive error (R&W §5.4.2) and not a likelihood. Given the hyperparameters, the posterior mean itself is standard (own implementation's MSE agrees to <= 1.9e-15; its f_bar agrees elementwise to <= 4.3e-13).
units_and_range: squared units of the target (SD^2 after z-scoring); >= 0; under default z-scoring in [0, about (T-1)/T]: independent pairs give (T-1)/T (0.996094 at T=256), interpolating fits give ~1e-10 ((w/(1+w))^2 (T-1)/T with w at the 1e-5 bound); scale-dependent when normalise=False (scaled_offset_T256 raw: 0.036 to 97.3); asymmetric (|A - A^T| up to 0.99 on narrowband_f0-0.4 and 0.97 on nonlinear_dependence); NaN matrix if the Cholesky fails.

score_rubric_note: Anchor 6: the code fits hyperparameters that the supplement fixes (fixed minus fitted up to 0.661, shared_envelope T64). The additive constant kernel and the single start depart from ML-II GP regression (multistart 0/11 pass).
what_changed: Given its hyperparameters the posterior mean and MSE are standard (fp-exact on an independent GP), and an independent single L-BFGS-B start from theta = 0 reproduces pyspi's values to <= 2.1e-7 (<= 1.7e-11 outside shared_envelope). The statistic nevertheless deviates from both references in an interpretable way (anchor 6). From the supplement: l, the constant and the noise are fitted, not fixed at 1. From canonical GP regression: (1) The constant kernel is added, not multiplied, so the RBF amplitude is fixed at 1. With that kernel the ML-II maximum is degenerate on pairs without strong dependence. The better optimum interpolates (w at 1e-5, l below the input spacing, MSE (w'/(1 + w'))^2 (T-1)/T about 1e-10) with no predictive skill. (2) pyspi uses a single start, not the ML-II maximum. The value is the fit reached from theta = 0, which is below the multi-start optimum on 100 of 128 pairs. That fit either sends l to the 1e5 bound and returns (T-1)/T for independent pairs, or misses cross-validated structure (narrowband_f0-0.1 T64 1->0: 0.483 against 0.023, LOO 0.520 against 0.056). (3) On noise-free periodic data, the single start itself lands in an interpolating optimum (shared_envelope T64 0->1: A = 1.1e-8, LOO 0.50). (4) The score is an in-sample MSE, so it is not bounded by the linear fit: on Gaussian and independent pairs it exceeds Ridge by up to 0.0063. Score 6, not 7: the optimiser unit fails the global optimality check, and local optimality fails marginally on 2 of 12 runs.

metric_name_standard: in-sample mean squared residual of the posterior mean of a Gaussian-process regression of y on x with a squared-exponential (RBF) covariance plus constant and white-noise terms, hyperparameters chosen by type-II maximum likelihood (single L-BFGS-B start)
canonical_ref: Williams & Rasmussen 1996, NIPS 8:514-520 (supplement ref [78], cited as 1995); Rasmussen & Williams 2006, Gaussian Processes for Machine Learning, MIT Press: Alg. 2.1 (p.19, posterior mean f_bar = K_*^T (K + sigma_n^2 I)^-1 y), eq. 2.31 (SE covariance with signal variance, k_y = sigma_f^2 exp(-(x - x')^2 / (2 l^2)) + sigma_n^2 delta), eq. 4.9 (SE kernel), §5.4.1 eqs. 5.8-5.9 (log marginal likelihood, ML-II, gradient; notes that multiple local optima exist and correspond to different interpretations of the data), §5.4.2 eq. 5.12 (leave-one-out predictive residual). There is no canonical pairwise "GP fit MSE" statistic; the canonical object is the GP posterior mean and its residual.
canonical_definition: With k(x, x') = c + sigma_f^2 exp(-(x - x')^2 / (2 l^2)) and noise variance s chosen by maximising log p(y | x, theta) (the global maximum, in practice approximated by several starts), the posterior mean is f_bar = K_f (K_f + s I)^-1 y; the score would be (1/T) sum_t (y_t - f_bar_t)^2, or the leave-one-out version r_t = [K^-1 y]_t / [K^-1]_tt if a predictive error is wanted.
documented_definition: supplement §1.6.2, p.18: 'we also use Gaussian process [78] model fits as a nonparametric measure of influence of x on y. Here, we use a combination of kernels (with parameters chosen from default settings) from the scikit-learn package [2] and compute the MSE of their fit. The fits are computed for ... the radial basis function (RBF) kernel with length scale l = 1 (RBF). Each of these kernels are separately combined with the constant kernel (with a constant of 1.0) and the white kernel (with a noise level of 1)'; keywords 'directed, nonlinear, unsigned, bivariate, contemporaneous'. GitBook spi-descriptions/miscellaneous.md lines 46-63 repeat the text verbatim and cite Williams & Rasmussen (WilRas96.pdf).
delegate_lib: scikit-learn==1.9.1 sklearn.gaussian_process.GaussianProcessRegressor.fit/predict with kernel ConstantKernel() + WhiteKernel() + RBF(); hyperparameters by scipy==1.17.1 scipy.optimize.minimize(method='L-BFGS-B'); score by sklearn.metrics.mean_squared_error
implemented_as: A[i, j] = mean((f_bar - z_j)^2) where f_bar is the GP posterior mean at the training inputs z_i (in-sample, not held out), on z-scored (ddof=1) data. Kernel = ConstantKernel(1.0) + WhiteKernel(1.0) + RBF(length_scale=1.0), k(x, x') = c + w delta + exp(-(x - x')^2 / (2 l^2)): the RBF amplitude is FIXED at 1 (the constant is added, not multiplied), so there is no signal-variance hyperparameter. c, w, l have bounds (1e-5, 1e5); the documented values 1.0 are only the L-BFGS-B starting point theta = (0, 0, 0) in log space. One optimiser run (n_restarts_optimizer=0), alpha = 1e-10 jitter, normalize_y=False, random_state=None (unused). The white term enters K(X, X) but not K(X_test, X_train) (kernels.py:1419), so the prediction is the de-noised posterior mean; an RBF with l below the input spacing, however, has Gram ~ I and is counted as signal, so the posterior mean then interpolates y. Probes: independent pairs give l -> 2e3..1e5 (upper bound 1e5), w ~ 1, A = (T-1)/T to 6 digits (0.996094 at T=256, 0.984375 at T=64); Gaussian pairs give l ~ 2-5 and A within 6.3e-2 relative of ((T-1)/T)(1 - r^2) at T=256; pyspi's own value equals the MSE of a from-scratch posterior mean at sklearn's fitted hyperparameters to <= 1.9e-15 absolute (the posterior-mean vectors themselves differ elementwise by up to 4.3e-13, np.linalg.solve vs sklearn's Cholesky; 24 RBF pairs). Fit warnings are suppressed by pyspi.

deviation_from_canonical: (1) No signal-variance hyperparameter: the RBF amplitude is fixed at 1 (R&W eq. 2.31 has sigma_f^2), because the constant kernel is added rather than multiplied. For z-scored data with no dependence the model cannot switch the RBF off; it can only make it a constant (l -> upper bound, acting as a random intercept) or a unit-variance white-noise-like term (l -> below the input spacing). The two modes have similar likelihood but opposite predictions (candidate below). score_rubric_note: Anchor 6: the code fits hyperparameters that the supplement fixes (fixed minus fitted up to 0.661, shared_envelope T64). The additive constant kernel and the single start depart from ML-II GP regression (multistart 0/11 pass).
what_changed: Given its hyperparameters the posterior mean and MSE are standard (fp-exact on an independent GP), and an independent single L-BFGS-B start from theta = 0 reproduces pyspi's values to <= 2.1e-7 (<= 1.7e-11 outside shared_envelope). The statistic nevertheless deviates from both references in an interpretable way (anchor 6). From the supplement: l, the constant and the noise are fitted, not fixed at 1. From canonical GP regression: (1) The constant kernel is added, not multiplied, so the RBF amplitude is fixed at 1. With that kernel the ML-II maximum is degenerate on pairs without strong dependence. The better optimum interpolates (w at 1e-5, l below the input spacing, MSE (w'/(1 + w'))^2 (T-1)/T about 1e-10) with no predictive skill. (2) pyspi uses a single start, not the ML-II maximum. The value is the fit reached from theta = 0, which is below the multi-start optimum on 100 of 128 pairs. That fit either sends l to the 1e5 bound and returns (T-1)/T for independent pairs, or misses cross-validated structure (narrowband_f0-0.1 T64 1->0: 0.483 against 0.023, LOO 0.520 against 0.056). (3) On noise-free periodic data, the single start itself lands in an interpolating optimum (shared_envelope T64 0->1: A = 1.1e-8, LOO 0.50). (4) The score is an in-sample MSE, so it is not bounded by the linear fit: on Gaussian and independent pairs it exceeds Ridge by up to 0.0063. Score 6, not 7: the optimiser unit fails the global optimality check, and local optimality fails marginally on 2 of 12 runs.

metric_name_standard: Johansen cointegration rank test statistics for r=0 in a bivariate VECM: lambda-max (max_eig_stat) and trace (trace_stat); unrestricted constant, 10 lagged differences
canonical_ref: Johansen S. 1988, J. Economic Dynamics and Control 12(2-3):231-254, "Statistical analysis of cointegration vectors" (LR trace test, eq. for -2lnQ); Johansen S. 1991, Econometrica 59(6):1551-1580 (deterministic terms, lambda-max); Johansen S. & Juselius K. 1990, Oxford Bull. Econ. Stat. 52(2):169-210 (models H1, H1*, constant restricted/unrestricted); Lutkepohl 2005, New Introduction to Multiple Time Series Analysis, §7.2 / §8.2 (statsmodels docstring reference)
canonical_definition: R0t, R1t = residuals of Delta y_t and y_(t-1) on lagged differences Delta y_(t-1..t-k) and deterministic terms D_t; S_ij = m^-1 sum R_it R_jt'; lambda_1 >= lambda_2 solve |lambda S11 - S10 S00^-1 S01| = 0; trace(r) = -m sum_(i=r+1..n) ln(1-lambda_i), lambda-max(r) = -m ln(1-lambda_(r+1)); here n=2, r=0. Deterministic case: unrestricted constant (H1(r)).
documented_definition: supplement §1.6.3, p.19 (heading supplement.txt line 885, text 886-899): "If two time series are individually integrated but some linear combination of them has a lower order of integration, then the series are said to be cointegrated [79]. We implement statistics for quantifying the cointegration of bivariate time series from two tests included in v0.12.0 of statsmodels [75]: the Augmented Engle-Granger (AEG, modifier aeg) [80] two-step test and the Johansen test (johansen) [81]." Keywords: "undirected, linear, unsigned, bivariate, time-dependent". [80] = Engle & Granger 1987 Econometrica 55, 251; [81] = Pesaran & Shin 1999 (ARDL bounds approach), not Johansen. GitBook spi-descriptions/miscellaneous.md:13-41 has the same text (Key References link to JSTOR 1913236 = Engle & Granger 1987 and to the Pesaran-Shin ARDL chapter). Johansen bullet (supplement.txt:896-899): "For the Johansen test, we output both the maximum eigenvalue (modifier max_eig_stat) and the trace (trace_stat) of the vector error correction model. Similar to the AEG test, we also assume a constant (order-0) or constant and linear trend (order-1) and fixed autoregressive lags of 1 (ardiff-1) and 10 (ardiff-10)." Listed as SPIs 221-228.

metric_name_standard: Johansen cointegration rank test statistics for r=0 in a bivariate VECM: lambda-max (max_eig_stat) and trace (trace_stat); unrestricted constant, 1 lagged difference
canonical_ref: Johansen S. 1988, J. Economic Dynamics and Control 12(2-3):231-254, "Statistical analysis of cointegration vectors" (LR trace test, eq. for -2lnQ); Johansen S. 1991, Econometrica 59(6):1551-1580 (deterministic terms, lambda-max); Johansen S. & Juselius K. 1990, Oxford Bull. Econ. Stat. 52(2):169-210 (models H1, H1*, constant restricted/unrestricted); Lutkepohl 2005, New Introduction to Multiple Time Series Analysis, §7.2 / §8.2 (statsmodels docstring reference)
canonical_definition: R0t, R1t = residuals of Delta y_t and y_(t-1) on lagged differences Delta y_(t-1..t-k) and deterministic terms D_t; S_ij = m^-1 sum R_it R_jt'; lambda_1 >= lambda_2 solve |lambda S11 - S10 S00^-1 S01| = 0; trace(r) = -m sum_(i=r+1..n) ln(1-lambda_i), lambda-max(r) = -m ln(1-lambda_(r+1)); here n=2, r=0. Deterministic case: unrestricted constant (H1(r)).
documented_definition: supplement §1.6.3, p.19 (heading supplement.txt line 885, text 886-899): "If two time series are individually integrated but some linear combination of them has a lower order of integration, then the series are said to be cointegrated [79]. We implement statistics for quantifying the cointegration of bivariate time series from two tests included in v0.12.0 of statsmodels [75]: the Augmented Engle-Granger (AEG, modifier aeg) [80] two-step test and the Johansen test (johansen) [81]." Keywords: "undirected, linear, unsigned, bivariate, time-dependent". [80] = Engle & Granger 1987 Econometrica 55, 251; [81] = Pesaran & Shin 1999 (ARDL bounds approach), not Johansen. GitBook spi-descriptions/miscellaneous.md:13-41 has the same text (Key References link to JSTOR 1913236 = Engle & Granger 1987 and to the Pesaran-Shin ARDL chapter). Johansen bullet (supplement.txt:896-899): "For the Johansen test, we output both the maximum eigenvalue (modifier max_eig_stat) and the trace (trace_stat) of the vector error correction model. Similar to the AEG test, we also assume a constant (order-0) or constant and linear trend (order-1) and fixed autoregressive lags of 1 (ardiff-1) and 10 (ardiff-10)." Listed as SPIs 221-228.

For each unordered pair the first call bivariate(i=hi, j=lo) runs statsmodels coint_johansen on the (T x 2) matrix [z_hi, z_lo] with det_order=0: levels demeaned (vecm.py:670, OLS on a constant), differences/lagged differences/lagged levels demeaned on the effective sample (f=0, vecm.py:665-667, :674, :678, :683) = unrestricted constant in the VECM. VECM Delta y_t = Pi y_(t-1) + sum_(i=1..1) G_i Delta y_(t-i) + D_t + e_t (VAR order 2); eigenvalues a_1 >= a_2 of S_kk^-1 S_k0 S_00^-1 S_0k from residual moment matrices over m = T-1-1 samples. Returned: max_eig_stat = -m log(1-a_1) and trace_stat = -m [log(1-a_1)+log(1-a_2)] (tests of r=0). One fit serves both identifiers. Column order does not matter (probe: max relative swap difference <= 1.3e-11). Critical values, rank decision and eigenvectors are discarded.

score_rubric_note: Anchor 10's second clause fails. The supplement calls the outputs the 'maximum eigenvalue' and 'trace' of the VECM and the parameter 'autoregressive lags of 1'. The code returns the rank-0 LR statistics with 1 lagged difference (VAR order 2). The numeric half holds: 8/8 against textbook RRR case 3 (max_rel 5.2e-14) and 8/8 against R urca ca.jo (max_rel 3.3e-13). No anchor-9 clause names this deviation.
what_changed: Value: none. pyspi stores the Johansen lambda-max and trace statistics for r = 0 with an unrestricted constant (Johansen-Juselius H1, urca ecdet='none'), fp-exact against the textbook RRR, the kernel and R urca. Score mapping (as for johansen_order-0_ardiff-10, whose note section covers both): the numeric half of anchor 10 is met (fp-exact against the textbook RRR case 3, 8/8 at max_rel 5.2e-14, and R urca ca.jo, 8/8 at max_rel 3.3e-13, both independent of statsmodels), and its second half, 'matches the pyspi supplement description', fails: the supplement calls the outputs the 'maximum eigenvalue' and 'trace' of the VECM and the parameter 'autoregressive lags of 1'. These are description errors, not one of anchor 9's trivial value conventions, so 9 is the nearest-anchor reading (score_rubric_note). The own kernel (_kernels_basic_misc.johansen, 19/19 at max_rel 1.35e-12) transcribes statsmodels' placement of the deterministic terms, so it does not carry the independent-impl label. Conventions: 'ardiff' counts lagged differences (VAR order k+1) where the supplement says 'autoregressive lags'; 'maximum eigenvalue' and 'trace' name the LR statistics. Interpretation limits (not value defects): the statistic is large for any pair of stationary series (confound runs) and its null distribution on driftless walks is not the tabulated case-3 one (size runs); pyspi discards the critical values anyway. Robustness defects: a duplicated channel blanks the whole matrix; an exactly collinear pair can return silent out-of-range values.

metric_name_standard: Johansen cointegration rank test statistics for r=0 in a bivariate VECM: lambda-max (max_eig_stat) and trace (trace_stat); statsmodels det_order=1 (pre-detrended levels), 10 lagged differences
canonical_ref: Johansen S. 1988, J. Economic Dynamics and Control 12(2-3):231-254, "Statistical analysis of cointegration vectors" (LR trace test, eq. for -2lnQ); Johansen S. 1991, Econometrica 59(6):1551-1580 (deterministic terms, lambda-max); Johansen S. & Juselius K. 1990, Oxford Bull. Econ. Stat. 52(2):169-210 (models H1, H1*, constant restricted/unrestricted); Lutkepohl 2005, New Introduction to Multiple Time Series Analysis, §7.2 / §8.2 (statsmodels docstring reference)
canonical_definition: R0t, R1t = residuals of Delta y_t and y_(t-1) on lagged differences Delta y_(t-1..t-k) and deterministic terms D_t; S_ij = m^-1 sum R_it R_jt'; lambda_1 >= lambda_2 solve |lambda S11 - S10 S00^-1 S01| = 0; trace(r) = -m sum_(i=r+1..n) ln(1-lambda_i), lambda-max(r) = -m ln(1-lambda_(r+1)); here n=2, r=0. Documented "constant and linear trend" most naturally maps to the restricted-trend case H*(r) (trend in the cointegration space, unrestricted constant; urca ecdet="trend").
documented_definition: supplement §1.6.3, p.19 (heading supplement.txt line 885, text 886-899): "If two time series are individually integrated but some linear combination of them has a lower order of integration, then the series are said to be cointegrated [79]. We implement statistics for quantifying the cointegration of bivariate time series from two tests included in v0.12.0 of statsmodels [75]: the Augmented Engle-Granger (AEG, modifier aeg) [80] two-step test and the Johansen test (johansen) [81]." Keywords: "undirected, linear, unsigned, bivariate, time-dependent". [80] = Engle & Granger 1987 Econometrica 55, 251; [81] = Pesaran & Shin 1999 (ARDL bounds approach), not Johansen. GitBook spi-descriptions/miscellaneous.md:13-41 has the same text (Key References link to JSTOR 1913236 = Engle & Granger 1987 and to the Pesaran-Shin ARDL chapter). Johansen bullet (supplement.txt:896-899): "For the Johansen test, we output both the maximum eigenvalue (modifier max_eig_stat) and the trace (trace_stat) of the vector error correction model. Similar to the AEG test, we also assume a constant (order-0) or constant and linear trend (order-1) and fixed autoregressive lags of 1 (ardiff-1) and 10 (ardiff-10)." Listed as SPIs 221-228.

For each unordered pair the first call bivariate(i=hi, j=lo) runs statsmodels coint_johansen on the (T x 2) matrix [z_hi, z_lo] with det_order=1: full-sample linear trend removed from levels by OLS on np.vander(linspace(-1,1,T), 2) (vecm.py:650-653, :670); differences, lagged differences and lagged levels then only demeaned (f=0). VECM Delta y_t = Pi y_(t-1) + sum_(i=1..10) G_i Delta y_(t-i) + D_t + e_t (VAR order 11); eigenvalues a_1 >= a_2 of S_kk^-1 S_k0 S_00^-1 S_0k from residual moment matrices over m = T-10-1 samples. Returned: max_eig_stat = -m log(1-a_1) and trace_stat = -m [log(1-a_1)+log(1-a_2)] (tests of r=0). One fit serves both identifiers. Column order does not matter (probe: max relative swap difference <= 1.3e-11). Critical values, rank decision and eigenvectors are discarded.

what_changed: det_order=1 is LeSage's/statsmodels' scheme: the levels are detrended by full-sample OLS on [1, t] and the VECM is then fitted with an unrestricted constant (reproduced exactly by ca.jo ecdet='none' on detrended levels). It is not Johansen's restricted-trend case 4 (urca ecdet='trend'): relative gaps up to 0.195 (trace, k=10, T=256) that persist at T=4096 (0.26-0.38 on non-cointegrated pairs). It approaches the unrestricted-trend case 5 (gap <= 1.2e-3 for k=1 and <= 1.1e-2 for k=10 at T=4096), and statsmodels' det_order-1 critical values are case-5 quantiles (cvmc). So the supplement's 'constant and linear trend' is implemented as a finite-sample approximation of case 5. On driftless walks the case-5 tables over-reject (trace 0.19-0.22 at the 5% value). Same robustness and confound limits as the order-0 units.

metric_name_standard: Johansen cointegration rank test statistics for r=0 in a bivariate VECM: lambda-max (max_eig_stat) and trace (trace_stat); statsmodels det_order=1 (pre-detrended levels), 1 lagged difference
canonical_ref: Johansen S. 1988, J. Economic Dynamics and Control 12(2-3):231-254, "Statistical analysis of cointegration vectors" (LR trace test, eq. for -2lnQ); Johansen S. 1991, Econometrica 59(6):1551-1580 (deterministic terms, lambda-max); Johansen S. & Juselius K. 1990, Oxford Bull. Econ. Stat. 52(2):169-210 (models H1, H1*, constant restricted/unrestricted); Lutkepohl 2005, New Introduction to Multiple Time Series Analysis, §7.2 / §8.2 (statsmodels docstring reference)
canonical_definition: R0t, R1t = residuals of Delta y_t and y_(t-1) on lagged differences Delta y_(t-1..t-k) and deterministic terms D_t; S_ij = m^-1 sum R_it R_jt'; lambda_1 >= lambda_2 solve |lambda S11 - S10 S00^-1 S01| = 0; trace(r) = -m sum_(i=r+1..n) ln(1-lambda_i), lambda-max(r) = -m ln(1-lambda_(r+1)); here n=2, r=0. Documented "constant and linear trend" most naturally maps to the restricted-trend case H*(r) (trend in the cointegration space, unrestricted constant; urca ecdet="trend").
documented_definition: supplement §1.6.3, p.19 (heading supplement.txt line 885, text 886-899): "If two time series are individually integrated but some linear combination of them has a lower order of integration, then the series are said to be cointegrated [79]. We implement statistics for quantifying the cointegration of bivariate time series from two tests included in v0.12.0 of statsmodels [75]: the Augmented Engle-Granger (AEG, modifier aeg) [80] two-step test and the Johansen test (johansen) [81]." Keywords: "undirected, linear, unsigned, bivariate, time-dependent". [80] = Engle & Granger 1987 Econometrica 55, 251; [81] = Pesaran & Shin 1999 (ARDL bounds approach), not Johansen. GitBook spi-descriptions/miscellaneous.md:13-41 has the same text (Key References link to JSTOR 1913236 = Engle & Granger 1987 and to the Pesaran-Shin ARDL chapter). Johansen bullet (supplement.txt:896-899): "For the Johansen test, we output both the maximum eigenvalue (modifier max_eig_stat) and the trace (trace_stat) of the vector error correction model. Similar to the AEG test, we also assume a constant (order-0) or constant and linear trend (order-1) and fixed autoregressive lags of 1 (ardiff-1) and 10 (ardiff-10)." Listed as SPIs 221-228.

VECM Delta y_t = Pi y_(t-1) + sum_(i=1..1) G_i Delta y_(t-i) + D_t + e_t (VAR order 2); eigenvalues a_1 >= a_2 of S_kk^-1 S_k0 S_00^-1 S_0k from residual moment matrices over m = T-1-1 samples. metric_name_standard: Engle-Granger two-step (augmented Engle-Granger, AEG) residual-based cointegration test statistic: ADF t-ratio on the residuals of the cointegrating regression (with constant, or constant + linear trend), lag order chosen by AIC or BIC up to 10
canonical_ref: Engle R.F. & Granger C.W.J. 1987, Econometrica 55(2):251-276 (two-step test, ADF on residuals, Table II); Said S.E. & Dickey D.A. 1984, Biometrika 71(3):599-607 (augmented DF); MacKinnon J.G. 1991/2010 (response-surface critical values, N=2); Phillips P.C.B. & Ouliaris S. 1990, Econometrica 58(1):165-193 (normalisation dependence of residual-based tests)
canonical_definition: Step 1: OLS y0_t = alpha (+ delta t) + beta y1_t + u_t. Step 2: OLS Delta u_t = rho u_(t-1) + sum_(i=1..p) gamma_i Delta u_(t-i) + e_t (no deterministic term); statistic = t-ratio rho_hat / se(rho_hat); reject no-cointegration for values below the Engle-Granger/MacKinnon critical value (more negative = stronger evidence). The statistic depends on which variable is the regressand.
documented_definition: supplement §1.6.3, p.19 (heading supplement.txt line 885, text 886-899): "If two time series are individually integrated but some linear combination of them has a lower order of integration, then the series are said to be cointegrated [79]. We implement statistics for quantifying the cointegration of bivariate time series from two tests included in v0.12.0 of statsmodels [75]: the Augmented Engle-Granger (AEG, modifier aeg) [80] two-step test and the Johansen test (johansen) [81]." Keywords: "undirected, linear, unsigned, bivariate, time-dependent". [80] = Engle & Granger 1987 Econometrica 55, 251; [81] = Pesaran & Shin 1999 (ARDL bounds approach), not Johansen. GitBook spi-descriptions/miscellaneous.md:13-41 has the same text (Key References link to JSTOR 1913236 = Engle & Granger 1987 and to the Pesaran-Shin ARDL chapter). AEG bullet (supplement.txt:892-894): "For the AEG test, we use a lag that is inferred via either AIC (modifier aic) or BIC (bic), with a maximum lag of 10 and obtain a t-statistic (tstat) of the unit-root test on the residuals. The time series is first detrended by assuming either a constant (c) or a constant and linear trend (ct)." Listed as SPIs 229-231; keyword "undirected".

implemented_as: Default pipeline z-scores (optionally detrends) each channel. For each unordered pair a<b the first call is bivariate(i=b, j=a), so coint(y0 = z_b, y1 = z_a): OLS of the HIGHER-index channel on the lower-index channel plus constant (c) or constant + trend (ct); ADF without deterministic terms on the residuals with lag p in 0..10 chosen by min AIC/BIC on the common sample T-11, then re-fit on T-1-p rows; returns the t-ratio on u_(t-1). R^2 >= 1-100*sqrt(eps) returns -inf. Cache stores the value for both (b,a) and (a,b), and the Undirected mirror copies it, so A[a,b] = A[b,a] = EG(dependent = z_max(a,b), regressor = z_min(a,b)). The p-value and critical values are discarded; the value is returned with its sign (no negation despite the comment at misc.py:99).

what_changed: The kernel is the canonical Engle-Granger ADF t-ratio (fp-exact against the numpy kernel and R urca at the selected lag; lag search on the common sample with re-fit, as statsmodels). The SPI is documented and labelled undirected, but EG is asymmetric and pyspi fixes the regressand by channel index (the higher index is y0 under multivariate, the first argument under bivariate). Reordering channels changes entries by up to 1.53 on cointegrated data (T=256), 7.41 on iid data and 60.9 on trending data (trend 'c'). The raw t-statistic is returned (negative, more negative = stronger) although the class is Unsigned and the comment says 'negative t-statistic'. Interpretation limit: stationary unrelated pairs score like or beyond the cointegrated pair. Collinear pairs give -inf.

metric_name_standard: Engle-Granger two-step (augmented Engle-Granger, AEG) residual-based cointegration test statistic: ADF t-ratio on the residuals of the cointegrating regression (with constant, or constant + linear trend), lag order chosen by AIC or BIC up to 10
canonical_ref: Engle R.F. & Granger C.W.J. 1987, Econometrica 55(2):251-276 (two-step test, ADF on residuals, Table II); Said S.E. & Dickey D.A. 1984, Biometrika 71(3):599-607 (augmented DF); MacKinnon J.G. 1991/2010 (response-surface critical values, N=2); Phillips P.C.B. & Ouliaris S. 1990, Econometrica 58(1):165-193 (normalisation dependence of residual-based tests)
canonical_definition: Step 1: OLS y0_t = alpha (+ delta t) + beta y1_t + u_t. Step 2: OLS Delta u_t = rho u_(t-1) + sum_(i=1..p) gamma_i Delta u_(t-i) + e_t (no deterministic term); statistic = t-ratio rho_hat / se(rho_hat); reject no-cointegration for values below the Engle-Granger/MacKinnon critical value (more negative = stronger evidence). The statistic depends on which variable is the regressand.
documented_definition: supplement §1.6.3, p.19 (heading supplement.txt line 885, text 886-899): "If two time series are individually integrated but some linear combination of them has a lower order of integration, then the series are said to be cointegrated [79]. We implement statistics for quantifying the cointegration of bivariate time series from two tests included in v0.12.0 of statsmodels [75]: the Augmented Engle-Granger (AEG, modifier aeg) [80] two-step test and the Johansen test (johansen) [81]." Keywords: "undirected, linear, unsigned, bivariate, time-dependent". [80] = Engle & Granger 1987 Econometrica 55, 251; [81] = Pesaran & Shin 1999 (ARDL bounds approach), not Johansen. GitBook spi-descriptions/miscellaneous.md:13-41 has the same text (Key References link to JSTOR 1913236 = Engle & Granger 1987 and to the Pesaran-Shin ARDL chapter). AEG bullet (supplement.txt:892-894): "For the AEG test, we use a lag that is inferred via either AIC (modifier aic) or BIC (bic), with a maximum lag of 10 and obtain a t-statistic (tstat) of the unit-root test on the residuals. The time series is first detrended by assuming either a constant (c) or a constant and linear trend (ct)." Listed as SPIs 229-231; keyword "undirected".

implemented_as: Default pipeline z-scores (optionally detrends) each channel. For each unordered pair a<b the first call is bivariate(i=b, j=a), so coint(y0 = z_b, y1 = z_a): OLS of the HIGHER-index channel on the lower-index channel plus constant (c) or constant + trend (ct); ADF without deterministic terms on the residuals with lag p in 0..10 chosen by min AIC/BIC on the common sample T-11, then re-fit on T-1-p rows; returns the t-ratio on u_(t-1). R^2 >= 1-100*sqrt(eps) returns -inf. Cache stores the value for both (b,a) and (a,b), and the Undirected mirror copies it, so A[a,b] = A[b,a] = EG(dependent = z_max(a,b), regressor = z_min(a,b)). The p-value and critical values are discarded; the value is returned with its sign (no negation despite the comment at misc.py:99).

deviation_from_documented: (1) Asymmetry hidden: the documentation calls the SPI undirected and does not say which series is the regressand; the code uses the higher channel index as y0 under multivariate (cache + loop order) but z[i] (the first argument) under a direct bivariate call. (2) Sign: labelled "unsigned" (class Unsigned -> issigned() False, base.py:146-150) and the code comment says "Return the negative t-statistic" (misc.py:99), but the raw t-statistic is returned: typically negative, more negative = more cointegrated, opposite orientation to the Johansen identifiers. (3) "The time series is first detrended" is implemented as including the deterministic terms in the cointegrating regression (equivalent by Frisch-Waugh for the residuals). (4) Metadata: class label "nonlinear" vs documented "linear". (5) statsmodels v0.12.0 documented, 0.15.0 installed.
deviation_from_canonical: Value: none against the Engle-Granger two-step ADF t-ratio with constant/trend in step 1, no deterministic term in step 2, IC lag search on a common sample and refit on the largest sample. Probe: from-scratch numpy implementation reproduces pyspi to <= 4.2e-13 over cointegrated, iid_gaussian, trending, var2_bivariate, delayed_noise at T=64..4096 for all three configs; a variant that does not refit on the larger sample differs by up to 2.27, so the refit convention matters for references (e.g. R urca ur.df). metric_name_standard: Amplitude envelope correlation (AEC): Pearson correlation of Hilbert amplitude envelopes, broadband, without leakage correction
canonical_ref: Bruns A., Eckhorn R., Jokeit H., Ebner A. 2000, "Amplitude envelope correlation detects coupling among incoherent brain signals", NeuroReport 11(7):1509-1514; power-envelope form in Hipp et al. 2012 Nat Neurosci 15(6):884-890 (supplement ref [82]), Methods "Power envelope correlation"
canonical_definition: r_xy(f) = corr_t(|x_f(t)|, |y_f(t)|), x_f = analytic (Hilbert or complex wavelet) signal of x band-limited around carrier f; Pearson correlation over time
documented_definition: supplement §1.6.4, p.19 (heading at supplement.txt line 915): keywords "undirected, linear, unsigned, bivariate, time-dependent"; "The envelope correlation [82, 83] is the correlation between the two amplitude envelopes of x and y. Power envelope correlation is computed using MNE, where we use six combinations of parameters, including whether the method was orthogonalized (modifier orth), the envelopes were squared and logs were taken prior to correlation (log), or the absolute of the correlation coefficient was used (abs)"; refs [82] Hipp et al. 2012 Nat Neurosci 15:884, [83] Khan et al. 2018 NeuroImage 174:57, [63] MNE v0.23.0. GitBook spi-descriptions/miscellaneous.md:92-113 repeats the text and lists pec, pec_orth, pec_log, pec_orth_log, pec_orth_abs, pec_orth_log_abs. Neither source names a frequency band, the orthogonalisation formula, or whether "abs" is applied before or after averaging the two directions.

implemented_as: Default pipeline z-scores each channel (optionally detrends first). Per channel: analytic signal z = x + iH(x) via scipy FFT Hilbert, zero-padded to the next 5-smooth length and truncated to T (no padding for powers of two); envelope e = |z| (amplitude, not power). Correlation row i: sum_t e_i(t) (e_j(t) - mean e_j) / ||e_j - mean e_j|| / ||e_i - mean e_i|| (seed uncentred; equal to Pearson in exact arithmetic). No band-pass, no lag, no symmetrisation step inside MNE; the stored upper triangle (i <= j) is mirrored by get_data, single-epoch mean is identity, diagonal NaN.

(3) Hilbert zero-padding to a 5-smooth length (no effect at powers of two; probe, max over pairs vs an unpadded analytic signal: 7.1e-3 on z-scored iid_gaussian_T4096[:, :1031], 2.2e-3 on z-scored np.random.default_rng(3).standard_normal((3, 1031))). metric_name_standard: Orthogonalised amplitude envelope correlation (Hipp 2012 pairwise orthogonalisation, "AEC-orth"), broadband; pec_orth_abs averages the absolute directional correlations
canonical_ref: Hipp J.F., Hawellek D.J., Corbetta M., Siegel M., Engel A.K. 2012, "Large-scale cortical correlation structure of spontaneous oscillatory activity", Nat Neurosci 15(6):884-890, Methods "Orthogonalization" (supplement ref [82]); MNE implementation and absolute option per Khan et al. 2018 NeuroImage 174:57-68 (ref [83]) [check stage: Online Methods re-read in the PMC author manuscript PMC3861400: Y_perp_X(t,f) = imag(Y(t,f) X(t,f)*/|X(t,f)|), power = |.|^2, log-transformed, Pearson correlation, computed in both orthogonalisation directions and averaged, Morlet wavelets 2-128 Hz in 1/4-octave steps]
canonical_definition: Y_perp_X(t,f) = Im(Y(t,f) X*(t,f) / |X(t,f)|); c(Y->X) = corr_t(env X, env Y_perp_X), c(X->Y) likewise; reported value (c(Y->X) + c(X->Y)) / 2 per carrier frequency f (Hipp 2012 correlates log-transformed power envelopes; that is the orth-log unit)

deviation_from_documented: Orthogonalisation method is not specified in the documentation; the code uses Hipp 2012 pairwise orthogonalisation (consistent with ref [82]). "the absolute of the correlation coefficient was used (abs)": implemented as the mean of the absolute directional coefficients, which is >= |pec_orth| and differs from abs(pec_orth) whenever the two directions differ in sign. Metadata: pec_orth labelled unsigned but signed (probe minimum -0.385 on shared_envelope_T256; extends REVIEW M8, which names only pec/pec_log); pec_orth_abs is in [0,1], consistent with the label.
deviation_from_canonical: (1) Broadband, no carrier frequency. (2) Amplitude envelopes correlated, not (log) power envelopes as in Hipp 2012. (3) pec_orth_abs is an MNE option (absolute=True default in the library), not part of Hipp 2012. (4) Hilbert zero-padding to 5-smooth length. (5) Exactly collinear channels give roundoff-driven values instead of 0/undefined (candidate).

what_changed: Hipp 2012 orthogonalisation reproduced to fp precision on non-degenerate input and matches the supplement (orth via MNE), but differs from canonical in value-changing ways: broadband instead of per-carrier (Morlet); the abs variant averages the absolute directional coefficients (|c_ij| + |c_ji|)/2, not |pec_orth_log|, and is positively biased under independence; pec_orth_log is signed (extends REVIEW M8); for bit-identical or exactly proportional channels the delegate's complex-arithmetic orthogonalisation a_i*(conj(a_j)/|a_j|) leaves a rounding residue that correlates with the envelope, giving 0.1-0.44 instead of 0 (any complex-multiply form does the same; only the explicit real form gives exactly 0)

metric_name_standard: Orthogonalised log power envelope correlation (Hipp 2012 "power envelope correlation of orthogonalized signals"), broadband; pec_orth_log_abs averages absolute directional correlations
canonical_ref: Hipp J.F. et al. 2012, Nat Neurosci 15(6):884-890, Methods "Orthogonalization" and "Power envelope correlation" (supplement ref [82]); MNE implementation and absolute option per Khan et al. 2018 NeuroImage 174:57-68 (ref [83]) [check stage: Online Methods re-read in the PMC author manuscript PMC3861400: Y_perp_X(t,f) = imag(Y(t,f) X(t,f)*/|X(t,f)|), power = |.|^2, log-transformed, Pearson correlation, computed in both orthogonalisation directions and averaged, Morlet wavelets 2-128 Hz in 1/4-octave steps]
canonical_definition: Y_perp_X(t,f) = Im(Y(t,f) X*(t,f)/|X(t,f)|); c(Y->X) = corr_t(log|X(t,f)|^2, log|Y_perp_X(t,f)|^2); value = (c(Y->X) + c(X->Y)) / 2 per carrier frequency f
documented_definition: supplement §1.6.4, p.19 (heading at supplement.txt line 915): keywords "undirected, linear, unsigned, bivariate, time-dependent"; "The envelope correlation [82, 83] is the correlation between the two amplitude envelopes of x and y. what_changed: Hipp 2012 orthogonalisation reproduced to fp precision on non-degenerate input and matches the supplement (orth via MNE), but differs from canonical in value-changing ways: broadband instead of per-carrier (Morlet); the abs variant averages the absolute directional coefficients (|c_ij| + |c_ji|)/2, not |pec_orth_log|, and is positively biased under independence; pec_orth_log is signed (extends REVIEW M8); for bit-identical or exactly proportional channels the delegate's complex-arithmetic orthogonalisation a_i*(conj(a_j)/|a_j|) leaves a rounding residue that correlates with the envelope, giving 0.1-0.44 instead of 0 (any complex-multiply form does the same; only the explicit real form gives exactly 0)

metric_name_standard: InterDependence Score IDS-max (IDS_inf): maximum absolute Pearson correlation between the first k Taylor-series feature maps of a Gaussian kernel applied to each variable
canonical_ref: Radhakrishnan A, Jain Y, Uhler C, Lander ES 2025, PNAS 122(34):e2509860122 (PMC12403096), "Efficiently quantifying dependence in massive scientific datasets using InterDependence Scores": Eq. 3 (Gaussian kernel exp(-(x-y)^2/(2B^2))), Eq. 6 (feature map), Eq. 11 (feature correlations), Eq. 12 (IDS_p as l_p norm, IDS_inf = max); main-text implementation choice: IDS_inf, B = 1, k = 6 terms, data min-max scaled to [0, 8]. Reference code: github.com/aradha/interdependence_scores (main, last commit 3c8d62b, 2025-03-18).
canonical_definition: phi_m(x) = exp(-x^2/(2B^2)) x^m / (sqrt(m!) B^m), m = 0..k-1; rho_ml = Corr(phi_m(x), phi_l(y)); IDS_p(x, y) = ((1/k^2) sum_{m,l} |rho_ml|^p)^(1/p), IDS_inf = max_{m,l} |rho_ml|; values in [0, 1], 0 iff all k^2 feature correlations vanish (population).
documented_definition: Not in the supplement (no section; the SPI post-dates it). GitBook miscellaneous.md:117-127: keywords "undirected, nonlinear, unsigned"; "a fast and scalable measure of dependence that captures both linear and various non-linear dependencies ... Based on the Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion (HSIC), the IDS offers a finite-dimensional approximation of the universal kernels that can detect any type of dependence"; "the IDS is normalized to a range of [0, 1] with a score of 0 indicating independence"; implementation "based on the code made publicly available" at aradha/interdependence_scores. Key reference: PNAS doi 10.1073/pnas.2509860122.

implemented_as: Data z-scores each process (ddof=1, default normalise=True; detrend off by default). multivariate transposes to (T, P), builds K*P feature columns f_k(z) = exp(-0.5 z^2) z^k / sqrt(k!), k = 0..5, ordered term-major (column index k*P + p), subtracts column means, computes the full (KP x KP) np.corrcoef, reshapes to (K, P, K, P), replaces NaN/inf by 0, takes abs, and returns max over both term axes: A[i, j] = max_{k,l} |Corr(f_k(z_i), f_l(z_j))| (36 correlations per pair). bandwidth=0.5 is the coefficient of z^2, i.e. paper B = 1; the missing B^m factor is irrelevant because correlations are invariant to per-column scale (probe: code vs Eq. 6 with B_paper = sqrt(1/(2*bandwidth)) agree to <= 4.4e-16 for bandwidth 0.25/0.5/1.0). No p-value (p_val=False). No mirroring: multivariate overrides Undirected.multivariate, symmetry comes from np.corrcoef, exact up to last-bit rounding (check stage: max |A - A^T| = 2.2e-16 over 65 square outputs, 52 of them not bitwise symmetric). Diagonal is 1 from compute_IDS (k = l term), set to NaN by Calculator.compute. Matches a from-scratch numpy reference to <= 8.9e-16 on 7 datasets x 4 lengths.

deviation_from_documented: (a) GitBook says 0 indicates independence; in finite samples IDS-max is positively biased under independence: probe on iid_gaussian off-diagonal mean 0.235 / 0.113 / 0.065 / 0.032 at T = 64 / 256 / 1024 / 4096; from-scratch Monte Carlo null mean 2.06/sqrt(T) (0.258 at T=64, 95% quantile 0.370), larger still for autocorrelated series. The [0, 1] range itself holds (abs of clipped correlations). (b) "finite-dimensional approximation of the universal kernels that can detect any type of dependence": with k = 6 truncated terms the statistic approximates, but is not, a universal-kernel HSIC; consistency against every alternative is not guaranteed (paper: "IDS_p is an approximation to a measure that is a statistically consistent estimate of independence"). (c) Parameters terms/pnorm/bandwidth and the bandwidth convention (coefficient of z^2, = paper B = 1) are undocumented; the identifier "ids" does not change with parameters. (d) Otherwise the code is the documented upstream implementation (verbatim copy of the numpy backend). Check stage: (b) is now shown by construction: a dependent law phi(x)phi(y)(1 + eps g(x)g(y)) with g orthogonal to 1 and to the six features has population IDS_p = 0 for every p while Corr(g(X), g(Y)) = 0.474; pyspi gives 0.0435 at T = 4096 (null mean 0.0324, q95 0.0477) (misc.ids|iid_gaussian|4096|pipeline|hidden-dependence).
deviation_from_canonical: (1) Preprocessing: pyspi feeds z-scored data (mean 0, sd 1, ddof=1); the paper's reported setting min-max scales to [0, 8] before IDS. Because the Gaussian damping is not scale/shift invariant, values differ materially: probe nonlinear_dependence T=4096 pair (0,1) 0.943 (z-score) vs 0.485 (min-max [0,8]); pair (2,3) 0.993 vs 0.313; contaminated 0.949 vs 0.592. The paper explicitly allows other normalisations, so this is a variant choice, not a code error. (2) Kernel parametrisation: bandwidth_term multiplies y^2 (exp(-0.5 y^2) = Eq. 6 with B = 1); Eq. 6 B^m and sqrt(m!) scalings cancel in correlations, so the default matches the paper's B = 1, k = 6, IDS_inf exactly (probe <= 4.4e-16). (3) No permutation p-value; the paper pairs IDS with permutation P-values for interpretation. (4) Application to autocorrelated time series violates the i.i.d.-sample assumption behind the null behaviour; IDS is zero-lag only (delayed_noise lag-1/3/5 copies score at the null level 0.03-0.05 at T=4096). (5) Constant features are mapped to 0 by nan_to_num (code convention; unreachable in pyspi because Data rejects NaN after z-scoring).
units_and_range: dimensionless, [0, 1], unsigned; symmetric up to last-bit rounding (check stage max |A - A^T| = 2.2e-16, not exactly 0); diagonal 1 from the library (k = l), NaN after Calculator; cannot be NaN off the diagonal (nan_to_num). Positively biased under independence (~2.06/sqrt(T) for i.i.d. samples). Not an upper bound on or generalisation of |Pearson|: for a standard bivariate Gaussian the population value is 0.2641 at rho = 0.3 and 0.7349 at rho = 0.8 (Gauss-Hermite quadrature probe; maximising pair (k, l) = (3, 3)); exact linear relations give 1 only after z-scoring makes the two series identical up to sign. Invariant to sign flips of either variable (odd/even features; probe diff 0.0) and, through z-scoring, to positive affine maps (scaled_offset reproduces bivariate_gaussian); not invariant to scale or shift at the kernel level (probe pair (0,1): 0.986 / 0.945 / 0.750 at scale 0.3 / 1 / 3).
